paragraphs.text: …of word and of life, having gone through the testimonies concerning our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, confirmed them by clear, credible and true demonstrations and arguments. Only at the end did it use a very few testimonies from the divine scriptures, which are believed both by the Jews and by us. There was no reason to set out abundant proofs from those scriptures for people who still wholly disbelieve them. The present books, however, have been worked out to supply what was lacking in those, for readers who, on the strength of the demonstration given there, ought by now to believe the sacred scriptures as divine and inspired. They contain a collection, in summary form, [?] … of the prophecy concerning our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, which it seemed good to gather together into one from [?] … of the Old Testament; [?] … and in some places the things concerning him were foretold through hidden meanings as well [?] … him and the dispensations relating to him. And not also [?] … which are shown to have reached their fulfilment. Such [?] … beginning; and scattered not only [in] prophecy [?] … stored up in histories; [?] … will be useful to not a few. For it is not easy, except by reading the scriptures through together [?] …, for all these passages to come to hand for those who wish to have them on their lips and carry them in their memory.

It should be known that before the present undertaking we composed Chronological Canons. Beside them we set an epitome of every kind of history, both Greek and barbarian, and through them we established the antiquity of Moses and of the prophets who came after him. Regarding the present work, scattered as it is [?], as following on from those, we have fittingly come after that to the present treatise. One might gracefully compare it to the natural industry of the wise bee, to which the sacred word in Proverbs sends us when it says: “Or go to the bee, and see how hard-working she is, and how dignified the work she carries on. Kings and ordinary people use her labours for their health. She is desired by all and held in honour; though weak in strength, she has been advanced because she honoured wisdom” (Prov. 6:8). That worker is attested to have honoured wisdom. She gathers what is useful from flourishing shoots, and out of the collecting and working of them all she provides her labours to kings and ordinary people, healthful, as the scripture says. In the same way, I think, our Prophetic Extracts concerning Christ, which are an anthology gathered from the rational meadows of God, will hold something similar. In their bare words they preserve the well-moulded craftsmanship of the wax, while within, as it were in secret, they store up the thoughts treasured in it, corresponding to the sweet and most healthful product of that wise creature. For which of the faithful would not confess that the saving passages concerning the Word of God surpass every bodily pleasure and benefit with an incomparable superiority, since they are suited to the acquisition of a truly beneficial and healthy orthodoxy? It is necessary to cherish this orthodoxy not only for those advanced in condition, who are called “kings,” but also for those of lower standing and those who are only now first approaching the divine word. For these, I think, the subject will be especially suitable, so that from it they may establish accurately the certainty of the words in which they have been instructed. For simple and pure faith holds its conviction more firmly when someone has first laid foundations in the reasoning by demonstration, [and leads on] to the acquisition [?] … of a precise grasp and knowledge of what is believed. For this reason, then, I say, [?] … necessary [?] … it seemed good, after the [?] … of each prophecy, to set out by way of introduction a brief narrative [?] … as concise as possible, concerning [?] … a refutation of those who boast that they believe the [sacred?] scriptures as divine, yet do not accept [?] … Jesus as being himself the one who was prophesied. [It will contain] difficulties raised [?] … against them, I mean those of the circumcision and those from the heresies [?] …, and refutations of whatever they might say when they try to explain the divine utterances in a more mythical fashion. There will also be a moderate exposition of our own, in few words. Sometimes it will contain a demonstration that the sacred predictions of God have been fulfilled in our Saviour alone, and sometimes it will indicate the opinion we hold about the passages to be set out.

But since we are about to take these matters in hand, we must first make a necessary distinction. In some places the sacred words teach that the Word of God existed beforehand, not only before the incarnation but before all generated being, and they call him God [?] … after the Father, and Lord. This is just what the church's preaching contains, in agreement with the testimony of the gospel, which says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being” (John 1:1). In other places they proclaim beforehand his two comings. The first is the one in which they expressly foretold that he would have neither form nor beauty and would be led like a sheep to the slaughter. They say clearly that in this way he would be condemned to death on account of the iniquities of the former people. The dispensations of his first coming in the time of Tiberius are shown to be exactly this. The second is no longer like the first, but more divine and far surpassing it in glory, and it will take place with an escort of angels and the array of heaven. In these matters the reader must sensibly hold to the apostolic preaching as a rule and a goal, for it preserves the doctrines of truth complete and unaltered. These are the doctrines concerning the first and unbegotten nature of the God of the universe, and those concerning the pre-existence and the ministry of the divine Word, which [he performed] in the creation of all generated things, as being the Word.

[?] … apart from the four letters that the Hebrews do not pronounce. The name signified by their combination is ineffable, though by a looser usage it is rendered “Lord,” and it has never yet been applied to an angelic power. You will need to consider this throughout the whole of inspired scripture, wherever God, or the Lord indicated by the four-letter name, is recorded to have spoken to anyone: should what is indicated be referred to the unbegotten nature of the God of the universe, or to his Word? Divine scripture customarily calls the Word, as the second cause of all things, both God and Lord, in the sense of the name that is ineffable among the Hebrews. So in the present passage, where the text says that “the Lord came down” and that “the Lord said” what is recorded (Gen. 11:5–6), one might reasonably ask whether what is indicated refers to one of the angels or to the first cause. It cannot refer to angels. First, here too “Lord” is taken from the unpronounceable designation. Second, the passage shows that the words were addressed to others ranked below the speaker. On the other hand, the meaning is unsuitable to the Father and God of the universe. It would not befit him to say, “Come, let us go down and confuse their language” (Gen. 11:7), and “the Lord came down to see the city” (Gen. 11:5) could in no way fittingly be said of the supreme authority. It remains, then, to understand that the divine Word is indicated in these passages as well. He was entrusted by the Father with the providence and governance of all things, and he has never ceased to serve the Father's will in whatever contributes to the benefit and salvation of the universe, sometimes by himself and sometimes through ministering angels. But the matters in this passage belong to a mystical and secret contemplation, and now is not the time to unfold them.

The first oracle recorded as given to Abraham is when the Lord said to him: “Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house into the land that I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you will be blessed; and I will bless those who bless you” (Gen. 12:1), and what follows. The second is when the Lord appeared to him and said to him: “To your offspring I will give this land” (Gen. 12:7). The third is when the Lord said to Abraham what is recorded after Lot had separated from him (Gen. 13:14). The fourth is the one in which it is said: “After these words the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision of the night, saying: Do not be afraid, Abram; I am your shield” (Gen. 15:1); and after other things: “I am the Lord who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans” (Gen. 15:7). The fifth is when the Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him: “I am your God; be well-pleasing before me” (Gen. 17:1), and the rest. The sixth is the one in which the Lord again appeared to him at the oak of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent at midday: “He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing over him. When he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them, bowed down to the ground and said: Lord, if I have found favour in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, and let them wash your feet” (Gen. 18:1). Then after some further words it continues: “The men rose from there and looked toward Sodom, and Abraham went along with them to see them on their way. And the Lord said: Shall I hide from Abraham my servant what I am doing? Abraham shall become a great and populous nation, and in him all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. For I knew that he would command his sons and his household after him, and they would keep the ways of the Lord, doing righteousness and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what he has spoken to him. And the Lord said: The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has grown great” (Gen. 18:16). And shortly after: “The men turned away from there and came to Sodom, but Abraham was still standing before the Lord. Abraham drew near and said: Do not destroy the righteous along with the wicked, so that the righteous fare like the wicked. If there are fifty righteous people in the city, will you destroy them? Will you not spare the whole place for the sake of the fifty righteous, if they are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous along with the wicked, so that the righteous fare like the wicked. Far from it! Shall not you, who judge all the earth, do justice?” (Gen. 18:33). And after other things the scripture says: “The Lord went away when he had finished speaking to Abraham. The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting at the gate of Sodom” (Gen. 19:1).

It is worth considering who is meant in these passages as the one who gave the oracles to Abraham. Is it some ordinary angel, or the God of the universe himself, or a third besides these, the Word of God? After the supreme Father and God of the universe, sacred scripture customarily calls the Word Lord and God. We should also ask which of the three men who appeared to Abraham was the one to whom he said, “Lord, if I have found favour in your sight,” and again, “Far from it! Shall not you, who judge all the earth, do justice?” Of him the divine scripture says, not once only but a second and a third time, “the Lord appeared to him.” Under the designation “Lord” stands the name that is unpronounceable in the Hebrew, and that name has never been applied to an angelic power. Take the place where Lot is recorded as saying to the angels who came to Sodom, “I beg you, lord, since your servant has found mercy in your sight” (Gen. 19:19). The word “lord” does stand in the Hebrew there. It is written, however, not with the four letters that the Hebrews use for the ineffable name of God, but with other syllables. These are the syllables the Hebrews use for anyone called “lord” among human beings, as a relative term, such as a servant's lord. The term used for the supreme authority of God, written with the four letters, has nothing in common with these. It occurs in the recorded visions of God to Abraham, and it clearly shows that the one who gave him oracles was neither an angel nor some divine power ranked only a little above an angel, but God himself. This is the very ineffable name, written in these passages with the four letters, that the high priest alone wore on his forehead. He bore it on the golden plate, in what is called the engraving of a seal, “Holiness of the Lord” (Exod. 28:32). Divine scripture does not use this designation for angels indifferently. That is evident from how carefully it relates at some times that God himself, or the Lord indicated by the four-letter name, appeared to the righteous and spoke with them, and at other times records that those who were seen were angels. Clearly, then, the one who appeared to Hagar in her wandering was an angel. She fell very far short of Abraham and was able to behold nothing more than an angelic vision, so it was fitting that her vision should suit her through the presence of an angel, while Abraham's came through the greater manifestation of God himself. Moreover, the other utterances of God to Abraham would not fit if anyone tried to refer them to angels; they would befit God alone. Examples are “I will make you into a great nation and bless you” and the like, and especially “I am the Lord who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans” and “I am God; be well-pleasing before me,” with what follows. No one could ever be so foolish as to suppose that an angel said these things. So when the three men came upon Abraham as he sat by the oak, Abraham went to meet them, yet he said “Lord, if I have found favour in your sight” not to the three but to one alone. None of the others is introduced as speaking with Abraham, for there was no reason for servants to speak in their master's presence; the Lord alone gives the oracle, saying, “Shall I hide from Abraham my servant,” and the rest. Then the men who were with the Lord, evidently the angels, turned away and went down to Sodom alone, and the Lord did not go with them. For how could the kind and merciful God dwell among the ungodly? The Lord remained in the company and conversation of the righteous man whom God loved. He took pleasure in Abraham's conversation and gave his protection to Abraham's most humane prayer. In that prayer Abraham, by saying “Far from it, you who judge all the earth,” shows most plainly that he knew well and precisely that he was speaking with God himself, and not with an angel or a lesser divine power. Next the text distinguishes the matters precisely and clearly calls those who went to Sodom angels, adding that “the two angels came to Sodom in the evening.” In what follows it records that neither the Lord nor God appeared to Lot or spoke with him, but the angels did. So it is entirely plain that the one whom scripture attests to have appeared to Abraham was Lord and God, and not one of the angels.

All who wish to sever the harmony between the Old Testament and the New seize on these passages as a windfall. They think these passages clearly establish that the Father of Christ, whom the voice of the gospel acknowledges to be invisible, is someone other than the God of Moses and the prophets. That God, they say, was seen in various ways: now by Abraham, now by Isaac (to whom he also gave oracles, foretelling things like those he foretold to Abraham), and likewise by Jacob. Perhaps he was seen also by Isaiah, who said, “I saw the Lord of Hosts” (Isa. 6:5), and in the same way by the other prophets. But in those very prophets of God of old a divine oracle is found speaking in the person of God: “For I am the Lord your God, and I have not changed” (Mal. 3:6), and “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jer. 23:24). And in his oracle to Moses he says, “No one shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20). We will therefore put the following difficulty to those just mentioned, together with those of the circumcision, and also to those who do not accept that a second divinity, that of the Son, pre-exists after the unbegotten nature. According to these very prophecies God is unchangeable and immutable. He says that he alone fills heaven and earth. According to the law itself he is clearly shown to be all but invisible, as in “No one shall see my face and live.” How, then, could he change again, as though altering his own essence, and come to be contained in small parts of the earth, and be seen now by Abraham and now by the other prophets? If these things were referred to the God of the universe, they would seem to disagree not only with the voice of the gospel but also with the voices of the prophets, which have declared him uncontainable, unchangeable and invisible to human beings. Perhaps someone will say that God himself was not seen at all by those recorded, but only produced an appearance for them. They would then seem to see and hear without truly beholding anything of what was thought to appear, and without truly hearing; they would be deceived even in this, merely supposing and seeming to hear. But that is unfitting and foreign to the truthful and undeceiving nature of the God of the universe. It is further shown to be untenable by the fact that God himself is recorded as saying about Abraham: “For I knew that he would command his sons and his household after him, and they would keep the ways of the Lord, doing righteousness and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what he has spoken to him” (Gen. 18:19). Here the Lord himself indisputably speaks as though about another Lord. How then is it possible to suppose that the God of the universe said this? What other Lord besides himself could these words be about? It is clear from this that what is described does not seem to belong to the God of the universe, and it has already been shown that it does not belong to the nature of angels either. For, as I said, the text knows how to speak accurately about appearances of angels, clearly marking the visions that came through them. If, then, these things seem to suit neither the angelic nature nor the supreme and unbegotten nature of the God of the universe, only one solution remains. We must reserve unchangeability, immutability and invisibility for the unbegotten essence, and transfer the oracles recorded as coming from God to the Word of God. We believe that the Word, even before the incarnation, was seen in various ways for the salvation of humankind and carried out the dispensations described in the divine scriptures. To him alone, after the God of the universe, have we found the four-letter name applied, since this divine title too befits the only-begotten Son and heir of the Father. Abraham was wise and was attested by God himself to be a prophet, so he knew well that the Father had given all judgment to the Son. He therefore worships him, and to him alone, as distinct from the others, he says, “Far from it! Shall not you, who judge all the earth, do justice?” It would be unfitting and most implausible to think this was said to an angel, who is lower than the divine Word. It would be most fitting, by contrast, for the divine Word alone to say, among other things, “Shall I hide from Abraham my servant what I am doing?” and “For I knew that he would command his sons and his household after him, and they would keep the ways of the Lord, doing righteousness and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what he has spoken to him.” And it befits him to say these things because he is teaching that everything human beings do in holiness must rightly be referred to the worship of the God and Father of the universe alone. From the Father all good things are supplied to the godly on earth [?] for their benefit and salvation. The divine Word says these things to teach about another Lord, his own Father. For he also acknowledged the Father as his own Lord and God to his disciples, saying, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God” (John 20:17). The law and all of scripture are full of this pattern: the Lord, that is, the divine Word, speaking as though about another Lord, evidently the Father. The matters in this passage call for much and very deep contemplation, but what has been said is enough for the present subject.

"And Hagar fled from her presence" (Gen 16:6), that is, from Sarah's. "And the angel of the Lord found her by the spring of water." In what follows it is said a second time, "And the angel of the Lord said to her," and a third time, "And the angel of the Lord said to her, I will greatly multiply your seed, and it shall not be counted for multitude." And again, "The angel of the Lord said to her, Behold, you are with child, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heeded your affliction." After all these words it is said, "And she called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her, You are God who looked upon me." If holy Scripture had not itself, speaking in its own voice, named as Lord the one who appeared to Hagar in her wandering, in the words "And she called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her," one might have supposed that Hagar mistakenly took the angel for God. As it is, Scripture testifies that it was the Lord who gave the oracle through the angel just named. Through him, being Lord and God, he said of himself, fittingly, "I will greatly multiply your seed"; for it would befit God alone to say this, and not an angel. It is likely that Hagar paid attention to this very word, understood that such an utterance could come from God alone, and so said, "You are God who looked upon me." A second time too, when she runs away taking her son with her, it is written, "And the angel of God called Hagar out of heaven," and said to her what is recorded, including the words "For I will make it a nation," meaning, clearly, the child. Again it would not be credible for the angel to say this, for again the promise is God's. Whose name as Lord, then, did Hagar call upon in "You are the God who looked upon me," when here too Scripture uses for "Lord" the name written by the Hebrews with four letters? Is it not clear from what was set out earlier that it was the Word who was in the beginning with God? He was present from the beginning, overseeing and ordering human affairs. To men who had ascended high and were perfect, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, he granted the visions himself, in his own person. To those who fell short of their virtue, such as Lot, and Gideon and Manoah in Judges, and any others like them, he granted the promises through the divine angels under him, using them as his ministers and servants in many parts and in many ways. So it was with Hagar: since she was not yet able to receive the vision of the divine Word himself, he declared through the angel the things recorded. And if he still appears to Jacob through angels, observe that he deals with him in this way at the beginning, as with one still being introduced. When Jacob has advanced and made progress toward perfection, he grants him his own converse naked and unveiled, no longer through angels and interpreters but himself, in his own person. It is the Lord and God the Word, who holds the second rank of the Father's divinity, who deems him worthy of his own vision.

"The sun had come out upon the earth, and Lot entered Zoar. And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven" (Gen 19:23). I do not think that anyone who has once believed the holy Scriptures to be sacred and inspired by God would invent quibbles over these passages, trying to contradict what has been handed down concerning the Word of God: that he existed beforehand with a subsistence of his own, and that before he became man he carried out the dispensations toward human beings. For here Scripture clearly presents two Lords, since the Lord rained from the Lord. The like can be found in the holy apostle, who says, "May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus" (2 Tim 1:16), and "May he grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day" (2 Tim 1:18). In these passages we must distinguish what is said of the Father and of the Son. To the unbegotten Father of all things we ascribe lordship and supreme authority over all things, and over the Son himself. To the Word we assign the second rank after the Father in rule and sovereignty over all things that have come into being. Here "Lord" is named twice, in "the Lord rained from the Lord," and in the Hebrew the four-letter name also occurs twice. It is therefore most clearly acknowledged that this ineffable designation is used of two persons, namely the God and Father of all things and his Word. So there can no longer be any doubt that wherever this name of God occurs, it is used not only of the unbegotten nature but also of the Word who was in the beginning with God.

In the blessing of Jacob, after some other words, Isaac says this as well: "And let nations serve you, and rulers shall bow down to you; and be lord of your brother, and the sons of your father shall bow down to you" (Gen 27:29). What is said as if to Jacob does not seem at all capable of being referred to him, nor indeed to the people of the circumcision descended from him. For what nations served him, and when? What rulers bowed down to him? And as whom would they have bowed down to him? When did he become lord of his brother? And who are the sons of his father who are said to bow down to him? Isaac is not found to have had any son besides Jacob except Esau alone. How, then, is it said in the plural, "the sons of your father shall bow down to you"? We have noted these things because Christ is often called Jacob in the prophecies, as will be shown in the proper places, and we suspect that these words too may somehow fit the testimonies concerning him. The holy apostle transferred what concerns Isaac to Christ, saying, "Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ" (Gal 3:16). In the same way, consider whether what is said here as if about Jacob might not rather fit Christ. Whether this is so, the studious reader will learn by examining each phrase according to the rules of allegory.

"And Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning" (Gen 32:24). A little later, when Jacob says, "I will not let you go unless you bless me," he says to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob." And he said to him, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have prevailed with God, and with men you are mighty." And again a little later, "Jacob called the name of that place Form of God, for I have seen God face to face, and my life was preserved." To this Scripture adds, "And the sun rose upon him as the Form of God passed by."

To Abraham the Lord gives oracles from the beginning while he is awake. He often converses with him, and he is recorded to have been seen by him three times, and seen not at night but in the middle of the day; indeed the third time he is even his guest at high noon. But to Jacob he appears first after the sun had set, in the middle of the night and in sleep, as Jacob was going down into Mesopotamia. In that vision he beheld the ladder reaching to heaven, with the angels ascending and descending on it and the Lord standing firm upon it, and he hears the Lord saying to him, "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father" (Gen 28:13), and the rest, which, as what follows shows, he said to him through an angel. The second time was in Mesopotamia, when the Lord signified by the four-letter name again stood by him and said, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you" (Gen 31:3). He said this to him in sleep and through an angel, as Jacob himself teaches. For as soon as he heard the divine voice he called Leah and Rachel, and among other things he related to them the oracle he had received, saying, "And the angel of God said to me in sleep, Jacob," and what follows, where he says, "I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God, where you anointed a pillar to me and vowed a vow to me. Now then arise, go out from this land, and go to the land of your birth" (Gen 31:11).

After this, as he returned from Mesopotamia, first, when it was already morning, the angels of God met him, and of them he said, "This is God's camp"; and it is likely that these were the same angels he had seen earlier on the ladder. Then the sun that had set earlier rises upon him, after the passage quoted above, in which the one who said to him, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because you have prevailed with God, and with men you are mighty," appears wrestling with him in sleep. So after the vision the sun rose upon him. When he had now advanced and been perfected, God gives him an oracle no longer in sleep, nor at night, nor through an angel, nor even in human form, but in the middle of the day and in the light, and says, "Arise, go up to the place Bethel and dwell there" (Gen 35:1). After all these things, then for the first time divine Scripture testifies that God appeared to him in Luz and blessed him, saying the things recorded. We shall inquire at leisure how, later on, when he was about to go down into Egypt, God again spoke in a vision and by night, saying, "Do not be afraid to go down into Egypt" (Gen 46:3).

We have had to set out these things, for they show that divine Scripture does not lightly relate that God was seen, nor does it say so of ordinary men. It is not recorded of Adam, nor of Enoch who was translated, nor of Noah, nor of Moses himself that God was seen by any of them, although he is recorded to have spoken with them often. Divine Scripture presents God as having been seen by no one else but Abraham, Isaac and Jacob alone. In Abraham's case he was not seen at the first oracle given him, but at the second, the fifth and the sixth. In Jacob's case he was seen only after all the things recorded. To Isaac the Lord gave oracles only twice, and both times he is recorded to have been seen by him, though the second time it was at night. It is plain from what we said earlier about Abraham that the visions must not be referred to the First Cause but to the divine Word. Not even him were those blessed and divine men yet able to receive; those very men who, as was said, saw him saw him only after a great deal of preliminary training. Who else, then, could the one in the present passage be, who wrestles with Jacob, contends with him and, as it were, fights as his ally, than the holy Word of God who spoke to the fathers in many parts and in many ways? He alone after the Father is called Lord and God, and he it was who blessed Jacob and named him Israel, adding, "for you have prevailed with God." This is how the divine men saw the Word of God, just as the apostles of our Savior did, who said, "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life" (1 John 1:1). Having beheld this Word and Life, Jacob adds, "For I have seen God face to face, and my life was preserved."

"Judah, may your brothers praise you; your hands shall be on the back of your enemies; the sons of your father shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up; having lain down, you slept as a lion and as a whelp; who shall rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him come; and he is the expectation of the nations" (Gen 49:8), and what follows.

We must hear the words of Jacob as the Holy Spirit's, foretelling the things concerning Christ and addressing him in person, from "Judah, may your brothers praise you" onward. That the patriarch was not addressing his words to just one of his sons is clear to those who attend to Scripture, which says in its narrative, "And Jacob called his sons and said, Gather together, that I may tell you what will befall you in the last of days." So he announces that he will prophesy to them about things to come. It is clear on other grounds too that the words of the prophecy do not fit the patriarch Judah. When did his brothers bow down to him, or why? For what achievement, or when, did they praise him? And how could anyone expound the rest of the prophecy so as to fit him? Nor could anyone reasonably refer the words to the tribe, since rulers of the people were not appointed from the tribe of Judah alone. The judges after Moses came from various tribes and continued as leaders for nearly five hundred years. After them Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, was the first of all to reign. After these the kings of the tribe of Judah reigned for not even a full five hundred years. Then, after the captivity in Babylon, those of the tribe of Levi presided over affairs for more than five hundred years, until the coming of Christ. Why, then, would the prophecy say these things about the tribe of Judah rather than about the others? So what is foretold would not fit the tribe either.

We know, however, that the true Judah, who appeared in the last of days, is our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God. Among the store of titles given to him, he was also named Judah, just as under one title he is called Israel, under another Jacob, and David, and now one thing, now another. Him the holy apostles, and all who were deemed worthy of the spirit of adoption, praised and worshiped. His hands, which we take symbolically to mean his deeds, came upon the back of his enemies, that is, of the spiritual foes who flee from him. He is also called a lion's whelp, either because of his birth according to the flesh from a royal tribe and from the root of David, a birth that took place in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom 8:3), or because of the divinity, emptying himself of which he became man; and on account of this Jacob fittingly exclaimed, "From a shoot, my son, you have gone up." When he was indicating the Savior's birth from a shoot and from his root, he called him a lion's whelp, saying, "Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up." But when he prophesies his lying down [?] and his sleep in the passion, he says he is both, as a lion and as a whelp, in the words "having lain down, he slept as a lion and as a whelp." For then he was lifted up not only as one belonging to a royal race but as being himself king, since the nations confessed that he was indeed the king of Israel, even if those of the circumcision were unwilling to.

It might also be explained another way. He was taking up war against the opposing powers and was about to destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, so the divinity of the Word had to be present in him who was born according to the flesh from the shoot of Jacob. The divinity, then, is fittingly compared to a lion, because it has subdued and conquered all the wild and untamable powers; and the frail flesh he had assumed, which belonged to the royal tribe of Judah, is compared to a lion's whelp. Again, if our adversary the devil is like a roaring lion, consider whether every sinner might not be called his whelp, since everyone who commits sin is born of the devil. The Savior too came in the likeness of sinful flesh and became a curse for us (Rom 8:3), and "him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us" (2 Cor 5:21). Consider whether, for these reasons and according to some deeper sense, the prophecy declares that at the time of the passion he became neither a lion nor a whelp, but as a lion and as a whelp. For he himself also compares his passion to the serpent, saying, "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up" (John 3:14). After this the prophecy silently hints at the mystery of his resurrection with the words "Who shall rouse him?" From the outcome it has become clear to us who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead: plainly, his God and Father.

Next come the words beginning "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs." If we read these as the start of a new thought, they would be said of all those of the Jewish race who led the people, and on this understanding the sense of the words before us would be something like this: the rulers and leaders from among the Jews who are set over the Jewish people will not cease until there comes the one who is the cause of the nations' expectation, that is, Christ, and at his coming the rulers just mentioned must fail. If this is so, let us examine our own times, to see whether kings and leaders are to be found now. But it is plain to everyone that the Jewish nation, along with the rest, is subject to the Roman governors province by province, and not one of the Jews has been entrusted with the authority to rule. This began from the time of our Savior's birth. Up to King Herod we find in the histories Hebrews, born of Hebrews, ruling their whole nation, leading in succession from Moses himself: first the so-called judges, then the kings until the captivity in Babylon, after which the high priests took over the rule and continued until the reign of Augustus. In his reign Herod, the first ruler of foreign race, was entrusted by the Romans with the kingship over them, and then our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was born. From that time to the present, then, ruler and leader among the Jews is clearly shown to have failed. It is plain that our Savior, who was prophesied, has come. From his time not only have the rulers of the Jews failed, but also all the worship they performed in Jerusalem according to the law of Moses. And plainly, from the time of his coming, the expectation of the nations who through him have taken refuge with the God of all things began to be fulfilled in fact, according to Jacob's prophecy.

That is the sense if we read the words beginning "A ruler shall not fail from Judah" as the start of a new thought. But if we join the passage before us to the sense of what precedes it, then, since Christ has been understood as Judah according to what was set out earlier, it would follow that "A ruler shall not fail from Judah" should be taken of the rulers and leaders of the church after Christ. The prophecy says they will not fail "until the things laid up for him come," as if it said more clearly: until the things laid up for him come, when the consummation arrives and he receives the kingdom over all things. That the divine Spirit also calls Christ's disciples leaders is clear from what is said about Judas: "But you, a man of like soul, my leader and my acquaintance" (Ps 54:13). Those who have believed the sacred words to be divine and true must attend to these things too, and must in no way be alarmed, nor let their faith be shaken by the persecutions that come from time to time. This holds above all for the present persecution, which has blown against us more violently than any before it and has inflicted on the churches and on all the people such things as no one has recorded, whether from Scripture or from the tradition of the ancients. We say this because in the present persecution the very opposite of what was said might seem to have happened, since there now seems to be no assembly gathered, nor any roll of the church's rulers. But since the God-inspired Scripture does not lie, we must be persuaded that those just mentioned have not utterly failed, even if to some they seem to have failed. When the prophet supposed that he alone was left and that the rest had been slain, God said to him, "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal" (Rom 11:4). The same God now too watches over those who are worthy of his providence, and for us also he preserves a remnant chosen by grace, guarded by him and seen by him alone. Of them we too might say, "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah" (Rom 9:29). For to suppose that those who preside over the word, whom the prophecy names rulers and leaders, have failed altogether is simply impossible, since a limit has been set: they shall not fail "until the things laid up for him come." These are the things promised by the Father to Christ when he said to him, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet" (Acts 2:35). Then every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10). For at that time the expectation of the nations who have believed in him in the present age will have its moment to receive the promises they hoped for, in the hoped-for kingdom of heaven. So much for this. What follows, beginning "Binding his colt to the vine," depends on an allegorical interpretation, and we shall leave it for the studious to investigate. We have already said more than enough in what has been said, not in keeping with the purpose we set ourselves, yet out of necessity, for the sake of a clear exposition of the passage.

"Now Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law" (Exodus 3:1). And shortly after: "And they came to Horeb, the mountain of God; and an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire." And after other things: "When the Lord saw that he was drawing near to look, he called to him out of the midst of the bush, saying..." And again: "And the Lord said to him, 'I am He Who Is.'" And after a great deal more: "And God spoke to Moses and said to him, 'I am the Lord. I appeared to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, being their God, and my name "Lord" I did not make known to them; and I established my covenant with them'" (Exodus 6:2), and so on. In these passages Scripture records with great care that it was not the Lord but the angel who appeared to Moses. Through the angel the Lord delivers his oracles as if through an interpreter, and he teaches that the power giving the oracle was not some subordinate power but He Who Is himself. And he shows more clearly who He Who Is is when he says, "I am the Lord; I appeared to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, being their God; and my name 'Lord' I did not make known to them." To me this seems to carry some such meaning as this: "To you, for the present, I make known only my name, saying, 'I am the Lord.' But to your fathers I did not make known my name, for they were worthy of something greater than that kind of knowledge. Rather, I myself appeared to them, and through myself I established my covenant with them." Now it is plain from what has already been set out who it was that appeared to the fathers. For when the argument examined the matter in this way, it showed him to be God the Word, who was in the beginning with God. So it is the same one who manifests himself now as well, though not in the same way as to the forefathers. To them, as greater and more perfect men, he appeared himself, and through himself he established his covenant with them. In the case of Moses, however, it was not the Lord who appeared but the angel, while it was no longer the angel who called him but the Lord. For the Lord was the one giving the commands, and the angel was the one who ministered the divine words. Hence, among the other wonderful things the holy apostle declared, there is also this: "the law, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19), and this: "For if the word spoken through angels proved firm" (Hebrews 2:2). Clearly, then, an angel is introduced, with the Lord giving his oracles through him. And not even once in the whole account of the lawgiving will you find Scripture noting that God or the Lord appeared to Moses. Evidently that is said of the three patriarchs alone. From this it is clear that the whole legislation was given to the people of that time as to souls who were still infants and beginners, and so was handed down as if through tutors and stewards. Divine things were hinted at to them figuratively and in images, by means of symbols, because they were unable to receive the more mystical and spiritual teaching. Since they were like children brought up in Egyptian ways and still in need of much correction, [they were told] that God is fire, as in "Our God is a consuming fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24). This is never said in the case of the patriarchs. Moreover, when he commands them to purify themselves so that they may see the glory of the Lord, it is not said simply, as with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that God appeared to them. Instead, these very things are recorded amid great terror and spectacle: "And it came to pass on the third day, as morning came, that there were thunders and lightnings and a dark cloud upon the mountain, and the sound of the trumpet rang out loud, and all the people in the camp were terrified. And Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke, because God had come down upon it in fire; and its smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and all the people were greatly amazed. And the sounds of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice. And the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, onto the top of the mountain, and the Lord called Moses" (Exodus 19:16), and so on. These words testify that the Lord came down. But they no longer say that he also appeared, for that is reserved for the patriarchs alone. So there was a presence of the Lord, but what was seen was not the Lord himself. Clearly it was the angels who attended him as his bodyguard. Through them he made the vision fearful and astonishing to the people for their benefit. He took care to strengthen reverence in them, together with fear and faith in him, so that they would guard and keep the laws that were about to be handed down to them. And that many angels served the Lord at the giving of the law Moses himself shows in the blessings, where he says, "The Lord has come from Sinai, and has appeared to us from Seir, and has hastened from Mount Paran with the myriads of Kadesh; at his right hand were angels with him" (Deuteronomy 33:2), and so on. That is why Stephen too, addressing the people in the Acts, says, "You received the law as ordained by angels, and did not keep it" (Acts 7:53).

"Then the angel of God who went before the children of Israel set out and went behind them. And the pillar of cloud also set out from before them, and went and stood behind them, and came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of the children of Israel" (Exodus 14:19). Then, in what follows, the divine Scripture teaches what the cloud was: "And the Lord said to Moses, 'Behold, I am coming to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you and may believe you'" (Exodus 19:9). And again: "And God led them by day in a pillar of cloud, to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light." And again: "And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud" (Exodus 13:21). From these passages, then, it is clear that the angel who went before the children of Israel was distinct from the cloud. The cloud was something other than the angel: it was, as it were, a bodily instrument of the Lord himself. Through it, though he is incorporeal by nature and beyond all perceptible and material substance, he honoured his servant with his own conversation by means of an audible voice. The Lord himself explains to Moses the reason for this arrangement when he says, "so that the people may hear me speaking to you and may believe you." With the people, who were of a more bodily cast, he conversed through an audible voice. With the patriarchs, who needed neither a cloud nor a pillar of fire, both the manner of the vision and the manner of his conversation with them were different. That it was not some angelic power giving oracles through the cloud, but God himself, is shown, besides what has already been demonstrated, by the following passage of Scripture: "And the Lord said to Moses, 'Go and lead the people to the place of which I have spoken to you. Behold, my angel will go before you'" (Exodus 32:34). And again: "And the Lord said to Moses, 'Go up from here, you and the people,'" and so on, "'and I will send my angel before you'" (Exodus 33:1). Such words are in no way fitting for an angel to speak. They belong to God alone, to the Lord who throughout the whole history is designated by the four-letter name. Did, then, the Maker of the universe and God of all things descend so far as to ride upon a material mountain and walk alongside men like a tutor, he who fills heaven and earth? Or is this neither possible nor holy to imagine? Is it not both more reverent and more possible to understand this as the divine Word, the minister of the Father's will? Since he is Lord, "Jacob became his portion, and Israel the allotment of his inheritance" (Deuteronomy 32:9). As one caring for his own portion and inheritance, he emptied himself and diminished his inborn greatness, so as to condescend to the salvation of men even before he became man. If we consider the matter fairly, we will find that sometimes he refers the commands to his own person, as when he says, "You shall not appear before me empty-handed" (Exodus 23:15), and "You shall make me an altar of earth," and "I will come to you and bless you" (Exodus 20:24). At other times he speaks as if of another Lord, namely his God and Father, as in the Ten Commandments when he says, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain," and "On the seventh day is a sabbath to the Lord your God; for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the Lord blessed the seventh day." And again: "Honour your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you, and you may live long in the land which the Lord your God gives you." It is believed that the Lord spoke these words in the Ten Commandments not through an angel but himself, in person. How, then, could it not be obvious that he was teaching the people about devotion to his own supreme Father, the God of all?

"Behold, I send my angel before you, to guard you on the way, so that he may bring you into the land which I have prepared for you. Pay attention to him and listen to him; do not disobey him, for he will by no means hold back from you; for my name is upon him" (Exodus 23:20). The Lord gives the people these commands along with the rest of his ordinances. Suppose that after the death of Moses the same Lord who gave oracles in the wilderness had not remained with the people, and that one of the angels had gone before them instead. In that case there would be nothing in these passages to inquire into. But the history shows that even after the death of Moses the same Lord gave oracles to Joshua. In his oracles to him he plainly says: "As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will not forsake you or neglect you. Be strong and of good courage, for you shall divide to this people the land which I swore to your fathers to give them" (Joshua 1:5). Throughout the whole of Scripture no angel is ever shown standing by Joshua or giving him oracles. Instead it is the Lord himself, the one who is also designated in Moses by the four-letter name. It seems to me that he is also the same as the one who appeared to Joshua only once, in the form of a man. Scripture records that he appeared to Abraham and to Jacob in this way, and so now too he reveals himself, to teach his servant not to take him for the first and unbegotten God, but for the commander-in-chief of that God's host. So throughout the whole book of Joshua no angel at all is named as present, but only the Lord who is designated throughout the whole lawgiving in Moses. Scripture testifies to this plainly when it says, "And the Lord was with Joshua" (Joshua 6:27). If that is so, of whom could it be said, "Behold, I send my angel before you, to bring you into the land which I have prepared for you" (Exodus 23:20)? It seems, then, that these words point to no one else but Joshua himself. For it was he who brought the people into the land of promise, as the words God spoke to him also show: "Be strong and of good courage, for you shall divide to this people the land which I swore to your fathers concerning it" (Joshua 1:6). So God gives the people this command in advance: "Pay attention to him and listen to him; do not disobey him" (Exodus 23:21). We should not be surprised that he called him an angel, since the prophecy also calls John by this title when it says, "Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare my way before you" (Matthew 11:10). And if the passage quoted above refers wholly to Joshua the son of Nun, see how the Lord says of him, "for my name is called upon him." What name could this be, if not the name Jesus itself? The name Jesus was not the proper name of the man who appeared at that time, for he was formerly called Hoshea. Moses, inspired by God, was the first to name him Jesus, plainly moved by a more divine Spirit. He did so in order that the oracle which said, "for my name is upon him" (Numbers 13:16), might be fulfilled. For Jesus was the name of the Lord who gave the oracles, whom we have often shown to be the pre-existent Word of God, and it was this name that Moses gave to Hoshea. The divine Scripture bears witness to this and records with great precision that he called him by this name at no other time than when he was sending him out as a messenger, in keeping with the oracle, to spy out the land of promise ahead of the people. Through these things, then, Moses clearly appears to have known the name of our Saviour Jesus. And just as the name Jesus is first found with him in the passages under examination, so too he appears to have been the first to use the title Christ. Before his time, from the beginning of the ages, no one among any people had ever been called either Jesus or Christ. And he evidently honoured these titles with divinely inspired reasoning. He bestowed these two titles on two men who stood out above the whole people and were distinguished before God, and who had other names of their own: his own brother Aaron, and the son of Nun, who was formerly called Hoshea. By God's will he appointed them rulers over the whole nation, ahead of all the people, and he glorified them with the titles of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Aaron he called Christ, because Aaron bore the image of the true high priest of all things, God the Word himself, who was in the beginning with God. His own successor he named Jesus, because this man too preserved a type of our Saviour Jesus. When the worship handed down symbolically through Moses had ceased, and Moses had, in a sense, died, our Saviour took over the work of devotion to God. He conquered in war and subdued all the invisible powers that opposed his word. Then he made his own possession the whole earth among all the nations that had lain under their tyranny, and allotted it as an inheritance to his own people through the churches throughout the whole world.

"Whenever Moses went into the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and stand at the door of the tent, and the people would stand and worship, each from his own tent. And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as someone might speak to his own friend; and Moses would go back to the camp, but his attendant Joshua son of Nun did not go out of the tent. And Moses said to the Lord, 'See, you tell me, "Lead this people up," but you have not shown me whom you will send with me. Yet you said to me, "I know you above all others, and you have found favor with me." If, then, I have found favor before you, reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly, so that I may be one who has found favor before you, and that I may know that this nation is your people.' And he says, 'I myself will go before you and give you rest.' And Moses says to him, 'If you yourself do not go with us, do not lead me up from here. For how will it be known that I and your people have found favor with you, except by your going with us? And so we shall be glorified, both I and your people, above all the nations that are on the earth.' And the Lord said to Moses, 'This word that you have spoken I will also do for you; for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you above all others, and you have favor with me.' And Moses said, 'Show me your own glory.' And he said, 'I will pass by before you in my glory, and I will call out in the name of the Lord before you; and I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.' And he said, 'You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see my face and live.' And the Lord said, 'See, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock; and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back; but my face shall not be seen by you,'" and so on (Exod. 33:8). To this the text adds: "And the Lord came down in a cloud and stood beside him there, and called out in the name of the Lord. And the Lord passed by before his face and called out: 'The Lord, the Lord, God compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true, keeping righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness and injustice and sins; and he will not clear the guilty, bringing the lawlessness of fathers upon children, and upon children's children, to the third and the fourth generation.' And Moses hastened, bowed down to the ground and worshiped, and said, 'If indeed I have found favor in your sight, O Lord, go with us face to face.'"

Moses is recorded as speaking to God with as much boldness and freedom of speech as a man might use in conversing with his own friend. This shows no ordinary progress on the prophet's part. But since the Lord spoke to him face to face, yet had not yet appeared to him as he had to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, for this reason he makes his request, saying, "If indeed I have found favor before you, reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly." By this he shows that God did not make his appearances to him in the same way as he spoke to him. For if, as someone might suppose, God's having spoken to him face to face were the same as his having been seen by him, so to speak, face to face, what room would still be left for his request, "If indeed I have found favor before you, reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly"? And how, if he had previously been seen by him face to face, as one might suppose, does the Lord go on to say to him, "You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see my face and live"? Let whoever wishes explain why the text does not once bear witness that the Lord was seen by him, as it has been careful to say in the case of the patriarchs. But by this it is evident that, even if the Lord spoke to him face to face, he nevertheless spoke to him through the cloud. For the scripture establishes this beforehand when it says, "The pillar of cloud came down and stood at the door of the tent, and spoke to Moses." So he spoke through the cloud, but was not seen by him as he was by Abraham or Isaac or Jacob. To them he is recorded as having been seen openly and distinctly, without any form; but to this man he was seen through what is called the form, and through the cloud, which the text also calls the glory of the Lord when it says: "When Moses was speaking to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they turned toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud, and the Lord spoke to Moses" (Exod. 16:10). And again: "Moses went up the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. And the glory of the Lord came down upon the mountain, and the cloud covered it for six days; and the Lord spoke to Moses on the seventh day from the midst of the cloud. And the appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a blazing fire on the top of the mountain" (Exod. 24:15). Clearly, then, these words say that what Moses beheld was not the Lord himself but the form of the Lord, and cloud and fire, which the text also calls the glory of the Lord. So he saw the form of the Lord and his glory, but by no means the Lord himself, the Word of the Lord himself who was speaking; yet he heard him speaking through the cloud, which is why it is said, "And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face." But it is not recorded that he was seen by him face to face; for Moses asks for this as something that had not yet happened, saying, "Reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly." And in another place the text teaches that God spoke to him mouth to mouth, but was not correspondingly seen; he was seen rather in a form and through his glory, described above. It says this: "And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the door of the tent of witness; and Aaron and Miriam were called, and both came out. And he said to them, 'Hear my words: if there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses; he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in form and not through riddles, and he has seen the glory of the Lord. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?'" (Num. 12:5). So then he saw the glory of the Lord, and heard him as he gave him oracles in a form and spoke mouth to mouth, but he had not yet seen the Lord himself as the fathers had.

And it is no wonder that God is recorded as speaking mouth to mouth with Moses, since Moses teaches in Deuteronomy that God spoke face to face with the whole people as well, saying: "Not with your fathers did the Lord make this covenant, but with you, you yourselves, all of you who are alive here today. Face to face the Lord spoke to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire" (Deut. 5:3). However, even if he gave oracles to Moses and to the whole people in this way, note that he is said to have spoken to them mouth to mouth and face to face, but not to have been seen by them without the fire or the cloud, as he was by the fathers; for to the fathers the Lord is recorded as having been seen openly and without the covering of cloud or fire. Indeed our Savior and Lord too teaches that seeing God belongs to those who are perfect and whose minds have been purified to the utmost, saying, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8). That is why the Lord calls himself the God of such men, saying to Moses: "Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and my memorial from generation to generation" (Exod. 3:15). So Moses, eagerly desiring the greater gifts and reaching for progress like theirs, makes his request to the Lord, saying, "Reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly." For he had some notion of the greatness and loftiness and the ineffable and unattainable transcendence of the Word of God who was giving him oracles, but he saw that the Word was presenting the visions to him through ministering angels. Therefore he begs him to reveal himself to him more distinctly and more purely: no longer through coverings, nor by means of other servants, but openly, in the same way as to Abraham and those with him, without the form that came through fire and cloud. This, at any rate, is what I think is meant by the phrase, "Reveal yourself to me; let me see you plainly." In the same sense, having already heard the Lord say to him, "Behold, my angel shall go before your face," he gently declines, reaching for the greater thing, and says: "If you yourself do not go with us, do not lead me up from here." When the Lord assents to his request and says, "This word that you have spoken I will also do for you," Moses perceives how ready the divine generosity is, its kindness coming to meet those who reach for great things. Then he makes himself small, and, reckoning himself not yet worthy of the greater things, he puts forward another request, which falls short by comparison with the first, saying, "Show me your glory." And the Lord, fulfilling his word, says: "I will pass by before you in my glory, and I will call out in the name of the Lord before you," and so on. He is teaching that the knowledge of the Father and God of the universe is greater than every vision Moses had previously beheld, and he promises to impart this knowledge to him: about himself he says, "I will pass by before you in my glory," and about the initiation into the mystery of the Father he says, "and I will call out in the name of the Lord." For since he himself is the Lord signified by the Tetragrammaton, in the name of what Lord does he promise to call out, if not that of the Father? And truly, unless the Word of God first passes through a person, and unless he himself calls upon the Father, it is not possible in any other way to receive the knowledge of the Father of the universe; since "no one has known the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son reveals him" (Matt. 11:27). He, then, is the door and the way, through whom alone it is possible to see the cause that is beyond and above all things, the Father himself. For even if the divine Word, as a kind of forerunner of the Father, comes first to dwell in the souls of the blessed and shares his own glory with them, he does not remain to the end taking the supreme authority to himself; rather, having prepared and made ready the dwelling beforehand, he withdraws and hands over the kingdom to God the Father. This he himself also confesses, saying, "I will pass by before you in my glory, and I will call out in the name of the Lord." Here, then, he promises in word to do this; and next the text adds the deed as well, where it says: "And the Lord came down in a cloud and stood beside him there, and called out in the name of the Lord. And the Lord passed by before his face and called out: 'The Lord, the Lord, God compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true, keeping righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness and injustice and sins; and he will not clear the guilty, bringing the lawlessness of fathers upon children, and upon children's children, to the third and fourth generation'" (Exod. 34:5). It is the Lord signified by the Tetragrammaton who says these things, having come down in a cloud and stood beside Moses. In keeping with the promise he had made, he passed by before his face and called upon his own Lord and Father, the one who is truly Lord Lord, named twice by the Tetragrammaton, saying, "The Lord, the Lord, God compassionate and merciful," and so on. But if someone should forcibly contend that it was not the Lord but Moses who said these things, let him take firm proof from the very words of Moses, who acknowledges that the words quoted above belong to the Lord. Praying in another place, Moses says: "And now let your hand be lifted up, O Lord, just as you spoke, saying: The Lord is long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true, taking away lawlessness and injustice and sins; and he will by no means clear the guilty, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation" (Num. 14:17). These words therefore show most plainly and clearly that the Lord himself spoke the words quoted above, calling upon a greater Lord, the one who is truly Lord, evidently his own Father. Or if anyone is reluctant to be persuaded of this, let him say whether he can offer any other explanation of these passages, while still holding that the one who gave the oracles was not an angel but the Lord himself, signified by the Tetragrammaton. For it is he who is recorded as having spoken face to face with Moses, and he is the one whom Moses entreats when he declines the guardianship of angels, saying, "If you yourself do not go with us, do not lead me up from here" (Exod. 33:15). But in fact it is impossible to refer these things to anyone other than God the Word alone, who was in the beginning with God. As Moses longed for great things, the Word shows him the knowledge of the Greater One, instructing him so that he might know the only true God, and God the Word whom he sent, who is himself also Lord and God, second after the Father. And this is the first and most necessary benefit he provides him: that Moses should never, because of the surpassing glory of what he beheld, transfer his notions about the God of the universe to the Word who was giving him oracles. Rather, he teaches him to regard as the first and only true God the one on whom he himself was calling, saying, "The Lord, the Lord, God compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true." Pay careful attention to the word "true," which is used in the same way as in "that they may know you, the only true God" (John 17:3), spoken by the same Savior in the Gospels. But the people as a whole could not have taken these things in. They were beginners, and so the one giving the oracles said to them, "I am, and there is no other besides me"; for they still needed an elementary introduction to the doctrine of God's sole rule, being in no way able to articulate the doctrines concerning the Father and the Son, since they had only recently turned away from the polytheistic error of the Egyptians. But "I am, and there is no other besides me" (Deut. 32:39) may be said in the person of God the Word, in the same way as "I and the Father are one," and "I am in the Father and the Father in me" (John 10:30). Just as whoever has seen him has seen the Father, according to the saying "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father who sent me" (John 14:9), so in the same way whoever heard him heard the Father who is in him saying, "I am, and there is no other besides me" (Deut. 32:39).

I have said this much, as far as such great matters allow, because I wanted to show beyond dispute that the one who spoke with Moses was neither the God of the universe nor some angelic power, but the divine Word himself. We firmly believe that, after the Father and Lord of the universe, he is the second God and Lord of all things. The evangelist John teaches us this still more clearly when he says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). It would take a great deal of leisure, more than the present occasion allows, to explain what the place and the rock are of which the Lord said, "Behold, there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock." The apostle, however, made clear what the rock is when he said, "And the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). I take the place to be nothing other than the rock, and to be the same as the place that Jacob came upon, where it is written, "Jacob went out from the Well of the Oath and journeyed to Haran. And he came upon a place" (Genesis 28:10). There he saw in a vision the ladder and the Lord standing firm upon it, and when he woke he said, "The Lord is in this place"; and again he said, "How fearful is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." There are further questions. What is the face of God the Word, which Moses, that is, the Law, could not behold, since it is human and rather bodily? What are his back parts, which alone the Law could take in, since it deals in types and [?] symbolizes intelligible things? And how was it said, "I will cover you with my hand," a veil and covering being laid over the Law, so that because of this veil it could see what is behind, but no longer what goes before and what is superior? Whoever cares to investigate these things will come to know them by attending to them privately at the proper time.

"A man shall come forth from his seed, and he shall rule over many nations; and the kingdom of Gog shall be exalted, and his kingdom shall be increased. God led him out of Egypt; he has as it were the glory of a unicorn. He shall devour the nations of his enemies, and he shall suck the marrow from their fatness, and with his arrows he shall shoot down the enemy. He lay down and rested like a lion and like a lion's whelp; who shall rouse him? Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed" (Numbers 24:7–9). Christ is the one who was born according to the flesh from the seed of Israel and who has ruled over many nations. For what nation has there been that has not known servitude to him, since the word of his disciples has gone out into all the earth, and their sayings to the ends [?] of the world? Among very many peoples, even among the barbarians themselves, one can see many who through faith in him have come to the knowledge of the one God, and who for the sake of their devotion to him have endured every kind of punishment, even to death. So this prophecy too is clearly shown to have found its fulfilment in our Saviour; or else let someone come forward and show to whom else these words could refer. For us it is plain that the spiritual kingdom and lordship of our Saviour grows day by day in the souls that have received his word. And at his coming the kingdom of Gog was also exalted. Some have taken this to be the dominion of the Romans; others, understanding it figuratively, have taken it to mean the heavenly commonwealth of the Gospel and the contemplation of intelligible doctrines, and for this reason they have understood it to be signified by "Gog," which is interpreted as "roofs." Moreover, God led him out of Egypt. Literally, this happened when Joseph, having received a divine warning, took Mary together with the child Jesus out of Egypt and returned to the land of Israel; thus was fulfilled both the present prophecy and the one in Hosea, which according to the Hebrew and the translation of Aquila says, "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1). In the spiritual sense, it happened when the Father took him up from the intelligible Egypt and the places of this world and led him to the heavens. And what is called the glory of the unicorns in the Saviour hints at the divinity in him that belongs to the sole sovereignty of the Father.

After this it is said, "He shall devour the nations of his enemies." For the nations that have come under his teaching were formerly the portion of his enemies, but after coming to faith in him he made them fit, as it were, to be food for himself. Their fatness, that is, everything material and earthly that had grown into them, he thinned away and drew out [?], while through his own husbandry he produced in them nourishing fruits. These things he accomplished with spiritual and rational arrows, shooting down the one who long ago ruled the nations and was his enemy, that is, the devil. The words from "He lay down and rested like a lion" onward were spoken almost word for word by Jacob as well, in his prophecies about Judah; since I have already set out what meaning they have, as far as it has occurred to me, I will not repeat myself. It is clear how we who bless Christ have been blessed by God. For even if people loathe us, as the Egyptians loathed God's people of old, nevertheless in our case too the words are fulfilled: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong" (Exodus 1:12). And it is plain in what way those who cursed him from the beginning, by saying, "Crucify him, crucify him," have received the curse. For the cross was a mark of a curse, according to the saying, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). But he who endured their curse has been highly exalted by the Father, while those who were cursed by God himself have received a ruin that lasts for ever. If anyone examines this ruin closely, he will see the greatness of the power of God, which still to this day pursues those who were once cursed by him. So much on the words, "Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed."

"A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise out of Israel, and he shall shatter the rulers of Moab and plunder all the sons of Seth" (Numbers 24:17). The Word of God, having emptied himself, taken the form of a servant, and been found in fashion as a man, rose as no small star, not for Jacob but out of Jacob. For he began from the bodily people, those of the circumcision, and then shone upon all the nations. Moving on from them, he waged no small wars, clearing away the opposing powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness. Having overcome them, he took plunder for his own inheritance, recovering all the nations that had formerly been under them. Concerning these nations the Father promised him, saying: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession" (Psalm 2:8).

"The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers; you shall listen to him in everything, just as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, saying, 'We will not hear the voice of the Lord our God again, nor will we see this great fire any more, and so we will not sin [?].' And the Lord said to me, 'They have spoken rightly in all that they have said. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my word in his mouth, and he will speak to them whatever I command him. And whoever does not listen to all that the prophet speaks in my name, I will exact vengeance from him'" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Whom from Israel could anyone point to as a prophet like Moses, that is, a lawgiver appointed for the human race, other than Jesus alone, our Savior and Lord? He has been revealed to all the nations as the lawgiver of the new covenant, of the life according to the gospel, in keeping with the prophetic prayer in the Psalm: "Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are but men" (Psalm 9:20). He also redeemed those who through him have come to the God of the universe from the spiritual Egypt, from its brickmaking, and from bitter slavery under the spiritual Pharaoh. In short, everything that is recorded as having happened bodily under Moses, our Savior and Lord accomplished according to the spiritual law. So he has come, the prophet still famous even now among Samaritans and Jews, whom Moses foretold, and about whom God testified in advance, saying, "And whoever does not listen to all that the prophet speaks in my name, I will exact vengeance from him." And indeed the blood of all, from Abel to Zechariah, who was murdered between the temple and the altar, has been avenged on the generation that rose up against the Savior, and above all on those who dared to raise against him the cry, "Crucify him, crucify him! Away from the earth with such a man! His blood be on us and on our children!" This came to pass at once: God, as he had foretold, avenged the blood of Christ on those very men and on their children, and justice overtook them, so that from that time until now the whole nation has not been able to lift its head at all. So another prophecy was also fulfilled, that of Amos, which says, "The house of Israel has fallen; it will no longer rise again" (Amos 5:1). Foreseeing this in the Spirit, the apostle too cried out, "But wrath has come upon them to the uttermost" (1 Thessalonians 2:16).
