"Rejoice, you heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice, you nations, with his people, and let all the sons of God give him strength" (Deuteronomy 32:43). Whom else would the divine Spirit command his angels to worship but Christ? At his coming the nations clearly rejoiced with his people, the choir of righteous patriarchs and prophets. Of these nations God speaks again in the same song, turning as if to address another people: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their idols. And I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them" (Deuteronomy 32:21). It is quite plain that after they were cast off, God chose the foolish things of the world to shame those who were wise among them. He chose the weak things of the world, the lowborn, the despised, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that formerly counted among them (1 Corinthians 1:27). For from the very time of Moses they had worshipped idols, angering God and provoking him to jealousy, and when his Christ came they did not receive him. But the nations, having come to know through him the Father and God of the universe, will rejoice, according to the prophecy before us, with his people of the saints. And all the sons of God gave strength to Christ: both those who had earlier prophesied about him, and all who after his coming received the spirit of adoption and proclaimed him throughout the whole world. So much, then, from the Pentateuch; let us move on to the books that follow.

"And it came to pass, when Joshua was at Jericho, that he looked up and saw a man standing opposite him, with his sword drawn in his hand. And Joshua went up to him and said, 'Are you one of ours, or one of our enemies?' And he said to him, 'I am the commander-in-chief of the army of the Lord; I have now come.' And Joshua fell on his face to the ground and said to him, 'Master, what do you command your servant?' And the commander-in-chief of the Lord said to Joshua, 'Loose the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy'" (Joshua 5:12). Who else could the commander-in-chief of the army of the Lord be but the Christ of God, the ruler of the whole holy and spiritual host of God? Consider whether the words spoken to Joshua do not suggest that he is the same one who spoke to Moses through the angel on the mountain. For what is now said to Joshua was said in the same way to Moses by the Lord through the angel when Moses was beginning his vision: "Loose the sandal from your feet," and what follows. The Christ of God has many names, and here he is called commander-in-chief of the army of the Lord. In Isaiah, likewise, he is called Angel of Great Counsel, in the passage: "And they will wish they had been burned with fire. For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel" (Isaiah 9:5). You would also find him named Angel of the Covenant in Malachi (Malachi 3:1), where it says, "And suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire."

"The Lord went up into the heavens and thundered; he will judge the ends of the earth, and he will give strength to our kings and exalt the horn of his anointed" (1 Samuel 2:10). The Lord, the Word of God, who came down from the heavens, himself went up again into the heavens. Having gone up, he thundered forth the gospel proclamation by his own divine power, so that it came to be heard throughout the whole world. He will judge the ends of the earth and those who dwell as far away as these, since he has received all judgment from the Father. He also gave strength to his own disciples, apostles and prophets, who are our kings. And he exalted the horn of his anointed: either of his people, who are so called by sharing in Christ, or of the humanity he assumed, whose horn was the Godhead, exalted, according to the holy apostle. In the eighty-eighth Psalm, too, God clearly says something similar to this passage about Christ: "And in my name his horn shall be exalted" (Psalm 88:24).

"And a man of God came to Eli and said, 'Thus says the Lord, the Lord'" (1 Samuel 2:27); and in what follows: "And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do all that is in my heart and in my soul. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall walk before my anointed all his days. And everyone who is left in the house will come to bow down to him for an obol of silver and for a single loaf, saying, 'Put me into one of your priestly offices, so that I may eat bread'" (1 Samuel 2:35). This is none other than Jesus Christ our Savior alone, the priest of God Most High after the order of Melchizedek, whom we have as a great high priest who has passed through the heavens (Hebrews 4:14), as the apostle says. He did all that was in the Father's heart, becoming obedient to him even to death (Philippians 2:8). For this reason the Father raised him up and built him a sure house: the church, made of stones that are rational, living, and faithful, stones in the truest sense. And those who have believed in him come to bow down to him, and he does not turn away the obol of silver. In the bodily sense, this is the widow who contributed her farthing for the relief of the needy. In the spiritual sense, it is the soul that rests on faith alone, or the soul that contributes, according to the measure of its spiritual possessions, whatever serves the upbuilding and benefit of others. For he chose the foolish things of the world (1 Corinthians 1:27), the weak and poor, the despised, and the things that are not. He did not disdain them, nor souls such as these. Rather, as the Word of God who loves mankind, he welcomes these too for their eagerness. By divine judgment he assigns them, according to their worth, to the various dwellings of his priestly offices, and counts them worthy of the bread of eternal life that comes from him. The words "and he shall walk before my anointed all his days" (1 Samuel 2:37) are spoken of the saints in the church, who are themselves also called anointed ones, as in "Do not touch my anointed ones" (Psalm 104:15). For it was to them that the Savior said in the gospel, "Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). These passages call for fuller explanation, but we shall be content with what has been said here as briefly as we could.

"And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come from your own body, and I will prepare his kingdom. He shall build me a house for my name, and I will set up his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. And if his wrongdoing comes, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the strokes of the sons of men. But my mercy I will not take away from them, as I took it away from those whom I removed from before my face. And his house shall be made sure, and his kingdom forever before me; and his throne shall be set up forever" (2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 88). Things like these are also said in the eighty-eighth Psalm. The Jews might well be at a loss over these passages. They will presumably suppose that the prophecy speaks of David, or of Solomon, who reigned after him. Then for what reason does God promise to make him a firstborn son? In the Psalm he says, "He shall call upon me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation.' And I will make him firstborn, high above the kings of the earth" (Psalm 88:26); and in the chapter before us, "I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me." Yet one would say that David differed in no way from the other prophets, since he even had to make confession over the matter of Uriah, saying, "Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil in your sight." Nor did Solomon, who, as the plain narrative of Scripture teaches, turned away from God and was drawn to idols through his desire for women. And how did the kingdom of David or of Solomon stand forever before God, and the throne stand set up forever? So says the prophecy here, and so too the one in the Psalm, which runs something like this: "I swore to David my servant: I will establish your seed forever" (Psalm 88:3), "and build up your throne from generation to generation." After other things it says, "Once for all I swore by my holiness that I would not lie to David. His seed shall remain forever, and his throne like the sun before me" (Psalm 88:35). And again: "And I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven" (Psalm 88:29). You would find similar things in Jeremiah too, where it is said: "For thus says the Lord: There shall not be cut off from David a man sitting on the throne of the house of Israel; and from the priests and the Levites there shall not be cut off a man before me, offering whole burnt offerings, sacrificing sacrifice, and making incense all the days" (Jeremiah 33:17, Complutensian edition; see the note on 40:13 in the editions of Bos and Holmes). One should examine these words alongside the present condition of the Jews and their history from the reigns of Hezekiah and Jeconiah. Under these kings the Jewish kingdom of David's line came to an end, at the time of the captivity in Babylon, and after that the Jews were never again ruled or governed as a kingdom by anyone of David's descent. Anyone who does this will find that the words in no way fit either David or Solomon. In that case God's prediction, made with oaths, would necessarily be proved false, which is unthinkable. But if we refer the so-called seed of David to the Christ who was born from him according to the flesh, it is clear how this seed, that is, Christ, will remain forever. It is also clear how his throne and spiritual kingdom stand forever before the Father, set up by him and built up from generation to generation in the souls of those who believe in him. The throne of this seed of David, which has been given to us, will endure before the Father like the Sun of righteousness, and like the days of heaven. That is why the Holy Spirit says to him in another Psalm: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions" (Psalm 44:6). And Christ built the church as a house for the Father out of living and intelligent stones, that is, holy and virtuous souls. He raised a temple far better than the temporary building of Solomon, which no longer exists, and far superior to it. The apostle too testifies that the saying "I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me" belongs to Christ. He took it from this passage in his letter to the Hebrews, where he says: "For to which of the angels did he ever say, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you'? And again, 'I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me'?" (Hebrews 1:5). The words from "And if his wrongdoing comes, I will rebuke him with the rod of men" onward (Colossians 1:24) are said of the people who have believed in Christ, since his church is also called the body of Christ, according to the apostle. To see that the words about visitation concern those who have believed in him, note carefully the plural in "But my mercy I will not take away from them." In the Psalm too, things like those here are clearly said about the sons of the one prophesied, in the passage: "If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their transgressions with a rod and their iniquities with scourges; but my mercy I will not scatter from them" (Psalm 88:30). See how Scripture has named the persecutions that come from time to time "rods of men" and "strokes of the sons of men." Yet God gives many encouragements and consolations through the Scriptures, and they do not allow us to lose heart at the persecutions carried out against us from time to time. For just as he foretold that he would visit the people of Christ with a rod when they sinned, so too he promised beforehand that he would not take away his mercy from them, saying, "But my mercy I will not take away from them, as I took it away from those from whom I took it away." One will ask upon whom the mercy of God rested before the people from the nations, the mercy that you [?] took away from them entirely; and he promises to do the like [?] in the case of the people of Christ.

"And David spoke to the Lord the words of this song" (2 Samuel 22:1). Then, in what follows: "And he bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet" (2 Samuel 22:10). And again, after this: "Deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will make me head of nations. A people whom I did not know served me; as soon as their ears heard, they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons shall be cast away, and shall stumble out of their enclosures" (ibid., v. 44). These things are said in almost the same words in the seventeenth Psalm, and they would be better examined when we come to gather selections from the Psalms. For now we note only this. The words "and he bowed the heavens and came down" may be understood of Christ's descent from the heavens. The words "deliver me from the contradiction of the people" are spoken in his person about those of the circumcision who did not believe in him. Of these he also says in Isaiah, "All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contradicting people" (Isaiah 65:2). The words "you will make me head of nations" and "a people whom I did not know served me; as soon as their ears heard, they obeyed me" are a prophecy about the church from the nations. The words "foreign sons lied to me" refer to the godless heresies, which have fabricated falsehoods about the Savior himself and about the God of the universe. Scripture says that these will be cast away, having stumbled out of their own enclosures, that is, having fallen away from their insidious and hidden false doctrines.

"And now, O Lord God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you spoke to your servant David my father: that God will truly dwell with men on the earth, though the heaven of heaven will not suffice for you" (2 Samuel 8:26; 2 Chronicles 6:17). Things like these are also said by Solomon in the second book of Chronicles, in his prayer to God. Here too, then, it is clearly prophesied that God will dwell with men on the earth. This too has been fulfilled in our own time at the coming of Christ, when God the Word became man and lived among the human race.

"And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come from your own body; and I will prepare your kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will set up his throne. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. And my mercy I will not take away from him, as I took it away from those who were before you. And I will make him sure in my house and in his kingdom forever, and his throne shall be set up forever" (1 Chronicles 17:11). These words are similar to the passage set out earlier from the second book of Kingdoms. Having noted them, we shall be content with what was said about that passage, since the two differ very little.

"And now, O Lord God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you spoke to your servant David: that God will truly dwell with men on the earth, though the heavens of heaven will not suffice for you" (2 Chronicles 6:17). We have already spoken about this once, when we set out the passages from the third book of Kingdoms, and we will not repeat ourselves now.

"Men, are not women strong? Great is the earth, and high is the heaven, and swift in its course is the sun, for it turns in the circle of the heaven and runs back again to its own place in a single day. Is not he great who does these things? And truth is great, and stronger than all things. The whole earth calls upon truth, and the heaven blesses it, and all works shake and tremble, and with it there is nothing unrighteous. Wine is unrighteous, the king is unrighteous, women are unrighteous, the sons of men are unrighteous, and all their works are unrighteous, all such things; there is no truth in them, and in their unrighteousness they will perish. But truth endures and is strong forever, and lives and prevails forever and ever. With it there is no respect of persons or partiality; rather, it does what is just, apart from all that is unrighteous and wicked. It holds aloof [?], and those who are pleased with its works [?]. In its judgment there is nothing unrighteous, and to it belong the strength and the kingship and the authority and the majesty of all the ages. Blessed be the God of truth" (1 Esdras [also called 3 Esdras] 4:31). Our Savior and Lord, being the Word of God, is recorded as having said, "I am the truth" (John 14:6). So we have fittingly set out the passage above about truth, since it shows that truth has a subsistence of its own, distinct from the Father. For truth, it says, "endures, and is strong forever, and lives and prevails; and with it there is no respect of persons," and so on. To this it adds, concerning God the Father, who is also God of the Word and of the truth, "Blessed be the God of truth." To this we ourselves will add the Amen.

So much, then, from the book of Ezra as well. From Esther, however, we have found nothing bearing on our subject. Having made our selections from the historical books, let us now move on to the books written in verse, since these come before the rest of the prophecies in time. Of these, let us first look at the passages from the Psalms.

1. Of the First Psalm: on the blameless life of Christ, and on his way of life at the very summit of virtue. 2. On the passion of Christ, and his heavenly kingdom, and the Father's promise to him concerning the nations. 3. On the passion of Christ and his resurrection from the dead. 4. On the knowledge of God sown through him among all people. 5. On the death of Christ and his resurrection from the dead, and how he is proclaimed lawgiver of the nations. 6. On the resurrection of Christ and the salvation of humankind. 7. On the blameless life of Christ. 8. On Christ's descent from heaven, and his appointment over the nations and the unknown people, and on the opposition of the Jews. 9. On the preaching of the apostles to the whole world, and on Christ as bridegroom. 10. On Christ as king. 11. Again on Christ as king. 12. On the events of Christ's passion, and on his apostles, and the turning of the nations to God, and on another generation and a people to come. 13. On his ascension into heaven. 14. Having set out the testimonies about our Savior drawn from the historical scriptures, we will next add to them, in this second section of the Selections, those gathered from the books written in verse, since these come before the remaining prophecies in time. And let us first examine those from the book of Psalms.

Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the pestilent; but his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night. Whom could anyone point to who has advanced to such extraordinary [?] virtue as to have fallen in no way into any sin whatsoever? That, it seems to me, is what is meant by "he has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly," and "he has not stood in the way of sinners," and "he has not sat in the seat of the pestilent"; through these words, I think, it is shown that the one called blessed had no taste of sin at all. For not only not to have walked in such things, nor, as it were, to have gone forward along them, but not even to have sat down, indeed not to have set foot in them at all to begin with, nor to have stood in them—how is this not a wonderful and rare thing? The praises of the man described present themselves to the mind rather as spoken of something continuous: for it says that he neither walked, nor stood, nor sat in such forms of wickedness, and this shows that the virtuous condition of the one called blessed is constant and unbroken. One might see many who have achieved virtue through watchfulness and discipline, but none such as the psalm describes. But if anyone considers how great a thing it is to prosper in everything and to have one's way made smooth according to God, stumbling in nothing and never falling short of the goal of virtue—so that in this sense the psalm says, "and whatever he does will prosper"—and further, if he considers what it is for someone to be so blended in harmony that his own will agrees with the law of the Lord, and to meditate on it not only all day long but also through the night, gazing into it with the wakeful eyes of the mind, and acting in accordance with it not only in his deeds and words by day but even in his thoughts and imaginings in sleep, he will understand the greatness of the one whom the divine Spirit attests to have achieved these things. But although what has been said admittedly surpasses all human nature, it would fit one man alone: the one born of the seed of David according to the flesh, Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior, of whom alone the divine Spirit in Isaiah has testified that he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isa 53:9). That this interpretation is acceptable is confirmed by the reading in the Hebrew, which carefully has "Blessed is the man," with the addition of the article. And it was indeed fitting that David, who was called the father of our Savior according to the flesh and had received the promise that the Christ would be born of his seed, should dedicate the beginning of his prophecy to him. Whoever wishes to understand precisely how what is said in the psalm refers to the Savior will learn it by reading those who have written commentaries on it.

Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his anointed (Ps 2). In the Acts of the Apostles, those who heard Peter and John recount the wonders that had happened to them bore witness that this prophecy too had been fulfilled. For, giving thanks for the marvels they heard of, they added to the words quoted above: For truly there were gathered together in this city against your holy servant, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the peoples of Israel (Acts 4:27). Yet it was not only those who plotted against our Savior at that time who gathered against him, but also the kings and rulers, and whole nations and peoples, from then until now, by blaspheming him and plotting against his teaching. And we must be convinced that it was not only the visible kings and rulers among men who plotted against him, but much more the spiritual and invisible rulers of this age, who were at work then and are still at work now in the nations and in the peoples of the circumcision, who meditated on the law of God vainly and to no purpose—peoples who took counsel not only against the Christ of God but, through him, also against the Father who sent him. Of all these the psalm goes on to say: He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and in his anger he will throw them into confusion. After this Christ himself, teaching us about the dispensation that came about concerning him after the passion, says: But I was appointed king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord. We must not, however, follow the earthbound notions of the Jews and think that Christ's kingdom is like the kingdoms of men, to be established on a physical Mount Zion. For to the one who asked him whether he was a king, he answered: My kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). That is why he promised the kingdom of heaven to those who believed in him; and that Mount Zion is heavenly is taught not only by the apostle but also by a great many other prophecies. Micah, for instance, having foretold that because of the impieties of the former people Zion would be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem would become like a watchman's hut in an orchard, and the mountain of the house like a wooded grove (Mic 3:12), then goes on in the same way to speak of another Zion and Jerusalem, saying: And in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be made manifest, and peoples will come to it, and many nations will go, for out of Zion will go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Mic 4:1). It is of this, then, that [?] Christ speaks here too: But I was appointed king by him on Zion, his holy mountain. And by whom was he appointed? Clearly by the Father, who said to him: You are my Son; today I have begotten you; and: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. That the prophecy is true and the promise does not fail can be seen from those of every nation who in so short a time have come over to the worship of God through our Savior. Otherwise, let those who shamelessly dare to turn their eyes from what is plainly happening tell us to whom they could apply the prophecy, if they will not accept that these things are so. For they could not show that David the king, of whom some have supposed these things to be said, suffered anything of the kind, as though rulers and kings, nations and peoples had plotted against him. And when, or for what great exploits, did the Lord say to David, You are my Son; today I have begotten you? And how could Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession be said to him, when his kingdom was plainly confined to Israel alone and the borders of Judea? Let them answer, too, why they do not accept the Christ who has come. Is it because he suffered, so that they must therefore expect another who will suffer nothing like what he suffered? Then how would the prophecies be fulfilled that foretell that the Christ of God would suffer a great many things—both in many other places and not least in the psalm before us? Or are we to suppose that he sowed the teaching about the God of the universe throughout the world without God [?]? Can one even imagine that a human impulse, the mere enterprise of an ordinary person, could have such strength and power that by his teaching alone, without divinity working with it, he could dispose the souls of every kind of hearer toward the God of the universe, could have sown these things [?] long ago, and could still now persuade people to abandon ancestral customs and a lawless, savage and licentious life, and to devote themselves to the worship of God alone, and to value it above not only their property but even life itself, which all hold dear? But I do not think that anyone willing to be even moderately fair-minded would fail to agree that such great things came about through our Savior with the help of a divine and superhuman power. From these things the divinity of the Lord who became man is demonstrated, and at the same time the proofs clearly appear that he has received from the Father the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession, in accordance with the prophecy before us. To expound everything in the psalm is not the business of the present occasion, especially since it has already received a very full exposition.

The third psalm, too, can easily be taken as referring to Christ. Following on from those before it, it teaches about the plot against him through the words, Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? (Ps 3), and about his resurrection, which is shown by the words, I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me. Each verse of the psalm would also fit Christ, if it were given the proper interpretation. And there is good reason why it is placed third, to prophesy the Lord's resurrection after the prophecies before it: for the first, as we have explained, teaches his blameless life and sinless way of living; the second, the events of the passion; and so, following these, the third prophesies his resurrection.

The first part of the eighth psalm, from O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth (Ps 8), seems to prophesy the calling from among the nations. That is why it is entitled "For the winepresses"—the winepresses being understood as the churches throughout the world, in which the rational grape-clusters of the true vine, Christ, and of his branches, as it were, the holy apostles, are pressed and yield the spiritual wine of their teachings, which brings about every kind of gladness. For otherwise it is impossible to apply what is said in the psalm to physical winepresses, since its wording contains no meaning of the kind found elsewhere, whether about a vine brought out of Egypt, or about the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, or anything like that. The part beginning What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and what follows, is taken in the Epistle to the Hebrews as referring to our Savior and Lord Jesus. There, after You subjected all things under his feet (Heb 2:8), it adds: But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death. One might say that he was made a little lower than the angels not only because of the suffering of death but also because of his very becoming man, when, being in the form of God, he did not count equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave (Phil 2:6), and lowered himself so far that, instead of the glory he had in the form of God, it was said of him: We saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honor, and fell short of the sons of men (Isa 53:2). In return for this the Father crowned him with glory and honor (Phil 2:10), highly exalting him and granting him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Heb 2:7). And he set him over the works of his hands (Heb 2:7). This too fits the person of our Savior because of God the Word within him, but it would not fit just anyone, since the sacred writings customarily count even the heavens among the works of God, as in And the heavens are the works of your hands (Ps 102:25). Besides this: and he subjected all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea (Ps 8:6). By these words, it seems, is indicated more allegorically the subjection, under the yoke and service of the Word, of the more irrational souls, which are of a lower order like beasts, or even of the opposing powers.

The title of the ninth psalm runs something like this: "For the end, concerning the hidden things. A psalm of David" (Ps 9). In its place Symmachus rendered: "A victory song concerning the death of the son. A song of David." And indeed the Hebrew seems rather to have this sense: lamanasse almauth ben masmora David. It would be well for those of the circumcision who use it to puzzle over what death, or what son, David spoke of in the psalm. To us it seems clearly to prophesy the passion of the Savior; and the Seventy, having understood this, hinted at it in a more veiled way. Aquila too, himself indicating some great exploit accomplished in the Savior's passion, rendered it: "To the giver of victory, of the youth of the son. A melody of David." And anyone who observes closely could apply all the words of the psalm to Christ, who calls himself poor and needy and prophesies his resurrection from the dead in the words: Have mercy on me, O Lord; see my humiliation at the hands of my enemies, you who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion—and which Zion is meant has been shown to us a little earlier. In it certain things are also prophesied about the nations that would be saved through him, as if about the poor and needy; among them is: Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are men. Here it is worth noting that the nations are not subject to the law of Moses. This text should be put to those of the circumcision who reproach those from the nations for not living according to the law of Moses, and it should be shown that the prophetic word knows that there will be a lawgiver of the nations other than Moses, since it says, as in a prayer, Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them—clearly, over the nations. For it adds, let the nations know that they are men, as if to say: let the nations regain knowledge and understanding of their own rational nature through the lawgiver who is to be appointed for them. And this would be Christ, who gave us the common covenant as law when he said, "It was said to those of old such and such, but I say such and such" (Matt 5:28). By divine and ineffable power he has been able to establish his laws not over one nation or a second, nor over some part of the whole world, nor yet for a short time, but, as can be learned from what has actually come about, perpetually and over all nations. If anyone does not accept that this is so, let him show whom else besides our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ he could name, in keeping with the prophecy before us, as appointed by the God of the universe to be lawgiver for the nations and as having become the teacher of all people in piety toward the creator of the universe.

Since in the eleventh psalm the Lord says, Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord; I will set them in salvation, I will speak boldly in it (Ps 11:5), let us consider whether these words too might fit the person of Christ teaching about his resurrection from the dead, with some such meaning as this: "For the sake of the nations, who have fallen into the misery of wickedness and are called poor in a reproachful sense because they have been deprived of the riches that are according to God, I emptied myself and took up the struggle on their behalf even to death; now I will arise, and, having received authority over all things from the Father, I will set all who have believed in me in salvation, and I will speak boldly in it"—that is, either in the Father, or in the great exploits I have accomplished for salvation. Such, then, might be the meaning of this text. But the opening of the psalm, which contains Save me, O God, for the holy one has failed, and what follows, shows what sort of time it was in which he suffered. For at that time the holy one had failed, and truths had dwindled away from among the sons of men; each spoke vain things to his neighbor; and everything that follows these words had been fulfilled at that time.

"I foresaw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken. Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also will dwell in hope. For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your holy one see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence." (Ps. 15:8) Peter testifies in the Acts of the Apostles that these words too refer to the person of Christ. There he says: "Jesus the Nazarene, a man attested to us by God with mighty works and wonders and signs, which God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this man, handed over by the set purpose and foreknowledge of God, you took and killed, nailing him up by the hands of lawless men. But God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. For David says, 'I foresaw the Lord always before me.'" (Acts 2:22) Then, after saying some things in between, he adds these words exactly: "Brothers, I may speak to you with confidence about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath to set one of the fruit of his loins on his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." (Acts 2:29) Since Peter, then, has applied the interpretation of the prophecy to the Saviour, anyone who does not treat the study of these things as a side matter has two choices. He may apply the whole wording of the psalm to the Saviour consistently with Peter's understanding, or he may consult what others have written in their commentaries on the psalm. Our purpose does not permit us to say anything more on these passages than what has already been said.

The words in the sixteenth Psalm, "You have tested my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tried me by fire, and no wrong was found in me" (Ps. 16), we have noted as spoken by the voice of Christ, since it is not fitting for human nature in any other case to say this. Indeed, anyone who examines all the words in the psalm closely can refer them to the Saviour.

Those of the circumcision will suppose that the seventeenth Psalm too is spoken by none other than David, because its title also seems to indicate this. We shall press them hard, since in his case they cannot make sense of the words: "You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will make me head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old." (Ps. 17:43) Over what nations could they show that David was made head? Who is this people whom he himself had not known before, which nevertheless served him, obeying him at the hearing of the ear? And who are those called foreign sons who lied to him, and who grew old and limped away from their paths? For us, however, nothing at all in the psalm will be a stumbling block. We take this prophecy too as spoken from the person of Christ, who was made head of the church gathered from the nations, and we see it plainly fulfilled. For we were, truly we were, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise (Eph. 2:12), and therefore unworthy of the knowledge of the Word of God. But now, having come to know God, or rather to be known by him, we who were once far off have been brought near (Gal. 4:9; Eph. 2:13). We have served him who formerly did not know us, and at the hearing of the ear we obeyed him, receiving the word of his new covenant, which he made with us. And wonderfully, after "a people whom I did not know served me" and our calling, he sets out what concerns the former synagogue with "foreign sons lied to me." This is equivalent to "I begot sons and raised them up, but they rejected me" (Isa. 1:2). These also grew old, limping away from their paths and refusing to receive the Christ of God. Rejected by them, he was made by the Father head of the nations that served him and obeyed him at the hearing of the ear, according to the prophecy that says elsewhere, "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner" (Ps. 117:22). I think too that his divinity and his descent among humankind are revealed in the first part of the psalm. Because these things are spoken more mysteriously, they would need more than a passing and cursory exposition. Such are the words from "And he bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet; and he mounted upon cherubim and flew, he flew upon the wings of the winds," and whatever else like them refers to the Word of God.

"There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world." (Ps. 18:3) We ask whose sound has gone out into all the earth, and whose words have reached the ends of the world, so that no words or speech remain among any people by whom their voices have not been heard. No one could point to any others than the holy apostles, in whom the prophecy has been fulfilled. Their teaching about Christ became renowned throughout everything under heaven when, during their lives, with the divine power working alongside them, they preached faith in the Christ of God throughout the whole world. After foretelling the preaching of his apostles, the text next teaches about Christ himself: that he set his tabernacle in the sun. The sun may be understood as the Godhead, in which he set his own abode and, as it were, his dwelling. Or it may be the body he took from the virgin, which was as it were a tabernacle for the divine power abiding in it. He also, "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run his course." He was like a bridegroom who rises from the Father's bosom for the sake of his bride, the church. He was like a brave and mighty giant who has fought out the contest set before him and conquered and overcome his adversaries. So he rejoiced at receiving his spouse and bride. His going forth was from the height of heaven, and again, his circuit reaches to its height. For no one else has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man (John 3:13). And again, according to the holy apostle, "He who descended is the same one who also ascended far above all the heavens" (Eph. 4:10). And "there is no one who will be hidden from his heat." Of this heat he himself also said, "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled?" (Luke 12:49) Anyone could easily work out the rest of the passage for himself along these lines.

The words in the nineteenth Psalm, "Now I know that the Lord has saved his anointed" (Ps. 19:6), point in some way to the salvation from death of our Saviour Jesus Christ. For it is also said to him, "We shall rejoice in your salvation" (v. 5). The whole passage could be applied to him if it were given the proper interpretation.

"O Lord, in your strength the king shall be glad" (Ps. 20) and what follows could, one might say, be referred to David. But "He asked life of you, and you gave him length of days for ever and ever" no longer fits David. His death is plainly evident, as is the span of his life, which was limited to not many years. So the king would be Christ, appointed by the Father to reign on Zion, the heavenly mountain. He asked the Father for life, not for himself, since he was himself the life, but for all who would believe in him. The Father granted him that all who believed in him could pass from death into eternal life, and into length of days with God, which last for ever and ever. The rest of the psalm, which is spoken about the king's glory and is no small matter, would suit Christ rather than David if it were given due explanation.

All who have soundly believed in Christ clearly agree that he spoke the opening of the psalm at hand at the time of his passion. It runs thus: "O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?" (Ps. 21) The cry on the cross, "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani," also showed this. But before we begin to take the prophecy in the psalm as referring to him, we shall ask those who boast of circumcision who the speaker of the psalm might be. He appears to be no ordinary person, for among other things he says: "For you are he who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother's breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God." He goes on: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." And again: "He did not turn his face away from me, and when I cried to him he heard me. From you comes my praise; in the great assembly I will confess you; I will pay my vows before those who fear him." Besides these, let them explain the other things in the psalm, if they can fit them to any of the holy men. Who has become such as the text foretold: "All who saw me sneered at me"? About whom did they speak with their lips and shake their heads, saying, "He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he delights in him"? Whom did many young bulls surround, and of what nature were they? Whom did dogs and fat bulls surround, opening their mouths against him like a lion ravening and roaring? Further, whom did the assembly of evildoers encompass, and encompass so as to dig his hands and feet, count all his bones, and divide his garments among themselves, casting lots for his clothing? Such are the things the speaker in the psalm says, and after suffering so much he adds: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." Let them resolve these things and at the same time explain the rest of the psalm. Let them explain especially the passage from "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him" down to "The generation to come shall be told of the Lord, and they shall proclaim his righteousness to a people yet to be born, whom the Lord has made." Let them show us the generation which did not yet exist at that time but was prophesied to come in the future. Let them show us the people which did not yet exist before but was foreseen to be born in later times. And let them say what they would say about the church gathered from all the nations through Jesus Christ our Saviour. Such great multitudes have come to know the God of all through Christ. In view of them, would they not admit that "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord" has been fulfilled, and "All the families of the nations shall worship before him"? It is time indeed for those willing to be fair-minded to admit that the prophecy has been fulfilled in none other than our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ alone. At his coming the turning of the nations began to take place, when the prophesied generation had arrived. The people that was to be born is foretold not only here but also in the hundred and first Psalm: "Let this be written for another generation, and the people that is being created shall praise the Lord" (Ps. 101). This is the people of which it was also said in the seventeenth Psalm: "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me" (Ps. 17). It was this our Saviour and Lord who took flesh and on its account was called a worm. He became the reproach of men and despised by the people, and "all who saw me sneered at me." This happened especially at the time of the passion, when the words of the prophecy came to fulfilment. Then those passing by blasphemed him and sneered, saying, "He saved others; let him save himself." Then too they spoke with their lips and shook their heads against him, saying in these very words, "He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he delights in him." The Gospels record that these very words were said about him at the passion. To him, then, and to him alone, it is fitting to say to the Father: "For you are he who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother's breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God." Besides this, the text teaches us that certain evil and bestial powers also worked the plot against him. Because of them he said, "Many young bulls surrounded me; fat bulls encompassed me." About the synagogue of the circumcision that rose up against him he says, "Many dogs encircled me; an assembly of evildoers encompassed me." These also dug not only his hands but also his feet. Or, in Aquila's version, "they disgraced": he says, "they disgraced my hands and my feet." This was truly fulfilled when they hung him on the wooden frame and pierced his hands and feet with nails. If anyone demands proof from scripture that Christ was foretold to endure even a cross, it is good to cite "they dug," and still more "they disgraced my hands and my feet," along with other evidence for it. Next to these words comes "They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." Aquila rendered this as "They will divide my garment among themselves, and over my clothing they will cast lots"; Symmachus as "They distributed my garments among themselves, and over my raiment they drew lots." This too was fulfilled at the passion. Those who crucified him took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and they also took the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be" (John 19:23). To this the evangelist adds, "that the scripture might be fulfilled: They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." So much for the prophecy. [?] Concerning this, the Hebrew contains "hosanna" [?]. Consistently with this, there follows in the psalm, just as in the Gospels, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" (Matt. 9:21). To me this seems to mean something like: "Save, then; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the Father and God of all."

"The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not set it aside: 'Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne.'" (Ps. 131:11) And again: "There I will make a horn spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. Your enemies I will clothe with shame, but upon him my holiness shall flourish." Here too God clearly gives David a promise with an oath concerning Christ, who would be born of his seed and would occupy his throne. These passages would need much examination, since Christ does not seem to have sat bodily on David's throne and in his kingdom. We shall set these questions aside, because it is not the business of the present treatise to spend our time on expounding the psalm, which is outside the purpose set before us. Yet in fairness one ought not to set aside what is clearly said about Christ in many places just because a single scripture cannot be applied to him in the bodily sense. Rather, those who follow true reason and stand by divine scripture itself should note how it speaks. Sometimes it prophesies that he will come poor, lowly and without honour, having neither form nor beauty; at other times it calls him a king held in honour. Some of these things can be fulfilled even bodily, others only according to the spiritual sense of scripture, and some we must expect to be fulfilled at his second coming. Nevertheless, our Lord was in fact called King of the Jews at his first coming, and not by chance. Pilate ordered that the words "This is the King of the Jews" be written on his cross in Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters.

The words here, "The righteous will wait for me until you reward me" (Ps. 141:7), seem to be spoken from the person of the Saviour. For whom else will the righteous wait until God rewards him, if not him? As is said somewhere about the righteous of old, though they were commended, they did not receive the promises, since God had foreseen something better for us, that they should not be made perfect apart from us (Heb. 11:39). The text clearly looks to him, because the psalm also foretells the events of his passion in agreement with the other prophecies. It is written: "I will pour out my supplication before him; I will declare my affliction before him. When my spirit was failing within me, you knew my paths. On the way by which I was walking they hid a snare for me." And again: "Rescue me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I" (Ps. 141:6). After this, praying also about his resurrection from the dead, he says: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name." To this he adds, "The righteous wait for me until you reward me" (Ps. 141:2). So all those righteous waited for Christ until the Father should reward him for having emptied himself and become obedient to him to the point of death (Phil. 2:8). And with what would he reward him but the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession (Ps. 2:8)? Then, when the full number of the nations has come in, all Israel too may be saved. Everything in the psalm could be applied to Christ, since it speaks of his incarnation, during which he was plotted against.

In the psalm at hand it is said, "Lord, bow the heavens and come down" (Ps. 143:5), and in the seventeenth, "And he bowed the heavens and came down" (Ps. 17). We noted the text there, and here we do the same: we have taken these words to be spoken about the Word of God. He bowed the heavens by emptying himself of the heavenly glory that was his in the form of God. In this way he came down to the lower parts of the earth, through the dispensation he undertook for the salvation of humankind. That is why, before the text just quoted, the psalm says in wonder: "Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him, or the son of man, that you take account of him?" (Ps. 143:3) The Word of God bowed the so-called heavens and came down for this purpose: that by becoming man he might be known to the human race, which had not known him before. He did not disdain the one who had become son of man or count him as nothing; that is, he did not disdain any rational soul made in the image of God. You will understand the rest of the psalm if you take it spiritually.

It also seemed right to note in passing the words "He who sends his oracle to the earth; his word will run swiftly" (Ps. 147). Here too scripture teaches that the Word of God has its own subsistence, being distinct from the Father who sends him. And see how there follows "his word will run swiftly." This too can be seen fulfilled after Christ's coming, since his teaching spread in a very short time. In not many years it prevailed throughout all the earth, even to the ends of the world.

We have gathered the words here, "Let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and they came into being, he commanded and they were created" (Ps. 148), among the testimonies about the Word who was God with God in the beginning. We have learned that the Word of God is also called his name, as one of the titles by which he is conceived. At any rate, after first saying "Praise the Lord," the Spirit goes on to urge one creature after another to praise his name after the Father, adding that "he spoke and they came into being, he commanded and they were created." The one who orders and commands would be the God and Father of all. The one who carries out the command would be the Word of God, serving the Father's will in fashioning created things. Note that the words "he spoke and they came into being, he commanded and they were created" also occur word for word in the thirty-second Psalm (Ps. 32). There, however, they are said about the earth and those who inhabit the world. Here they are said about the things in the heavens, the angels and powers said to be in the highest, and also the sun, moon and stars and everything listed with them. In these passages divine scripture teaches us what the holy apostle teaches: that all things were created through the Word, both in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities; all things have been created through him and in him; and without him not one thing came into being (Col. 1:16).

So much, then, for the passages from the Psalms. Since this part of the work has now reached a moderate and sufficient length, we shall make a fresh start and set out the selections from the remaining poetic books, and after them those from the prophets.

Having finished the selections from the Psalms, let us now, in this third treatise of the Prophetic Selections concerning Christ, which is the eighth book of the General Elementary Introduction, gather selections from the remaining books written in verse and from the prophecies that follow them. First, however, we note that the words of the prophets cannot be shown to be true unless faith in our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ is taken together with them. Nor can our faith in Christ be given firmer rational grounds unless the prophets of old confirm the proofs concerning him. So one might rightly blame both the Jews who have not received Christ and the heretics who reject the prophecies, for both end up in incoherent positions. The Jews accept the prophecies as coming from God, yet they make them false by leaving them unfulfilled, since they cannot accept that the prophecies came true in Christ. The heretics confess Christ, but they hold a faith in him that is incoherent and unproven, because they make no use of God's wonderful prophets, who bore witness to him beforehand. We, however, confirm the prophecies by the coming of Christ, and his coming by the prophecies, and so we set out the clear and firm truth with proofs that cannot be refuted. So much by way of preface; let us turn to the matter at hand.

The whole book of Proverbs seems to be spoken in the person of Wisdom. At times she sets out the moral life, and at times she voices the words of others. Sometimes she poses riddles, and at other times she teaches something about herself and instructs us about her own divine dignity. From these we shall select the passages that teach us that Wisdom is a divine living being, wholly virtuous in nature. She is the same as the second cause of all things after the first God, the same as God the Word, who was with God in the beginning, and the same as God's providence, which governs and orders all things and reaches even to the affairs of earth. She was created before all being and substance, and she is the beginning of the ways of the whole creation. The words spoken as if by Wisdom herself run as follows: "I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and knowledge, and I have called upon understanding. The fear of the Lord hates evil, insolence and arrogance and the ways of the wicked, and I have hated the crooked ways of evil men. Counsel and security are mine; I am understanding, and strength is mine. By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just. By me great men are made great. I love those who love me, and those who seek me will find favor. Riches and glory are mine, and great possessions and righteousness. It is better to have my fruit than gold and much precious stone, and my produce is better than choice silver. I walk in the ways of righteousness and go about in the midst of the paths of justice, so that I may give wealth to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things. If I declare to you what happens day by day, I will remember to recount what has been from of old. The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works. Before the age he established me, in the beginning, before he made the earth and before he made the depths, before the springs of the waters came forth, before the mountains were set in place; before all the hills he begets me. The Lord made the lands and the uninhabited places and the inhabited heights of the earth under heaven. When he prepared the heavens I was there with him, when he marked out his own throne upon the winds, when he made the clouds above strong and made the springs of the earth under heaven secure, when he set for the sea its boundary so that the waters would not pass beyond his command. When he made the foundations of the earth strong, I was beside him, setting things in order. I was the one in whom he delighted day by day, and I rejoiced before him at all times, when he rejoiced at having completed the world and rejoiced among the children of men" (Prov 8:12–31). These things Wisdom teaches about herself. But the holy Apostle teaches who she is, saying, "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24), and again, "who became for us wisdom from God" (1 Cor 1:30). So it is Christ who speaks the words quoted above. He is the Wisdom and Word of God, through whom all things came into being: "For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him" (John 1:1–3). And according to the Apostle, "in him all things were created, things in the heavens and things on earth, whether visible or invisible" (Col 1:16). Under one aspect he is called the Word of God, under another Life, and again Truth and the true Light, along with all the other names the divine Scriptures give him. In the same way he is also called Wisdom, since he serves the Father in the providence and ordering of the universe.

"In the light of the king's son is life, and those accepted by him are like a cloud of late rain" (Prov 16:15). In the light of what other king's son is there life, if not in the Word of God, who is the son of God, the King of all? For he is "the true light that enlightens every person coming into the world" (John 1:9). In this light there is life, according to the saying of the Gospel: "In him was life, and the life was the light of men" (John 1:4). Those accepted by him we take to be his apostles and disciples. They have become like a cloud of late rain at the end of days and at the close of the age. They have watered the land that was once desert and waterless, that is, the church of the Gentiles, with the spiritual rain of his godly teaching.

"These are the words of the man to those who believe in God, and I cease. For I am the most foolish of all men, and human understanding is not in me. But God has taught me wisdom, and I know the knowledge of holy things. Who has gone up to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the winds in his bosom? Who has wrapped up water in a garment? Who has taken hold of the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is the name of his children?" (Prov 30:1–4). Who else could the man saying these things be but our Lord, who became man? He calls himself foolish either because of our follies, which he took upon himself, or because of "the foolishness of the preaching" (1 Cor 1:21), which is wiser and stronger than human wisdom. Here he says, "For I am the most foolish of all men," and in Psalm 68, "You know my folly" (Ps 68:5). He also says, "human understanding is not in me," as if taking pride, as in a noble deed, in having none of the understanding of those men who have been compared to senseless beasts and made like them. Or he means those whose wisdom God made foolish, who think of nothing beyond earthly things, all that naturally belongs to flesh and matter. That is why it is said of them that they are wise in their generation: they seek earthly things alone and devise evil from their youth. So there was no human understanding at all in this man, but clearly a divine understanding beyond the human. That is why he adds, "But God has taught me wisdom, and I know the knowledge of holy things." Then he asks, "Who has gone up to heaven and come down?" In this way he rouses us to inquire into the one who teaches such great things about himself. The words that follow are also about him, but they need separate treatment. Now the divine Apostle, teaching us about him, says, "He who descended into the lower parts of the earth is the same one who ascended far above the heavens" (Eph 4:9–10). The Apostle puts his descent first and then adds his ascent, but this passage says that he ascended and afterward came down. For after his resurrection from the dead he said to Mary, "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17). After this he appeared to the disciples for forty days and ate with them. Clearly, then, he had gone up to the Father and come down again for the sake of the work of salvation he was carrying out. This is why it is also said, "Having ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts among men" (Eph 4:8). What are these gifts but the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which he brought down from heaven? For this reason Aquila's version of this verse reads, "Who has gone up to heaven and brought down?" He also took hold of the ends of the earth, so that "his word went out into all the earth, and his words to the ends of the world" (Ps 18:4). Whoever has been given the word of knowledge will know how to understand the rest of the passage. The passage urges us to ask what his name is, and the name of his children. To this we shall answer, having learned it from what actually happened, that his name is Jesus, which means "salvation of God." His kin according to the flesh gave him this name in obedience to Gabriel's message, and the angel also gave the reason for the name: "For he will save his people from their sins" (Matt 1:21). And what is the name of his children? He said to them, "Little children, I am with you only a little while longer" (John 13:33). Their name, and the name of their sons and grandsons and descendants after them in all the churches, can be nothing other than the blessed name Christian.

"Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take heed. For he will come out of the house of prisoners to reign, since even in his kingdom he became poor. I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second youth, who will rise up in his place. There is no end to all the people, to all who were before them, and those who come later will not rejoice in him. This too is vanity and a striving after wind" (Eccl 4:13–16). Christ, who is "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24), became poor for our sake though he was rich. So I think the words "Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king" are said about him. The king I take to be the devil, who has grown old in evil days. He is king over those whom he rules through the sin he works in them, but he is foolish because he lacks the virtuous understanding that comes from God. The good and wise youth came out of the house of prisoners, meaning either the earthly region or the regions of Hades, at his resurrection from the dead. Then the Father established him as king upon Zion, the heavenly mountain of God. And in his very kingdom he became poor. He "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped" (Phil 2:6), but humbled himself and came down from the highest glory for the sake of those who could not take in the riches of his wisdom. The second youth, who is said to rise up in his place, I take to be the Antichrist. With him, the text says, it saw all who live and walk under the sun. Who could these be but all who cling to what is called the vanity of vanities under the sun?

"This too I saw as wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me. There was a small city with few men in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built great siege-works against it. And he found in it a poor and wise man, and that man saved the city by his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man. And I said, 'Wisdom is better than might, yet the poor man's wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard'" (Eccl 9:13–16). Here too the one who wages war is called a king, and the one who saves the city he besieges is called a poor and wise man. In the preceding chapter it was said, "Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king." There we took the foolish king to be the devil, and the poor and wise one to be the Word of God, who emptied himself and became poor for our sake. That is why we have noted the present passage as well. We think the warlike king described here is none other than the foolish king spoken of there. Likewise, the one who saves the besieged city by his own wisdom here is none other than the poor and wise man there, whom we said was Christ. The small city is the earthly region, which is tiny compared with the whole cosmos. Those in it are few compared with the multitude of all rational beings, since all the nations are like a drop from a bucket. They were besieged by the kingdom of the devil, who surrounded the earthly region and its people on every side and built great siege-works against it: "the principalities, the powers, the world-rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness" (Eph 6:12). Christ redeemed them. No one else but the poor and wise man alone pulled down these siege-works. He is our Savior and Lord, who emptied himself and became poor for us in the riches of his mercy. Having pulled them down, he saved by his wisdom the small city and the few who are in it. On another interpretation, the small city may reasonably be taken to be the Church, whose members are few, since "narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, and few are those who travel it" (Matt 7:14). Those who see so great a work of salvation say, "Wisdom is better than might," meaning, clearly, the might of the enemies. The text also says, "no one remembered that poor man." It was God who remembered him through the prophets and announced beforehand his coming to dwell among men. But of those moved by the wisdom of the rulers of this age, not one ever remembered him. They could not even know the mystery hidden before the ages, the plan by which the Word of God would become man. It is also said that "the poor man's wisdom is despised," for God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. And further it says, "his words are not heard." Not everyone can hear the Savior's words, but only those who have ears to hear. For the gospel of Christ is veiled, though not to his disciples; it is veiled to those who are perishing.

The subject of the whole book is a bride's love for her bridegroom. She confesses that she has been wounded by love for him, and he in turn declares that she alone out of many is his perfect dove, set apart from those called queens, concubines and maidens. Those of the circumcision are convinced that this book too is one of the twenty-two divinely inspired scriptures they have accepted. Yet I do not know whether they could point to anything said in it that is worthy of divine inspiration, since they imagine nothing beyond the obvious meaning of the passages. But someone may be able to remove the veil that lies over this book too, to turn to the Lord, who is the Spirit, and with unveiled face to behold the glory of the Lord here as well, as in a mirror. Such a reader will see in it the mysteries of the spiritual bride, who is clearly the Church of Christ. He will see what is said about the perfect bridegroom of such a bride, and about the difference among his queens, concubines and maidens. He will see all the other more secret teachings hidden in the book. These have already been explained most fully in the commentaries of the most diligent interpreter of the divine Scriptures.

Among other things, Job says of the Lord: "He commands the sun, and it does not rise, and he sets a seal upon the stars. He alone stretched out the heavens and walks on the sea as on dry ground" (Job 9:7–8). And again: "he who is to subdue the great sea-monster" (Job 3:8). It is unworthy of a lofty idea of the God of the universe to suppose that he who fills all things walks on a sea, as though the sea could hold so great a magnitude [?]. It remains, then, to understand these words of the Word. By his power Joshua son of Nun, who was a type of him, spoke to the sun, and it stood still at Gibeon. And at the time of his passion the sun was darkened over all the earth, as if at some divine command. He is the one who stretched out the heavens. He is also the one who walked on the sea as on dry ground, when he had become man and performed his wonders, as the Gospels record. If one applies these passages wholly to the Word of God, it follows that one should apply to him not only the sayings we have quoted but everything Job says in this section. For he alone subdued the great sea-monster when he loosed the pangs of death and destroyed the truly great dragon, the devil. Long ago the devil, in his strength, swallowed the souls of men, like the sea-monster that swallowed Jonah. But afterward he was subdued by the one who wrestled him down, and he brought forth again those he had once swallowed, just as the beast gave Jonah back safe. In this was fulfilled the prophecy that says, "Death in his strength swallowed them up, and again God took away every tear from every face" (Isa 25:8). And we say this because of our Savior and Lord, who subdued the great sea-monster spoken of here.

The Lord, in his message to Job, recounts the works of his own providence and ordering of the world, saying: "Did you take clay from the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth with the power of speech? Did you take away the light from the ungodly and break the arms of the proud? Have you come to the source of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the deep? Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" (Job 38:14–17). The Lord says these things to Job about himself, as though no one but he alone could do such great things. For who took earth and formed a living creature, if not God, who took dust from the earth and formed man? At the same time we are taught here that he who formed man is the same one who descended into the lower parts of the earth, into what is called its heart. This, I take it, is what is here named the source of the sea. He is also the one who walked in the tracks of the sea. To him alone the gates of death were opened in fear, because it was impossible for death to hold him. The gatekeepers of Hades cowered at the sight of him, as they saw death's victory, its sting and its pangs being destroyed by him. Perhaps it was to these gatekeepers of the gates of death mentioned here that certain divine powers said, at the time of the passion and of our Savior's descent into Hades, "Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory will come in" (Ps 23:7). The gates are called everlasting, I take it, because from all ages they had been opened to no one else but to him alone. He rescued and brought to life even those whom death had swallowed long ago. It is of him that this passage says, "Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" And Psalm 106 says, "For he shattered gates of bronze" (Ps 106:16), which I think are none other than the gates of death, "and broke bars of iron," clearly the bars of those same gates. We have taken these things as referring to Christ, since they fit no one else but him. He is the one to whom the Father has given all judgment, so that he takes away the light from the ungodly and breaks the arms of the proud. But suppose someone thinks these things are said of the God of the universe. Let him consider whether it is reverent to think so. The Lord says, "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Heaven is his throne, and the earth is the footstool of his feet. Would this God, who encompasses all things, say, or even think, that he had walked in the tracks of the sea? What would be remarkable, or worthy of the unbegotten nature, in boasting as of something great that the gates of death had been opened to him? Would it befit the God of the universe to recount about himself, as something great and marvelous, that the gatekeepers of Hades [?] cowered when they saw him? I do not think these things are said of him. But they can be applied reverently and without forcing to the Word of God, our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ. He became man, endured death, and rose from the dead with divine power and with the authority given him by the Father.

Again, in his message to Job, the Lord speaks of the dragon and says, "Are you not afraid? For he has been made ready for me" (Job 41:2). The dragon he speaks of is none other than the devil. Consider, then, whether it is fitting to suppose that the God of the universe says this. It would better fit our Lord and Savior. For him alone the devil has been made ready, the devil whom no one else had conquered and who had overpowered almost everyone. The Word of God alone, stronger than all, subdued him, according to the words "he who is to subdue the great sea-monster." Having subdued him, he urges his disciples to take courage, saying, "Take courage; I have conquered the world" (John 16:33).
So much for the passages from the books in verse that come after the Psalms. It remains to gather passages from the prophetic writings, beginning with those from the Twelve Prophets.

"For I am like a panther to Ephraim, and like a lion to the house of Judah" (Hosea 5:14). Since in another place of the same prophet the Lord also says of himself, "And I will be like a panther" (Hosea 13:7), it is necessary to look at what is recorded about this animal. These things should be cited from the first book of Didymus's *Physics*: "The panther is an animal that is not only beautiful in body, spangled as if with stars, but also, because it naturally has a sweet breath, surpasses even the spices of India in fragrance. Until it is hungry, it stays in its den, content to keep at home. But when it wants to take food, it comes out and simply walks about. The other beasts, captivated by the fragrance of its body, follow it as if enchanted. Then, glancing sideways, it looks around for a beast that suits it to catch, leaps on it, and has it."

Such, then, is the nature of this animal. How these things might be applied to the power of the divine Word and to the fragrance that breathes forth from it would take too long to explain now. The passage should be cited against those of the circumcision who, by way of slander and abuse, claim that our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was born of Panther. Perhaps they have received this from some tradition that signified something more mystical, but they do not grasp its meaning, because they pay no attention to the wording of the prophecy before us, in which the Lord himself calls himself a panther.

"And destruction will rise up among your people, and all the walled places of your temple will be gone. As the ruler Shalman from the house of Jeroboam, in the days of war, dashed the mother to the ground upon her children, so will they do to you, house of Israel, because of your wickedness" (Hos 10:14). "For Israel is a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called back his children. As I called them, so they went away from my presence" (Hos 11:1). In place of "and out of Egypt I called back his children," Aquila, following the Hebrew, rendered, "Out of Egypt I called my son." We have had to note this passage, since Matthew sets out the prophecy word for word and says that it was fulfilled with great precision in our Saviour: Joseph, having been warned, took Mary and her son and returned from Egypt to the land of Israel (Matt 2:21). Consider, then, Aquila's version too, which reads, "At dawn the king of Israel was silenced, for Israel is a boy and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son." It plainly shows the casting off of the kingdom of Israel, which lasted until the appearing of our Saviour and from that moment was cast off and silenced. That is why it says, "At dawn the king of Israel was silenced": the prophecy calls "dawn" the appearing, the first rising of the divine Word upon all people at that time.
