The words "the king of Israel was silenced" can also be a prediction about Herod, on account of the deception he suffered at the hands of the magi at the birth of our Saviour. These things happened because of the Father's love for his own child, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is called Israel here as in other prophecies. At the proper time the Father arranged for him to depart to Egypt together with Joseph and his mother, when need required that the king who was plotting against him, clearly Herod, should be silenced; and again, once Herod had died, he called him back, in accordance with the prophecy before us. But if anyone refers these things to the Jewish people, saying that they were spoken about the people of Israel of the circumcision, let him attend to the sequence of the passage. For it says these things after first saying, as if to Jerusalem herself, "And destruction will rise up among your people, and all your walled places will be gone"; and that what such a ruler suffered in the war that came upon him, in which they dashed the mother to the ground upon her children, "I will do the like to you yourselves because of your wickedness, O house of Israel." And they were indeed cast off together with their king, and suffered all these things. Then: "because," it says, "Israel is a boy and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son." Let whoever wishes show what coherence the phrase has on that reading. Rather, just as Christ is called Jacob and Israel in countless other prophecies, so too here. "Since, then," he says, "this one became obedient to me, took the form of a servant, and became a child beloved by me, accomplishing all my will, therefore I called him back, as a true and beloved son, from the spiritual Egypt into which he had come down by becoming man; but you, to whom the word is addressed, I will hand over, together with your kingdom, to ruin and destruction." So much for the prophecy. But it is plain how, from the times of our Saviour, when Jerusalem was besieged, the kingdom of the Jews, which had stood until then, was destroyed and cast off completely, so that this prophecy too has been fulfilled along with the others.

"I will not abandon Ephraim to be blotted out; for I am God and not man, the Holy One among you, and I will not enter into a city. I will walk after the Lord" (Hos 11:9). The same one who said, "For I am God," goes on to say, "I will walk after the Lord." Who else could be the God who walks after the Lord than the Word of God, who follows the Father's will? He also teaches that we should not think that through the incarnation he became a mere man, like one of the righteous and holy men of old. He says that he will not enter a city, showing that he did not live the common, human way of life. He teaches his disciples to do the same, saying, "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans" (Matt 10:5).

"I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire, and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord" (Amos 4:11). Here too the Lord himself says, as though about another, "as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah." In Genesis as well the divine scripture has kept the two persons, saying, "And the Lord rained sulphur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord" (Gen 19:24). From these the orthodoxy of the church's faith concerning the Father and the Son is made manifest.

"Prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, he who makes the thunder firm and creates the wind, and announces his anointed to humankind, who makes the dawn and the mist and treads upon the high places of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name" (Amos 4:12). These words too clearly prophesy Christ's coming to dwell among humankind; but each phrase could be explained more precisely at leisure.

"The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord God to Idumea: I have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent out a message to the nations" (Obad 1). Since here too the Lord God heard a report from the Lord, we have reasonably noted the passage.

In the present book we have found no prophecy dealing specifically with Christ. But when the generation that asked the Saviour for a sign was told that no sign would be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet, he added, "For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so too will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights" (Matt 12:40). For this reason we have had to note this scripture too among the testimonies about Christ.

"For behold, the Lord, the Lord, is coming forth from his place; he will come down and tread upon the heights of the earth, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire" (Mic 1:3). We have understood these words to be spoken about the second coming of Christ.

"Hear these things, you leaders of the house of Jacob and you who remain of the house of Israel, who abhor justice and twist everything that is straight, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with injustice. Her leaders judged for bribes, her priests gave answers for hire, and her prophets divined for silver; and they leaned on the Lord, saying, 'Is not the Lord among us? No evil will come upon us.' Therefore, because of you, Zion will be ploughed like a field, Jerusalem will become like a watchman's hut in an orchard, and the mountain of the house a wooded grove. And in the last of days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, set ready on the tops of the mountains, and it will be lifted high above the hills; and peoples will come to it, and many nations will go to it and say, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and they will show us his way, and we will walk in his paths.' For out of Zion will go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he will judge between many peoples and rebuke a strong people far and wide; and they will beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles; and nation will no longer lift sword against nation, and they will no longer learn to make war" (Mic 3:9). The word has said that because of the impieties of the Jewish people Mount Zion will be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem, formerly regarded as the holy city, will be like a watchman's hut in an orchard. Next it prophesies about another mountain of the Lord, which already existed at the time of the prophecy but was not visible to ordinary people, since it would appear in the last of days and be lifted high above the hills and the mountains. And to this new mountain, the word foretells, there will come no longer that old Israel, but peoples and many nations, saying, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord"; and not only to the mountain of the Lord, but also to the house of the God of Jacob, which is clearly a different one from the one in Jerusalem, for a little earlier he had said that Jerusalem would be made desolate and become like a watchman's hut in an orchard. Consistently with the prophecy that Mount Zion and Jerusalem would be made desolate and others would appear in their place, it is said that another law, different from the one given by Moses from Mount Horeb, will go forth from the new mountain, which is itself also called Zion, by the same name as the former one. Further, the word of the Lord, together with the new law, is said to go forth from the new Jerusalem, which he called above the house of the God of Jacob. This word, going forth to all the nations, is foretold to judge between many peoples and to rebuke a strong people, and to benefit so greatly by its judgement and rebuke those it rebukes that they would change from their former savage [?] and warlike condition to a calm and peaceful [?]. So much for the prophecy. One may consider whether [?] the coming of our Saviour, because of those who built [?] with the blood of the prophets and of Christ himself and of [his apostles] [?], whom the [people] of the Jews killed in Jerusalem itself [?], because of those who [?] the other things contained in the prophecy [?] Mount Zion, as never at any other time [?] Jerusalem was besieged. After their desolation, the [?] and the heavenly Mount Zion of God, of which they were [?] shadow, types and patterns, has been revealed to all who have come to [?] God through Christ.

"And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are least to be among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who will be ruler in Israel; and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity" (Mic 5:2). [?] These words present proofs about Christ: one [against] the error of Marcion and the other heretics [?], the other [against that] of Artemon and the Samosatene [?] and of those Ebionites who [?] have supposed that he did not exist before the incarnation. For those who do not confess him [?] God, the prophetic word clearly refutes [?], [saying] that his goings forth are from the beginning and from the days of eternity [?]. To those led astray by Marcion and the other [heresies] [?], who do not confess his [?] birth, nor that he was known by the [?] of the Creator [?], one must set forth the [place] of his birth that was prophesied [?], [pointed out] clearly to this day even by the local inhabitants [?], as from tradition, the place in Bethlehem where [he] was born [?], and [attested] by the holy evangelists themselves [?]. The passage must also be put to the Jews [?] to show who the one prophesied might be [?], as [the prophecy remains] unfulfilled according to them; plainly the divine prediction is then also shown to be false [?]. Yet the saving and gospel word of Christ was established as ruler of the spiritual Israel, properly of the Jew who is one inwardly, and of every virtuous and discerning soul understood as Israel [?].

"Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my resurrection as a witness; for my judgement is for gatherings of nations, to receive kings" (Zeph 3:8). I think these words too indicate the resurrection of Christ from the dead, after which, it is prophesied, the congregations of the church from the Gentiles will be established everywhere. Perhaps [?] of his second coming and of the [?] of all [?] the things in this passage might also be taken.

[?] Almighty: "After glory he has sent me to the [nations] that plundered you" (Zech 2:8). Then shortly after he adds, "[You will know] that the Lord Almighty has sent me." The one who says [?] me is the Lord Almighty; likewise the one who sends [?], being [?] of the one sent, is named Lord Almighty [?]. Rightly, then, [we have noted] the passage among those concerning the Father and the Son [?], because the [?] of God is also Lord Almighty, just as he was also called God through the prophets.

"[?] and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many [?] will flee to the Lord on that day, and they will be [?] people, and they will dwell in your midst, and you will know that [?] Almighty has sent me to you" (Zech 2:10). And who [?] is the one who says this and confesses that he was sent by the Almighty, if not the Word of God, sent by the Father for the salvation of the human race? He [?] the foregoing [?] the heavenly Zion, of which the mountain on earth was [?] a pattern; and he also addresses the church from the nations, [?] to her the calling of those who would be saved through him [?] and ruled by him within her.

"And [?] Jesus the high priest standing before [?] of the Lord, and the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him" (Zech 3:1). And a little later: "And he said to those standing before [?], saying, 'Take the filthy garments off him.' And he said, 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities; and clothe [?] a full-length robe, and put a clean turban on his head.'" And again a little later it is said to him: "Hear now, [?] the high priest, you and your companions who sit before you; for they are men who watch for portents; for behold, I am bringing my servant the Dayspring" (Zech 6:9). And again, after other things: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying, 'Take what is from the captivity, from the rulers'" (Zech 6:11). And shortly after: "And you will take silver and make crowns, and set them on the head of Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest, and say to him, 'Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, a man whose name is Dayspring, and from beneath him he will spring up, and he will build the house of the Lord, and he will receive virtue, and he will sit and rule upon his throne, and the priest will be at his right hand, and there will be a counsel of peace between them both. And the crown will be for those who endure'" (Heb 4:14). Since the wonderful apostle named our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, the one in the prophecy, honoured with the same name and the same rank, might reasonably be referred to him [?]; and in this way [?] being called. This one, then, the Lord showed to the prophet [?] clothed in filthy garments, hinting at our Saviour's descent into our captivity, in which [he came] [?] to proclaim release to captives; for since he took our sins upon himself, he wore filthy garments taken from us. The Father commands him to take these off and to put on the divine garments of the Godhead, worthy of the heavenly high priesthood. These things presumably also happened typologically in history to [?] the Jesus of that time; and then the word, beginning afresh, says to the man Jesus himself and to the [?] portent-watchers with him (by whom I think are meant those deemed worthy of the spiritual [?]): "Behold, I am bringing [?] the Dayspring." And going further on, after placing the crowns on the head of Jesus himself, he adds, saying: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, a man, Dayspring is his name; and from beneath [?] he will spring up and will build the house of the Lord, and the [?]." These words too might be referred to Christ, given the proper exposition. But also to those of the circumcision [?] to set forth, since they could not point to any prophet at all raised up from the [?] kingdom of the Persians [?] and from the times of the prophecy [?], let alone John and our Lord Jesus Christ. So it is time for them to say who the one prophesied is. [?] And if they say that these things refer to Jesus son of Jozadak, it must be shown to them that what is said does not fit him in any way. For when was his name called Dayspring? And why is he deemed worthy of this title? And how will the words "and he will sit and rule upon his throne" fit him? Above all, how will "and the priest will be at his right hand" fit him? For if he himself was the high priest, who would be the one at his right hand, a priest other than him? And the text clearly teaches that the one called Dayspring is someone other than him; for to that same [?] and those around him the word says: "Hear now, Jesus the high priest, you and your companions; behold, I am bringing my servant the Dayspring." If, then, these things were said to him, how could there still be room to think that "Behold, a man, Dayspring [is his name]" [?] is said about him? Clearly, then, these words present two persons: one to whom the Deity speaks, and another about whom it prophesies; and the latter could be referred beyond dispute to Christ, the true son of [?], which is interpreted "righteousness of Iao." This would be the Father [?], who places the crowns of victory on Christ [?] and calls [?] because of the teaching that dawned upon humankind [?]; and the first and great high [priest] [?], his firstborn Word, being God and Lord of [?], but priest of the first and unbegotten Godhead. [?] he says that he is [?] of the man whom he assumed, who is also called [?] great high priest because of his union with the only-begotten of God. The things in this passage need much explanation, but these remarks are enough for the present subject.

"Rejoice [?], daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, [your king] [?] is coming to you, righteous and saving; he is gentle and [mounted] [?] on a beast of burden and a young colt. And he will utterly destroy chariots from Ephraim and horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be utterly destroyed; and abundance and peace from the nations; and he will rule from sea [to sea], and from rivers to the ends of the earth" (Zech 9:9). The daughter of Zion whom the word commands to rejoice is every soul that dwells in the spiritual and heavenly Zion, or else the church from the nations, established on earth through Christ. Likewise, again, the daughter of Jerusalem is she who bears kinship with the heavenly Jerusalem, such as was the soul of Paul, who says, "But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother" (Gal 4:26). To such souls, then, the word proclaims in advance that the Christ of God will come, mounted on a beast of burden and a young colt, by which is meant the human nature that he assumed when he came. With it he destroyed every warlike power from every soul that belongs to the church and is able to bear holy fruit; for Ephraim is taken to mean fruitfulness, and Jerusalem in the Greek language means "vision of peace." And having destroyed the evil demons that formerly ruled over humanity, he brought countless multitudes from all the nations once subject to them under the pious yoke of his teaching. So much for the spiritual sense. But literally too, Christ, having become man and fulfilling in bodily fashion the prophecies about himself, brought this one to completion as well, when, according to the evangelist, he said to his disciples, "Go into the village opposite, and you will find a donkey tied, and a colt; untie her and bring her; and if anyone says to you, 'What are you doing?' say, 'The Lord has need of them.' And they went and did as he had commanded them" (Matt 21:2). This being so, the passages must be set before those who imagine, in a merely bodily and Jewish way, that the foregoing will happen at Christ's coming. And it must be shown how at our Saviour's coming the prophecy that says, "And he will utterly destroy chariots from Ephraim and horse from Jerusalem," was also fulfilled [?] in bodily fashion along with the others. At any rate, the divine and heavenly power of Christ, by an ineffable working, after the [?] plot against him, utterly destroyed Jerusalem itself together with the [?], in which [?] with the military force that was there. Then [?] the people in it, often called Ephraim [?] commandment; multiplying horses in Jerusalem and chariots [?] for the battle lines in wars [?] horses that had become [?]; like senseless beasts [?], all of whom the coming of our Saviour plainly destroyed [?]. At any rate, after the saving coming, when those had been destroyed, [?] the multitude from all the nations received the [?] in their souls [?]; God having ruled and [?] the whole world, according to the [?] prophecy of the divine word.

"And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and in [his] name [?] they will boast, says the Lord" (Zech 10:12). Again the Lord, the Word of God, promises to strengthen the worthy in the Lord their God, by which he means his own God and Father. Therefore let this passage too be noted among those concerning the Father and the Son.

"And the Canaanites will know the sheep that are kept for me, for it is the word of the Lord. And I will say to them, If it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or else refuse. And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And they cast them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace. And I cast away the second rod [?] to dissolve the covenant between Judah and Israel." Zech. 11:11. For what is there of the things [?] concerning our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ that was not foreknown and foretold by the holy prophets of God? [?] For his birth from a virgin, and the [?] of his birth [?] and the root from which he was born according to the flesh; and the [?] wonders worked by him when he came among us [?] were thought worthy to be recorded by the divine Spirit through the prophets of old. Above all, they foretold both his death and the manner of it, not leaving out [?] even the scourgings and the spitting, the blows and the insults that he endured. They even pointed out the one who betrayed him to those plotting against him, one of his own disciples. Indeed, the divine Spirit publicly branded him by name through Jeremiah, saying, "The sin of Judas is written with a pen of iron, with a point of diamond." Jer. 17:1. You would find these words in the Hebrew itself and in the other translators, though not in the Seventy; and in various Psalms too you could learn what is revealed about him. And now no less, in the present passage, divine Scripture clearly foretells even the number of the pieces of silver for which Judas betrayed his teacher to those plotting against him. The present words might be spoken in the person of Christ, as though concerning those who plotted against him, whom elsewhere the word of prophecy calls "rulers of Sodom" and "people of Gomorrah" (Isa. 1:10), but here names Canaanites because they had become like the Canaanites. So, having said, "And the Canaanites will know," the prophecy goes on to teach us whom it means, and says, "the sheep that are kept for me." And what were these sheep, formerly kept for the Lord, if not the people of the circumcision? Having now called them Canaanites, the word continues as in the person of Christ: "And I will say to them" what is written there. This he might well say to those who plotted against him, as though asking them for wages in return for the benefits he had done them, that is, for faith in him and a life in keeping with it; for that is how I understand "Give me my wages." But they, as he says of them elsewhere ("In return for my love they slandered me, but I prayed; and they repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love" Ps. 108:4), weighed out thirty pieces of silver and handed them to the traitor, as though in their most impious judgment they valued him at that price. But since the fire will test what sort of work each one has done, the Lord for this reason commands that they be cast into the furnace, that is, into the fire of judgment and of punishment. And whom does he mean, if not those who plotted against him? "And consider," he says, "whether it is approved," meaning clearly what they did against him. He says that they will be tested in the fire, just as the Lord himself was tested on their behalf through his coming in the flesh and his passion; for indeed it was first and foremost for the salvation of the lost sheep of the house of Israel that he became man and suffered. Next, signifying their rejection after the passion of our Saviour, the word says, "And I cast away the second rod." To teach what this rod is, it adds "the measuring line," of which it is said, "Israel is the line of his inheritance." It makes this still clearer by adding, "to dissolve" God's former covenant, the one "between Judah and Israel." And this is plainly shown to have been abolished from the times of our Saviour, since all the worship prescribed by the law has been destroyed from then until now.

"Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty. Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the shepherds." Zech. 13:7. The evangelist took from here the words "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered" (Matt. 26:31) and taught that they were fulfilled at the time of the saving passion, when the disciples deserted him and were scattered. For this reason we too have noted the passage; but since it needs much examination, we shall put it off to a suitable occasion.

"And the Lord will go forth and fight against those nations, as on a day of battle; and the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him." Zech. 14:3, 5. We have noted these words too, supposing them to be spoken of the second coming of Christ.

"I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty; but you profane it." Mal. 1:10. Just as in the divine Scriptures the Word of the God of all is called his hand, his right hand, his arm and his power, so the same Word is also called the name of God. That this divine name has been glorified among the nations, as it were from the rising of the sun to its setting, is plain to everyone from those everywhere who bear the name of Christ. In every place they offer to God, through the true High Priest, spiritual incense and the pure, bloodless and rational sacrifice of prayer. And since these worship him in this way, God says that he will turn away from the bodily sacrifices of the former people. And it is clear that after the coming of Christ the prophecy has been fulfilled in both respects: in the rejection of the former people, when, as Daniel foretold, sacrifice and libation were taken away from them, and in the turning of the nations to the God of all.

"My covenant of life and peace was with him, and I gave him to fear me with fear and to stand in awe before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips; he walked with me in peace and uprightness, and turned many away from wrongdoing. For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty." Mal. 2:5. We have set these words out too, supposing them to belong among the testimonies concerning Christ. For the covenant of life and peace was with him; and the spirit of fear, together with the other spirits, rested upon him, according to the saying in Isaiah, "and the spirit of the fear of God will fill him" (Isa. 11:3). This law of truth, and not the law of types, was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips; for, as Isaiah says, "he committed no sin, nor was deceit found on his lips." Being one with the Father's power, he walked with him in peace and uprightness, bringing to conversion many of those who formerly did not know God. And since he is High Priest and guards the knowledge of all things, those who care for the knowledge that comes from him have sought, and will seek, the divine law from him. For he is the Messenger of great counsel, who serves and announces the Father's will to every created being.

"Behold, I send out my messenger, and he will survey the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight. Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty. And who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears? For he comes in like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap; and he will sit refining and purifying as silver and gold." Mal. 3:1. These words too prophesy the second coming of Christ, when [?], sent out by the God and Father of all, the Christ of God himself, who is here called the messenger of the covenant, will survey the way before the Father's face: that is, he will make ready and prepare beforehand the souls of men for the Father's kingdom. Then, when he has built the spiritual temple, that is, the church, out of rational and living stones, the Lord and God the Word himself will come, together with the messenger of the covenant himself, to the temple just described. Then, as though announcing beforehand his second coming, the Word says as if to sinners, "Behold, the Lord Almighty comes; and who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears?" and what follows. We must pay careful attention to these words, since they are spoken by the Lord Almighty himself as though about another. And we must ask those of the circumcision whom they could possibly say is the lord indicated here, and the messenger of the covenant with him, of whom the Lord Almighty says, "Behold, he comes," and the rest. In our view, these words proclaim the second coming of Christ. Being the Word of God, he will come and enter into the soul of each person, judging each for what he has done in his life, washing out and refining in fire, as gold is refined, the ruling faculty of every soul, and purifying it. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son, according to the word that says in the Psalms as well, "O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, to judge your people in righteousness, and your poor with justice" (Ps. 71:1). There the Godhead, God the Word himself, is called the king, and the man whom he assumed is called the king's son.

"And for those who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings." Mal. 4:2. The sun of righteousness is "the true light that enlightens every man coming into the world" (John 1:9). It is said to rise only for those who fear the name of his Father. For those who are not such, he threatens that it will set, according to the words spoken in one of the prophets: "And the sun will set upon the prophets who lead my people astray" (Mic. 3:5–6).

So much, then, for the passages from the twelve prophets. But since we intend to collect the passages from Isaiah in a separate work, because there are so many of them, let us now move on and examine those from the remaining major prophets.

"O Lord, make it known to me, and I shall know; then I saw their practices. But I was like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, and I did not know. They devised plans against me, saying, 'Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more.'" (Jer. 11:18) Our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, according to the prophecy in Isaiah, "was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer" (Isa. 53:7); and according to the passage before us, "like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, I did not know." His suffering on the cross can also be indicated by the words "Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us wipe him out from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more," which are spoken in the person of those who plotted against him. For if his body was bread, as he himself teaches his disciples when he says, "Take, eat; this is my body" (Matt. 26:27), and if this was what was exposed to shame on the wood of the cross, then the words "Come, let us put wood into his bread" may fittingly be said about him. And even if the passage admits of a deeper interpretation, what has been said here does nothing to hinder it.

"I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me; therefore I have hated her. Is not my inheritance to me a hyena's den, or a den all around her? Go, gather all the beasts of the field, and let them come to devour her. Many shepherds have ruined my vineyard, they have defiled my portion, they have turned my desirable portion into a trackless wilderness; it has become a desolation of destruction. Because of me the whole land has been utterly laid waste, because there is no one who takes it to heart." (Jer. 12:7) This too seems to be the voice of our Lord and Savior. He says "I have forsaken my house" about the temple in Jerusalem, and "I have abandoned my inheritance" about the former synagogue, which had once been his portion and the measured lot of his inheritance. This accords with the words "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing! Look, your house is left to you desolate" (Luke 13:34). And the same one who said, "No one takes my soul from me; I have authority to lay it down" (John 10:18), also says, "I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies." To him the former inheritance became like a lion in the forest, and she raised her voice against him when, having handed him over to Pilate, they stood there accusing him and all but shouting, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" And he says, "Therefore I have hated her," because of her works, which deserved hatred, and because she showed him nothing that deserved love. What follows, and especially the words "Because of me the whole land has been utterly laid waste," seems to point to the complete capture and captivity of the former people, which came about on account of the Savior after his passion, and to the utter desolation of Jerusalem.

"O Lord, my strength, my help, and my refuge in the day of troubles, to you the nations will come from the end of the earth and say, 'How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them!' Will a man make gods for himself? Yet they are not gods. Therefore, behold, at this time I will show them my hand and make known to them my power, and they shall know that I am the Lord. ※ The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the breast of their heart." (Jer. 16:19) Having prophesied about those who through Christ have come to know the God of the universe, the word next adds something about the sin of the Jewish people against the Savior, and in the words set out with asterisks it signifies that this sin would be indelible. These words could also be applied to Judas the traitor, as one foreknown and foretold even by name by the divine Spirit.

"Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous Dawn, and a king shall reign and shall understand, and shall execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. In his days Judah too shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence; and this is the name by which the Lord will call them: Josedek among the prophets. On that day, said the Lord, I will break the yoke from their neck and burst their bonds, and they shall no longer serve strangers, but shall serve the Lord their God; and I will raise up for them David their king." (Jer. 30:8) Similar things are said in another passage of the same prophet, in these words: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for you my good word which I spoke to the house of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Dawn to rise for David." (Jer. 33:14; 40:14 Breiting.) To this it next adds: "For thus says the Lord: There shall not be cut off from David a man sitting on the throne of the house of Israel; and from the priests, the Levites, there shall not be cut off a man before my face offering whole burnt offerings, sacrificing sacrifices, and making offerings all the days." (Jer. 33[40]:17) And again: "Thus says the Lord: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that there are no day and night in their season, then my covenant with David my servant may also be broken, so that he has no son reigning on his throne, and my covenant with the Levites, the priests who minister to me. As the host of heaven cannot be numbered, nor the sand of the sea measured, so will I multiply the seed of David my servant and the Levites who minister to me." (Jer. 33[40]:20) And once more, shortly afterward, it is said: "Thus says the Lord: If I have not established my covenant with day and night, and the ordinances of heaven and earth, then I will also reject the seed of Jacob and of David my servant, so as not to take a ruler from his seed." (Jer. 33[40]:25) What, then, is the Dawn that the Lord will raise up for David? It is the divine Word, of whom it is also said elsewhere, "Behold a man whose name is Dawn." He is prophesied to reign, to understand, and to execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. He it is who will make light dawn for the souls sitting in darkness, in keeping with his heavenly kingdom. And when, as the apostle says, the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Rom. 11:25), and all the true Israel, together with the spiritual Judah, is saved, the Lord will also call them by name, those whom he judges worthy, by the name "Josedekin," which is interpreted "the righteous of God." On that day, after God has freed those just mentioned from their captivity under the devil, so that they no longer serve him but serve the Lord their God alone, God promises to raise up David as king for them. This is none other than our Savior, born of the seed of David, whom the Scriptures in various places have also called by this name. So in the prophecy "David" means the human being understood in our Savior, while the righteous Dawn is the Godhead at work in him, which elsewhere is called "the sun of righteousness"; for the true light that enlightens every man coming into the world (John 1:9) is likewise none other than he. The prophecy says, then, that there shall never be cut off for God a man who leads and presides over his church, which is the spiritual house of Israel. Nor, the word prophesies, will there ever fail priests of God in the spiritual sense, who offer the spiritual incense and the fragrant, bloodless, and pure sacrifice made up of good works and words. For if we do not take these things in this way, it is time to convict the prophecies of falsehood, since neither the throne of David in a bodily sense nor the priestly service of the types still stands today. The kings of David's seed failed from the very times of Jeremiah, and the Levitical and priestly service not long after the coming of our Savior; from that time to this the Jews are not even allowed to set foot in Jerusalem. And if those of the circumcision should claim that the seed of David has not failed, because of the man they call the patriarch, they must be refuted, since they cannot show him sitting on the throne of David, reigning on his throne, and ruling over Israel. For these are the things the prophecy says will never fail, and they have plainly failed since the times of the captivity: from then on not a single person of the seed of David can be shown to have reigned over Israel. And what would they say about the priesthood, which at the present time has clearly been abolished, though the prophecy foretells that it will never be cut off?

"Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach each his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the Lord,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord; for I will be merciful to their iniquities and will remember their sins no more." (Jer. 31:31) The Lord clearly foretells that in the days to come he will make a new covenant. It is new because it has nothing like the old one, which we have learned was given through Moses in the wilderness. What would those of the circumcision say to this? They try to look at the prophecies in their plain sense, and they prefer to show them unfulfilled rather than yield to the truth by accepting the new covenant of our Savior's gospel. At its coming the first covenant was made old, and it began to come to an end from the time when Christ came and fulfilled the law and the prophecies about himself. So the Lord says that days will come in which he will make the new covenant, that is, the one written within the books of the Gospels. Next the same Lord adds that after those days he will write his own laws in the very minds of those who accept the new covenant, so that they will be a people to God and he will be God to them. They will not come to know the Lord through human teaching at all, but will be as though self-taught, or rather taught by God. One can see this, too, being fulfilled at the present time. One could also see how the new covenant and the laws of the Lord have been written on the minds and hearts of those who through Christ have believed in God, by observing among us a multitude of entirely unlettered men who display a virtuous and philosophic way of life, such as is not easily found among those who have trained in scholarship and pride themselves on their study of the Scriptures.

"The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in their corruptions, of whom we said, 'In his shadow we shall live among the nations.'" (Lam. 4:20) Here too the divine Spirit names Christ explicitly and foretells the Jews' plot against him in the words "he was taken in their corruptions." And the prophets foresaw in the spirit that they themselves would live under his shelter and shadow, and would live among the nations that were going to believe in Christ and through him to accept the writings of the prophets.

"Who has gone up into heaven and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds? Who has crossed over the sea and found her, and will bring her back for choice gold? There is no one who knows her way, nor anyone who ponders her path. But he who knows all things knows her; he found her out by his understanding. He who prepared the earth for all time filled it with four-footed creatures. He sends forth the light, and it goes; he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling. The stars shone in their watches and rejoiced; he called them, and they said, 'Here we are'; they shone with gladness for him who made them. This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men." (Bar. 3:29) "Who has gone up into heaven," it says, "and taken her, and brought her down," and so on. We are taught by the holy apostle that Jesus Christ, who descended, is the very one who also ascended far above all the heavens (Eph. 4:10). He received the gift of the Holy Spirit and brought it down and poured it out on the souls of those who accepted it. This is why it is said in the Psalms, "You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men" (Ps. 67:18). Next in the scripture before us the word says, "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him." Who is this, if not the one who ascended into heaven and descended? For the answer to the question "Who has gone up into heaven?" is "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him." What is said next shows this more clearly: "Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men." Clearly, then, beside this one, the Word of God, none of those who have received the title "god" as something acquired shall be reckoned. "Afterward," it says, "he was seen on earth": that is, clearly, after he had given the whole way of the promise through the law and the prophets. For "he found out," it says, "the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved"; then, after this, he was seen on earth and lived among men.

"Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will judge between the strong sheep and the weak sheep. You shoved with side and shoulder and butted with your horns; you crushed all that was failing. And I will save my sheep, and they shall no longer be a prey, and I will judge between ram and ram. And I will raise up over them another shepherd, and he shall shepherd them, my servant David, and he shall be their shepherd; and I will be their God, and David a ruler in their midst. I the Lord have spoken. And I will make with David a new covenant, a covenant of peace." (Ezek. 34:20) Since in other places too we refer the prophesied David to none other than our Savior, born of the seed of David, for this reason we have noted this passage here as well. For who else could be the one who is to shepherd the Lord's sheep after he has judged them, if not the only good shepherd? He did not disregard the rational sheep of his own flock when they were being shoved and destroyed by the opposing powers, but laid down his own life for their salvation. His God and Father promises to establish him as their ruler after the time of judgment, making with him a covenant of peace, when his enemies have been subjected to him and, last of all, death itself, which now opposes the Word, Wisdom, and Life, will be abolished.

"Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am taking the whole house of Israel from among the nations to which they went, and I will gather them into the land of Israel, and I will make them into nations in my land and on the mountains of Israel; and there shall be one ruler over them, and they shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they ever be divided into two kingdoms, so that they may no longer defile themselves with their idols. And I will deliver them from all their lawless deeds in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them from all their sins in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them, and they shall be my people, and I the Lord will be their God. And my servant David shall be ruler in their midst, one shepherd of them all, for they shall walk in my ordinances and keep my judgments and do them. And they shall dwell in the land which I gave to my servant Jacob, where their fathers dwelt, and they themselves shall dwell on it; and David my servant shall be their ruler forever. And I will make with them a covenant of peace, and it shall be an everlasting covenant with them; and I will set my holy things in their midst forever, and my dwelling shall be among them, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them, when my holy things are in their midst forever." (Ezek. 37:21) After the dispersion of the spiritual and true Israel has been gathered together, and after the lost sheep of the house of Israel have been found, once the fullness of the Gentiles has first come in, then the Lord promises that he himself will be God to the people who are to be his, and that he will set his servant David as ruler in their midst, to shepherd them and rule over them, not for a little while or some short time, but forever. Let those of the circumcision suppose, then, that the word promises them that man, the son of Jesse, imagining once again a bodily kingdom of his, and expecting God's promises to consist in things perishable and earthly and unworthy of a divine promise. But we are persuaded that what is said as though about David in no way befits divine promises and cannot be referred to David himself. So we take the prophecies as referring to our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of David's seed according to the flesh, believing that the things presented in the sacred Scriptures as though in the person of David fit him rather than the David of old. Such are the words "The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you" (Ps. 2:7), and "You will make me the head of nations" (Ps. 17:43), spoken in the seventeenth Psalm, where again, as though in his person, it is said, "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And about whom else is it fitting to suppose that God says, "He shall call upon me, 'You are my Father,'" and "I will make him firstborn," than about our Savior, his only-begotten Son? For what exceptional thing had David accomplished beyond the other prophets and righteous men, that these things should be said of him alone, and that it should be prophesied that he would rise again as king and shepherd of God's sheep? Taking all this together, and attending to the prophecy of Isaiah, which after David's death proclaims, among other things about Christ, "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him" (Isa. 11:1), and what follows, we are persuaded that the things here too, prophesied as though about David, are fittingly said about the same one. For only the Christ of God, who by a transfer of name was also called David, has been shown to be the good shepherd, having become the leader and savior of God's flock and church. And it is prophesied that the Father will establish him as king over the whole spiritual Israel after the Lord has brought back his people from captivity.

"And in the times of those kings the God of heaven will raise up another kingdom, which shall be forever and shall not be destroyed; and this kingdom shall not allow another people, but it shall strike and do away with the kingdoms, and it shall stand forever, just as you saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands, and it crushed the clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver, and the gold." (Dan. 2:44) These words too point to the kingdom of Christ that will come at the consummation of the ages. For the stone cut from the mountain without hands would be a symbol of the Word of God, who is also called a stone in other prophecies, as in "Behold, I lay in Zion a chosen and precious cornerstone" (Isa. 28:16), and "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner" (Ps. 117:22). The present passage says, then, that he will bring down and crush the kingdoms of the world, the principalities, the powers, and the world-rulers, and will hold the kingdom of the saints forever.

King Nebuchadnezzar threw Hananiah and his companions into the furnace of fire. When he learned that the fire had done them no harm, he became an eyewitness of the marvel, and he is recorded as saying to his friends, "Did we not throw three men into the midst of the fire?" (Dan. 3:24) When they agreed, he says, "Look, I see four men unbound and walking about in the fire, and they are not harmed at all, and the appearance of the fourth is the likeness of a son of God." The Hebrew likewise has "the likeness of a son of God," and the other translators have rendered it the same way. For this reason we have marked the passage, since here too the title "Son of God" is signified.

In the visions Daniel says: "I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming on the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days and was brought before him. And to him were given the authority and the honor and the kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues will serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority that will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed" (Dan. 7:13). This agrees with the prophecy of the same Daniel which foretold the kingdom of Christ under the image of the stone cut out of the mountain without hands. For who else could be the one like a son of man coming on the clouds and reaching the Ancient of Days, if not our Lord Jesus Christ, who took the form of a servant for our sake and became a son of man, and who said, "I came forth from the Father, and I am going to God" (John 13:4)? While his disciples were present and looking on, he was taken up, and a cloud received him (Acts 1:9). Then, as they were gazing into heaven, behold, two men appeared in shining garments and taught them about his second coming, foretelling that he would come again in a cloud. To Christ alone, then, were the authority and the honor and the kingdom given by the Father, so that all the nations should worship him and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

When Daniel prayed about the captivity of the whole people in Babylon and about the desolation of Jerusalem, the archangel Gabriel appeared to him and revealed to him at once the end of the seventy-year captivity, the restoration of Jerusalem, the time from the restoration to the coming of Christ, the second capture of the city that would take place after these things, and, on top of all this, the enslavement of the whole nation, which was carried out after the coming of Christ. His words run as follows: "Daniel, I have now come out to give you understanding. At the beginning of your supplication a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are a man greatly desired. So consider the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been decreed for your people and for the holy city, to bring sin to an end, to seal up sins, to blot out iniquities, to make atonement for wrongdoing, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophet, and to anoint a holy of holies. And you will know and understand: from the going out of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until an anointed leader there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and it will return, and street and wall will be built, and the times will be emptied out. And after the sixty-two weeks an anointing will be destroyed, and there is no judgment in it; and he will destroy the city and the sanctuary together with the leader who is coming, and they will be cut off in a flood, and until the end of a war cut short by devastations. And one week will confirm a covenant with many; and in half of the week sacrifice and libation will be taken away, and upon the temple there will be an abomination of desolations, and until the consummation of the time a consummation will be given upon the desolation" (Dan. 9:22).

Of those who have taken up the weeks under discussion, we know only Africanus to have examined them with the greatest precision, and with more success than the rest. So it seems to me necessary first to set out his account of these passages, and only then to consider whether we ourselves can contribute anything to the discussion. In the fifth book of his Chronography he writes, word for word, as follows:

"This passage, then, as it stands, points to many remarkable things. For now, however, we shall discuss only what is needed concerning the dates and the matters connected with them. It is clear that these things are said about the coming of Christ, who was to appear after seventy weeks. For in the time of the Saviour, or from him onward, transgressions are made old and sins are brought to an end through forgiveness; lawless deeds, together with iniquities, are wiped away by atonement; an everlasting righteousness is proclaimed, beyond the righteousness that comes from the law; visions and prophecies last until John; and the Holy of Holies is anointed. Before the Saviour's coming these things did not exist; they were only looked for. The angel lays down that the count of the numbers, that is, of the seventy weeks, which are four hundred and ninety years, begins from the going forth of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem. This happened in the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. For Nehemiah, his cupbearer, made his request and received the answer that Jerusalem should be built, and a word went forth commanding it; up to that time the city had lain desolate. After the seventy years of the captivity, Cyrus had sent back everyone who wished to go, of his own free will. But those who went up with Jeshua the high priest and Zerubbabel, and those who came after them with Ezra, were at first prevented from building the temple and from putting a wall around the city, on the grounds that this had not been commanded. So matters remained until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of Artaxerxes' reign, which was the hundred and fifteenth year of Persian rule and the hundred and eighty-fifth year after the capture of Jerusalem. Then King Artaxerxes ordered the city to be built, and Nehemiah was sent down and put in charge of the work; and the street and the surrounding wall were built, as had been prophesied. Counting from that point, we find that the seventy weeks are completed at Christ."

For if we begin counting from some other point and not from here, the time will not fit, and a great many absurdities will follow. If we start counting the seventy weeks from Cyrus and the first return, there is a surplus of a hundred years and more. The surplus grows if we count from the day on which the angel prophesied to Daniel, and grows much more if we count from the beginning of the captivity. We find that the kingdom of the Persians lasted 230 years and that of the Macedonians extended to 300 years, and from there to the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar there are 60 years. But from Artaxerxes the seventy weeks are completed at the time of Christ, according to the Jewish reckoning. Nehemiah was sent by Artaxerxes to resettle Jerusalem in the 115th year of the Persian kingdom, which was the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes himself and the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad. From then until this time, which was the second year of the two hundred and second Olympiad and the sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, 475 years are reckoned. These make 490 Hebrew years, because the Hebrews count their years by the lunar month, which is, roughly speaking, twenty-nine and a half days. Since the solar cycle is 365¼ days, the twelve-month lunar year falls short of it by 11¼ days. For this reason both Greeks and Jews insert three intercalary months every eight years, for eight times 11¼ days makes three months. So the 475 years make 59 eight-year periods and 3 months. With three intercalary months for every eight years, this comes to fifteen years less a few days. Added to the 475 years, these complete the seventy weeks.

That is how the man mentioned above has handled these passages. Come, then: now that his interpretation has been given, let us also see whether the passages can be approached in another way. We would not want to seem to make the explanation rather forced by quietly dropping the years from Cyrus to Artaxerxes. Nor would we want to seem to leave unexplained the reason for dividing the weeks into seven and sixty-two. The divine word surely made that division with some reasonable purpose and the deepest understanding when it said: "And you shall know and understand: from the going forth of the word to answer and to rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed leader, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and it shall return, and street and wall shall be built." See, then, whether our account would not prove unforced if we count the years from Cyrus himself, under whom Daniel prophesies. For Cyrus was the first to issue the answer about raising Jerusalem up again, according to the scripture in Ezra, which runs as follows: "In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the word of the Lord from the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and in writing as well, saying: 'Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judea. Who is there among you of all his people? His God will be with him, and he shall go up to Jerusalem,'" and so on. To this is added: "And King Cyrus brought out the vessels of the house of the Lord, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his god. Cyrus king of the Persians brought them out by the hand of Mithridates and counted them out to Sheshbazzar, the ruler of Judah." (Ezra 1:1) Scripture then relates that those who went up first laid the foundations of the temple, and that in the time that followed they were kept from pressing on with the work, until the seventh week of years. Forty-six years, then, are reckoned from Cyrus to the sixth year of Darius, when the building of the temple was brought to completion. So the word fittingly set the first seven weeks apart from the rest, wishing to mark the interval between the first laying of the temple's foundations and its full completion. Cyrus reigned thirty-one years and then handed the rule to his son Cambyses. After Cambyses had reigned nine years, Darius received the kingdom and, following Cyrus, again ordered by decree that Jerusalem be built. In the sixth year of his reign, which was the forty-sixth from Cyrus, the building was completed. This is why they said to our Saviour, "This temple was built in forty-six years (John 2:20), and will you raise it up in three days?" According to Josephus, however, exactly forty-nine years are reckoned from Cyrus to the ninth year of Darius. In the eleventh book of the Antiquities he says that the building of the temple was finished in that year, stating in so many words that the temple was built in the seventh (sic) month of the ninth year of the reign of Darius. To this he adds: "They settled in Jerusalem, living under an aristocratic constitution combined with oligarchy, for the priests presided over affairs until the descendants of Asamonaeus came to reign." (Josephus 11.4.8) These, then, are the seven weeks mentioned in the prophecy, ending at the aforementioned year of Darius, and it is plain why they have been set apart from the rest. Let us also see to what point in time the remaining sixty-two extend. The history of the Greek chronographers shows that the ninth year of Darius falls in the sixty-seventh Olympiad. From then to the one hundred and sixteenth Olympiad, in which Seleucus took control of all Syria and Babylonia after the death of Alexander, there are 200 years. From there to the death of Simon, high priest of the Jews, 177 years of Syrian rule passed, as the first of the so-called books of Maccabees indicates, for it carries its history down to this point. From there onward Josephus, recording the successions of the priests with the greatest precision, says that after the Simon just mentioned, John, also called Hyrcanus, led the people for 29 years. Aristobulus succeeded him and reigned for one year. After him came Alexander, for 27 years, and after him his wife Alexandra. Down to her, the total from the ninth year of Darius comes to 434 years, which is the number that results from the sixty-two weeks. In those weeks the anointed leaders, who would be the high priests, presided over the affairs of the nation, beginning from Cyrus. For it is plain from holy scripture, and indeed also from the words of Josephus cited above, that after the return from Babylon, beginning with Jeshua the great priest himself, the people had leaders and rulers in succession. This continued down to those whom Josephus calls the sons of Asamonaeus and scripture calls the Maccabees. The first of these to be high priest was Judas, called Maccabaeus, who also led the people after routing the generals of Antiochus. After him his brother Jonathan took over both the high priesthood and the leadership of the people together. His brother Simon was high priest next, and after Simon came Hyrcanus. After Hyrcanus, Judas, also called Aristobulus, succeeded, and he was the first to put on a diadem in addition to holding the high priesthood and the kingship. After him Alexander took over the high priesthood and the kingship together, and he died leaving his wife as his successor. With him, as the weeks in Daniel came to their end, the rulers drawn from the priests, who were called "anointed," ceased. So the oracle that says "until an anointed leader" shows that there would be this many weeks. It is as if it had said more plainly that sixty-nine weeks of years would pass, that is, a period of 483 years, during which an anointed one and high priest, leading by succession, would preside over the affairs of the people. It is clear to anyone from what we have set out that this is exactly the number of years from Cyrus to the death of Alexander, the last high priest who led them. After him a woman, alone of all who had ever ruled, took over the kingdom of the nation at that time, and from her onward both the government of the Jews and the high priesthood, which had passed down steadily from their ancestors, fell into confusion. Once she had taken power, this woman gave the high priesthood to her son Hyrcanus, while she herself held the kingship for nine years and then died. After her, Aristobulus, her other son, after much strife with his brother, took the high priesthood away from him. He himself, in his third year, lost both the priesthood and the kingship. For Pompey, the Roman general, came at once, took Jerusalem by siege, defiled the holy things by advancing into the innermost sanctuary of the temple, and sent Aristobulus in chains to Rome with his children. After him, when Hyrcanus too had been carried off captive by the Parthians, Herod, the first man of foreign birth to do so, was entrusted with the kingdom over the Jews by the Roman senate. Josephus relates that Herod was an Idumaean on his father's side and an Arabian on his mother's. But according to Africanus, whom we mentioned a little earlier, those who have precise knowledge about him say that Antipater, who was Herod's father, was the son of a certain Herod of Ascalon, one of the temple servants of the shrine of Apollo. (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 1.7.8) When the rule of the Jews had passed to such a man, at that very time, along with the predictions of the other prophets, the prophecy of Jacob recorded by Moses was also fulfilled: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he is the expectation of the nations" (Genesis 49:10). It is plain both from the histories and from what we have set out that until Herod, in whose time Christ was born, the rule of those who led the whole nation in succession from among the Hebrews themselves did not fail. But when Herod, the first of foreign race, became their king, the coming of Christ was at once fulfilled, and the foretold expectation of the nations began to be accomplished in deed through the teaching of our Saviour, which spread to every nation. Then too the prediction in Daniel that follows the weeks we have discussed received its seal. It says: "And after the sixty-two weeks anointing shall be destroyed, and there is no judgment in it; and he shall destroy the city and the sanctuary together with the leader who is coming; and they shall be cut off in a flood, and until the end of a war cut short by destructions."

We have shown, as far as we are able, how the prophecy reached its end in the times of Herod: the prophecy of the foretold weeks, both the first seven [?] and the sixty-two that follow them, during which [?] (the text here repeats a phrase found below: "it was fitting to receive by succession of family, and the history down to the times of Herod, showing the high priests in succession throughout") an anointed one and high priest led the people, which is why the oracle said "until an anointed leader." It remains to show how, after this, when the time of the weeks already mentioned was complete, anointing was destroyed because there was no judgment in it, as the oracle indicates. The oracle means that the anointing belonging to the high priesthood would be brought to an end, by a reasonable judgment, at the time indicated. This will become clear to anyone who considers two things. The first is the ordinance of the law, which prescribes that those to whom the high priesthood belongs by succession of family should hold it for life, until their very death. The second is the history down to the times of Herod, which shows that the high priests in succession were held worthy of the honour throughout their whole lives, in keeping with the legislation concerning them. It shows also how under Herod himself the ordinance concerning the high priests was not only confounded and corrupted, but Herod also took from them their authority over the holy vestment, which belonged to the high priest alone [?], since no one else but he alone was permitted to minister in it. Herod brought it under his own control, though he was a foreigner. If proofs of these things must also be set out, accept the words of a witness: Josephus, one of the Hebrews themselves, who was himself honoured with the priesthood and came of the most distinguished family among them, set them down in the twentieth book of the Antiquities. About the alteration of the high priesthood he writes, word for word, as follows:

Herod, when he had been entrusted with the kingdom by the Romans, no longer appointed high priests from the line of Asamonaeus. Instead he assigned the honour to certain obscure men who were not of priestly descent, with the single exception of Aristobulus. He appointed this Aristobulus, the son of the Hyrcanus who had been taken captive by the Parthians, as high priest, and he married his sister Mariamme, seeking to win the goodwill of the people through their memory of Hyrcanus. Then, fearing that everyone would turn to Aristobulus, he killed him at Jericho, contriving to have him drowned while he was swimming, as we have already related. After him Herod never again entrusted the high priesthood to the descendants of the sons of Asamonaeus. His son Archelaus acted as Herod had in appointing high priests, and so did the Romans after him, once they had taken over the rule of the Jews. (Josephus, Antiquities 20.11.5)
That is what Josephus says on these matters. About the high-priestly vestment he relates the following in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities:

When Herod became king, he lavishly rebuilt this citadel, which lay in a convenient place, and named it Antonia. He found the high-priestly vestment kept there, and he went on keeping it there as he had received it, confident that because of it the people would never rise against him. Archelaus his son, who was appointed king after him, did the same as Herod. When the Romans took over the rule from him, they held possession of the high priest's vestment, which was stored under seal in a house built of stone. (Josephus, Antiquities 18.4.3)

From these things we have an indisputable proof that what the prophecy marked out came to pass at the times indicated. If those of the circumcision do not agree, we must ask them for an interpretation of the scripture different from ours. We must also show them that, on their reckoning, the predictions of so great a one as Gabriel would have to be exposed as false, if nothing he foretold has happened from his time until now, when nearly a thousand years have passed. For us, however, the word is clearly shown to be true by the unforced accounts we have set out. In keeping with them it is easy to explain how the single week added last of all strengthened a covenant for many. That covenant is the new covenant of the saving proclamation, which spread through the whole world and was preached no longer to the single nation of the Jews alone but now to many nations as well. That is why it was said, "One week shall strengthen a covenant for many." It is worth noting that this last single week, which the word says will strengthen a covenant for the many, is not joined directly to the other weeks. The word did not treat the single week as it treated the seven and the sixty-two weeks. In their case it divided the whole number of the time into the seven and then the sixty-two weeks, but made the division continuous: it joined the sixty-two to the seven and left no time or event between them. No interval of time is introduced to divide them and break the continuity of the history covered by those weeks. With the single week added afterwards, however, there is a long gap that sets it far apart. For after the sixty-two weeks it says first, "anointing shall be destroyed, and there is no judgment in it," and it is plain how this reached its end in the times of Herod. Then it says, "and he shall destroy the city and the sanctuary together with the leader who is coming." Who shall destroy them, if not the devil, the destroyer of souls? And who is the coming leader, if not Herod, the first of foreign race to lead them, together with those after him who have held government over the Jews down to the present? The prophecy riddlingly called the high priests who led them of old "an anointed leader." In the same way it called those of the gentiles who ruled them after the high priests had ceased "a coming leader," when it said, "and he shall destroy the city and the sanctuary together with the leader who is coming." Aquila rendered this more clearly: "and the people of a coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary." It is plain how the people and the army of the gentile leaders, who succeeded the anointed leaders in rule over the Jews and lived by the laws of the gentiles, destroyed both the city and the sanctuary. It is plain too how the destroyer, who leads souls in their thoughts, worked every kind of corruption together with the leader who came as the prophecy foretold. He corrupted first the people themselves and the citizens who lived in the city, and then also the temple and the worship that was once performed in it. A divine oracle somewhere foreshadows this as the reason for the coming of Christ that took place soon after. It says: "The Lord looked down from heaven on the sons of men, to see if there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one" (Psalm 13:2). Then, since those already mentioned had become corrupt, the word teaches in advance what would overtake them. It says, "and they shall be cut off in the flood," and they shall be cut off to such an extent that it lasts "until the end of a war cut short by destructions" (Daniel 9:26). And while these things were still being accomplished and carried out, "one week shall strengthen a covenant for many." This would be the week of the saving proclamation, through which our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ strengthened the handing on of the new covenant among the many who became his disciples. He did this at one time before the passion, when he was with them and shared their life, and at another time after his being taken up, when he appeared to them over forty days, ate with them, and spoke of the things concerning the kingdom of God. That is why he also commanded them not to leave Jerusalem (Acts 1:3). In the middle of this week, through the plot he suffered at the hands of the Jews, the rest of the divine prediction was fulfilled, for the scripture of the Gospels also shows that he preached for about three and a half years. That is why it is said, "and in the middle of the week sacrifice and libation shall be taken away." It is clear how, at the moment of the passion, sacrifice and libation were in effect taken away from them. According to the scripture of the Gospels, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom then (Matthew 27:51), and according to the history of Josephus,

At Pentecost itself the priests entered the temple by night for their ministrations, as was their custom. They said that they first sensed a movement and a crash, and after that a voice as of many together, saying, "Let us depart from here." (Josephus, Jewish War 6.5.3)

Josephus recorded these things word for word in his histories, along with others like them. They would support our proof that after the saving passion the bodily worship of the people was in effect dissolved and brought down. I also know of another interpretation that has been given of the week that strengthened a covenant for many. This account took it as a week of decades and so made the whole period of the apostles extend to seventy years. During that time the proclamation of the new covenant was preached no longer to one nation but to many, and was strengthened throughout the whole world. Indeed, the histories show that John, the disciple of the Lord, lived for seventy years after the Lord's ascension, for the account says that he remained alive until the reign of Trajan. On this interpretation it is plain how, in the middle of this week of decades, sacrifice and libation were taken away, and the so-called abomination of desolation stood in the holy place. The period from our Saviour's resurrection to the final siege under Vespasian comes to thirty-five years, which would be half of the week so understood. It was then, when the ancient sacred and holy temple had suffered complete destruction by fire and been razed to the ground, that these words received their seal: "sacrifice and libation shall be taken away, and upon the temple an abomination of desolations." The oracle shows that this abomination of desolation will remain until the end of the age, for it says, "and until the end of time an end shall be given upon the desolation." But we have set these things out in abbreviated form. It is now time to move on to Isaiah, who alone remains for us out of the whole of the Old Testament scripture.

Now that we are trying to gather the Prophetic Extracts from Isaiah, which are all that remain for us, we will first set out a few points for those who disbelieve the prophecies, to show that the prophets spoke the truth. To begin with, I will present an argument that those before us rightly noted. They seem to me to have said well that, for those under the law of Moses, the law itself solemnly declares that the nations among whom they will live listen to omens and divinations: "But to you," it says, "the Lord your God has not granted this" (Deut. 18:14). And the divine word, holding them back from augury and from every meddlesome divination worked through demons, adds: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers." Suppose these things had been written for them but had not come about in fact, and no prophets had been present among them. Could they then have believed the law, and the word that promised these things, when it was so plainly and obviously lying? Is it not clear that, drawn by their very craving to know the future, they would have despised their own traditions as holding nothing true or divine, since they had no prophets, and would have gone over of their own accord to the divinations and oracles of the nations? But in fact they plainly accepted as prophets of God not only Moses but also many after him. Clearly the only reason was that they had experienced the divine power in these men. For the prophets not only foretold things that would happen long afterward, but also predicted ordinary, everyday matters: lost donkeys, whether people who were dangerously ill would live or not, a coming time of plenty for the people, and countless other things recorded in the histories about them. If these things had not happened in this way, let someone answer: for what reason did they regard them as prophets and call them so, or why did they think their words worthy of being written down? And what made them hand down these men's writings to their children after them, as divine? For it is the most implausible thing of all to suppose that people who had seen nothing divine or extraordinary in these men formed such views about them at random and for no reason. If someone travels back in thought to those times, what would he think as he saw rustic men in plain dress, goatherds and shepherds, coming forward into the midst of the whole nation? They spoke as if in the person of God and cried out, "Thus says the Lord." They addressed kings and the whole people with undaunted boldness. They showed a more than human wisdom, which is still preserved in their prophecies today.
