They taught countless other hidden truths through riddles and parables, and handed on to the people moral and doctrinal teaching in the Hebrew tongue. Besides all this, they showed a life in keeping with their words, spoke to everyone without flattery, and rebuked the ungodly to their faces, so that the ungodly plotted against them even to the point of death, while they stood by the word of truth with strong and noble courage. Who, considering these things fairly, would not admit that all this happened to them by truly divine inspiration? It was natural, then, that sensible people admired them in their own day, that the sacred scribes kept their words in writing, and that even now the whole nation believes they were prophets of God. Our treatise on Christ establishes this most clearly of all. In it we show that the whole dispensation concerning him, including his teaching and the calling of all the nations through him, was precisely foreknown and foretold countless years before by those inspired men. The Jews, who would be more credible witnesses than we are, preserve and bring forward the sacred books of these men with all reverent honor. Having usefully set these things out first, we must now proceed to our subject.

"The word that came to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem. For in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains, and it will be raised above the hills, and all the nations will come to it. And many nations will go and say, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it.' For out of Zion will go forth a law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he will judge between the nations and rebuke many people, and they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles, and nation will not take up sword against nation, and they will never again learn to make war" (Isa. 2:1). Let those who boast in circumcision show us what this law is that is prophesied to go forth from Zion, what kind of law it is, and to whom it will be given. For "out of Zion," it says, "will go forth a law," which is clearly different from the law given through Moses in the wilderness. And what is this word of the Lord? According to the prophecy, it no longer stays in Jerusalem but goes out from Zion itself and passes over to all the nations. It is to judge between them and rebuke many people. Then the deepest peace will come upon the nations judged by the word of the Lord, and those found worthy of peace will refashion their former weapons of war and turn their minds to cultivating their own souls. I do not know whether those people have any answer to this. But for us, who have soundly believed in Jesus the Christ of God, it is easy to make the whole prophecy plain and to show that it is truly divine and wonderful. We believe that what was prophesied has been fulfilled, and we do not fall away from the truth by putting off the fulfillment of the prophecies to some endless future. For we say that at the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ the law of the new covenant, the law of the gospel, went forth from Zion, even in a bodily sense, and from there was proclaimed to all the nations. Then the saving Word himself, who is called the Word of the Lord, went out from Jerusalem, where he had stayed and taught, in keeping with the saying "Behold, your house is left to you desolate," and poured out his grace on all the nations (Acts 10:45). These nations were judged by him and rebuked for their former sins, and came to awareness of them and to repentance. They have stopped devoting themselves to the wars of the passions, and now live in the deepest peace of soul, tending their own minds, cultivating them and bearing fruit. If someone wishes to take these words literally, a sound sense results. If he takes them according to their deeper meaning, it is much easier, since we must be convinced that the passages are fulfilled primarily and more fully in this sense [?]. In any case, what has been said may also make clear the beginning of the passage at hand. For in the last days, which clearly means now, at the consummation of the ages, the spiritual mountain of God has become manifest, that is, the divine and heavenly Word. So has his house, the church built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, which is therefore said to be above the mountains. These things became manifest after the people of the circumcision were cast off and the kingdom of heaven was taken from them. That was when the words that come before the passage just quoted were fulfilled, where it is said: "The daughter of Zion will be left like a booth in a vineyard, like a watchman's hut in a cucumber field, like a besieged city" (Isa. 1:8). It was also when these words were fulfilled: "Hear the words of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord," and so on. To this it adds: "My soul hates your new moons and your feasts. You have become a surfeit to me; I will no longer forgive your sins. When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood." Notice how, after saying all this at length, the word does not charge them here with idolatry or any other sin, nor even with shedding much blood. It charges them with shedding one particular blood, clearly that of Christ, and plainly convicts the people of it when it says, "for your hands are full of blood." For this reason it goes on to say: "How has the faithful city Zion, once full of justice, become a harlot? Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers." After all this, the word concludes by foretelling their rejection once again: "For they will be like a terebinth that has shed its leaves, and like a garden that has no water. Their strength will be like a stalk of tow, and their works like sparks, and the lawless and the sinners will be burned up together, and there will be no one to quench the fire." After first pronouncing so many grave things against them, the prophecy then adds the passage we have just set out, where it says, "For in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest" (Isa. 2:2). After their complete and final rejection and desolation, it clearly points to the dispensations of the new covenant, under which the mountain of the Lord has become manifest to all the nations. And what mountain is this, if not God the Word, who was with God in the beginning? It is our Savior and Lord himself, as we have already explained. Of him it is also said in the Psalms, "The mountain of God, a rich mountain" (Ps. 67:15–16), and "the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell." Together with this mountain, the house of God has also become manifest. The house of God would be the church, firmly set on the tops of the mountains, that is, on the words of the apostles and prophets. When these became manifest, those who came to this very mountain, to the divine Word, were not Israel, which did not possess the Word, nor the house of Jacob so often mentioned, but quite simply all the nations. It is plain, then, how and in what way the things foretold were fulfilled through the appearing of our Savior, when the mountain and the house we have identified became manifest. We from the nations have come to the God of all through faith in Christ the Son of God. Once we were ignorant of such great things, but now we have come to know them through divine grace, and we have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. We have been taught by the Word of God, who went out, or rather came down, from the heavenly Jerusalem, that "the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother" (Gal. 4:26). So we stir one another up and urge one another on toward this heavenly house of God and toward Zion, which is itself the heavenly mountain of the Lord, and through teaching and exhortation we say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it" (Isa. 2:3). Now that these things have been fulfilled and, by God's grace, have become manifest to us all, another prophecy has also been fulfilled. In it the saving Word himself bears clearer witness to the passage of Isaiah's prophecy before us, saying: "I became manifest to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me; I said, 'Here I am,' to a nation that did not call on my name" (Isa. 65:1). If someone does not take these passages in this way, what other mountain or house of God could he point to as the subject of the prophecy, when nothing of the kind was then physically manifest? These things can also be applied in another way to the second coming of Christ, on the view that the prophecies will be completely fulfilled then rather than now. It should be noted that almost the same words are found in the prophecy of Micah as well.

"Behold, the Master of Hosts will take away from Judea and from Jerusalem the mighty man and the mighty woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water, the giant and the mighty man, the warrior and the judge, the prophet and the diviner, the elder and the captain of fifty, the wonderful counselor, the wise master builder, and the intelligent listener. And I will set youths as their rulers, and mockers will lord it over them" (Isa. 3:1), and so on. To this God adds: "I will not be the leader of this people, for Jerusalem has been forsaken and Judea has fallen, and their tongues are full of lawlessness, disobedient toward the Lord. Therefore their glory has now been brought low, and the shame of their face has risen up against them. They have proclaimed and displayed their sin like that of Sodom. Woe to their soul, because they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us.' Therefore they will eat the fruits of their works." The so-called Wisdom of Solomon says something similar to what is said here about the righteous one: "Let us lie in wait for the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us and opposes our words" (Wis. 2:12). The context there clearly shows that those words were spoken about Christ. So the words here also prophesy about those who plotted against him and who devised an evil plan against themselves rather than against him. That is why the word fittingly pronounces woe on them, saying, "Woe to their soul." It also sets out the punishment that awaits them, saying, "Therefore they will eat the fruits of their works." For whatever they sowed against Christ, they will also reap at the judgment seat of God. And consider whether, even in this present life, after their plot against Christ, the word of prophecy before us has not been fulfilled in them: "Behold, the Master, the Lord of Hosts, will take away from Judea and from Jerusalem the mighty man and the mighty woman." For truly the divine and heavenly grace that once dwelt among them has been taken away from them, and among them one can no longer find either a prophet or a diviner. Where now is their warrior or their judge, the wonderful counselor or the intelligent listener? And though they seem to share in spiritual bread when they read the sacred words of God, consider whether the power and strength stored up in the divine Scriptures has not been taken away from them. Clearly, along with this, Jerusalem too has been forsaken, and everything else has been fulfilled in them because of that one sin against Christ. For "woe to their soul," says the word, and it adds the reason for the woe: "because they have devised an evil plan against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us.'"

"My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the path of your feet. But now the Lord will take his stand for judgment, and he will make his people stand. The Lord himself will enter into judgment with the elders of the people and with its rulers" (Isa. 3:12). The words "now the Lord will take his stand for judgment" do not seem to refer to the God of all, and still less the words "the Lord himself will enter into judgment with the elders of the people and with its rulers." It would be fitting for these things to be prophesied about God the Word, who is also called Lord. For indeed the Word of God himself, who has been proclaimed to all under heaven, will take his stand for judgment with everyone. He will leave not one of the ungodly any room for excuse, since his teaching has reached the ears of all. But Jesus Christ will enter into judgment above all with the elders of the people and with its rulers, since they gathered together against him and contrived the plot against him. It was they who led astray the people under their rule by calling them blessed, calling evil good and declaring that our Savior's good words were evil.

"And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying, 'Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height.' And Ahaz said, 'I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.' And he said, 'Hear then, O house of David! Is it a small thing for you to weary men? How then do you weary the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel. He will eat butter and honey; before he knows or prefers evil things, he will choose the good. For before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness, to choose the good'" (Isa. 7:10). Let those of the circumcision who do not accept the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ tell us who the virgin is who, according to the prophecy, will conceive in her womb and bear the son named Emmanuel. If they claim that the Hebrew has "young woman" rather than "virgin," we must reply that those who first translated the Scripture by divine dispensation were no ordinary men. They were seventy in number, chosen by merit from the whole people, and had won no small reputation for wisdom in their own day. Besides, what extraordinary sign would the word be promising, solemnly declaring that the Lord himself would give it to the house of David as something wonderful, if it were speaking about a mere young woman? Yet even if, as they say, the Hebrew has "young woman," nothing prevents us from holding that the words refer to a virgin. For in Leviticus you will find that a woman who was admittedly a virgin, betrothed to a man but violated by another, is called a "young woman" by the Scripture. Understood this way, it would be a sign worthy of the Lord to give to the house of David because of their unbelief: that a virgin should, against all expectation, give birth. This is also why the child to be born is declared to be someone wonderful, since it is prophesied that from childhood, and even, so to speak, from his very birth, he will refuse wickedness and choose the good. His name too is wonderfully proclaimed in advance as Emmanuel, which means "God with us." We who confess him, and who perceive his divine and ineffable visitation to all people through his power, would say this too. Again, he might be called Emmanuel, God with us, because the Father and God of all is beyond not only mortal nature but all rational nature, while the Son is fittingly named God with us because he came all the way down to us. I remember hearing one of the circumcision say that these words were prophesied to Ahaz about Hezekiah, his son, who reigned after him. We must therefore point out that Hezekiah can be shown to have been born long before Ahaz became king, and before this very prophecy was spoken to him. Ahaz reigned sixteen years, and Hezekiah succeeded him at the age of twenty-five when he began his reign, so that his birth came nine years before his father's accession to the throne. But the words before us were prophesied to Ahaz when he was already king, and they concern the extraordinary and most wonderful birth of Christ that we have described. The diligent reader will learn the meaning of each phrase by reading the commentaries of that admirable man on these passages.

"And the Lord said to me, 'Take for yourself a large new scroll (of papyrus), and write in it with a man's pen, "To make swift plunder of spoils"; for it is at hand. And make for me faithful men as witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Barachiah.' And I went in to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me, 'Call his name: Despoil quickly, plunder swiftly. For before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians.'" (Isaiah 8:1). To record the extraordinary thing that was going to be accomplished, the prophet is commanded to take a scroll that is new, large and unwritten, and by this I think the Gospel of the New Covenant is meant. He is also to make faithful men witnesses for the Lord. One of them is said to be a priest, and the other, I think, was a prophet; at any rate the book of Chronicles also mentions him. I take these men too to be a symbol of the prophets who bore witness to the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the priests who were appointed long ago as a type of him. After this it says, "And I went in to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son," and so on. But it is utterly unfitting, and foreign to the dignity and purity of a prophet, to suppose so casually that the prophet, at the very moment he was inspired by God, went in to a woman, herself a prophetess, for shameful intercourse in front of the witnesses just mentioned. And how could anyone plausibly venture to claim that when he went in she conceived and bore a son? Rather, I consider that this prophecy too keeps to the sense of the one set out before, where it was said, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive." There it was foretold that the virgin would conceive and bear a son; here the way the prophecy reached its fulfillment is shown, for she conceived, it says, and bore a son. Who, then, would be the one saying "I went in to the prophetess" but the Holy Spirit who speaks in the prophet, of whom it was said to Mary, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35)? So she too might not unfittingly be called a prophetess, since she conceived from the Holy Spirit and bore the one who there was called Emmanuel but here is named otherwise. "Call," it says, "the name of the child that is born: Despoil quickly, plunder swiftly." And truly he did despoil and plunder the opposing invisible and spiritual powers by an ineffable and divine power, so that he could say, "I have conquered the world" (John 16:33). From them he took as spoils and plunder the souls they had long held under their tyranny, so as to proclaim release to the captives (Luke 4:18), and he acknowledges that he has received from the Father the nations as his inheritance (Psalm 2:8), which might readily be called spoils, and the ends of the earth as his possession, which might also fittingly be called plunder. Besides this, "Before the child knows how to call father or mother," it says, "he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians." I think these words too are meant in a purely spiritual sense. They refer either to certain evil powers, which the divine power of our Savior overthrew at his very birth, or to the different kinds of souls among those who have believed in him. On this reading, those who turned from idolatry to the life of the Gospel are likely to be what is called the power of Damascus, and those from the circumcision who received the Christ of God are what are called the spoils of Samaria. He took these souls as spoils and plunder from his spiritual enemies, in opposition to the spiritual king of the Assyrians, that is, the devil, and he armed them and made them ready to wage war against him. Anyone who wishes may learn these matters in detail from the commentaries on these passages by the holy man. But if those of the circumcision demand that these things be taken more literally, they must be questioned in turn. Can they themselves show, in a literal sense, how Isaiah went in to the prophetess for bodily intercourse in front of the witnesses mentioned? Who was this prophetess, and how did she conceive immediately and give birth at once? What sort of child was this whom the Lord commands Isaiah to call by the name "Despoil quickly, plunder swiftly"? What meaning does so grand a name have? Or how is it possible, on the obvious sense, to imagine any child at all physically seizing what is called the power of Damascus and the so-called spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians, and doing these things before it knows how to call father or mother? And further, if they dispute what we have set out, let them show how the Christ they expect will, when he comes, physically take the power of Damascus according to the prophecy, and what spoils of Samaria he will take, and before what Assyrians, since none of these is active any longer in the present times.

"Behold, I and the children whom God has given me; and there will be signs and wonders in the house of Israel from the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion" (Isaiah 8:18). The words "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me" are rightly taken in the Epistle to the Hebrews as spoken in the person of the Savior about the apostles and those who afterward believed in him. At any rate, here the words are added, "And there will be signs and wonders in the house of Israel" (Hebrews 2:13). And it is clear that at the time of the Savior's coming there were signs and wonders in the house of Israel such as had never before been accomplished.

"And they will wish that they had been burned with fire. For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, whose rule has come to be upon his shoulder; and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel. For I will bring peace upon the rulers, and health to him. Great is his rule, and of his peace there is no limit: upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to set it right and to uphold it with judgment and with righteousness, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do these things" (Isaiah 9:5). I think the child spoken of here is none other than the one prophesied above as to be born of the virgin, whom a little earlier the prophetess was also said to bear. But above, his name was Emmanuel, and after that, "Despoil quickly, plunder swiftly." Here this same one, according to the translation of the Seventy, is called Angel of Great Counsel. According to Aquila and the Hebrew itself, however, his name is Wonderful Counselor, Strong, Mighty, Father Still, Prince of Peace. And according to Symmachus, the name of the child will be called Marvel of Counsel, Strong, Mighty, Father of the Age, Prince of Peace. So those of the circumcision must be challenged to show what child they have to whom they could apply titles of such greatness. For in our view these are names for aspects of the divine power of Christ. Those who did not believe in him will wish that they had been burned with fire rather than see their own rejection and the salvation of the nations, which, it is said, the zeal of the Lord of hosts will bring about. With this you may compare what was said in Moses, roughly as follows: "They provoked me to jealousy with their idols, and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a senseless nation I will anger them" (Deuteronomy 32:21). But it is not a task for the present occasion, nor indeed within our purpose, to explain each word of the prophecy [?]. That includes how it is said, "upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to set it right," a phrase at which those of the circumcision might well stumble, because our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ did not physically sit on the throne and kingdom of David. So we refer the studious to the commentaries on these passages, and we shall carry through what we have set before us.

"Behold now, the Master, the Lord of hosts, will throw the glorious into confusion with strength, and those lofty in insolence will be crushed and humbled, and the lofty will fall by the sword, and Lebanon will fall with its lofty ones. And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him: a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit of knowledge and godliness shall fill him, a spirit of the fear of God. He shall not judge by appearance, nor convict by what is said, but he shall give judgment to the lowly and convict the lowly of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall destroy the ungodly. And he shall be girded about his waist with righteousness, and wrapped about his sides with truth. And the wolf shall graze with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the bull and the lion shall graze together, and their young shall be together, and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And an infant child shall put his hand on the hole of asps and on the nest of the offspring of asps, and they shall do no harm, nor be able to destroy anyone on my holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as much water covers the seas. And on that day there shall be the root of Jesse, and the one who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope, and his rest shall be honor" (Isaiah 10:33). Not even those of the circumcision have supposed that the one prophesied here is anyone other than the Christ. But because they imagine, on the bare letter of the prophecy, that the contents of the passage will come about in a more bodily way, they do not confess faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. We, however, are persuaded that the whole prophecy is worthy of God, and we have believed that these things are said of human transformations: of those who, through the appearing of our Savior, have changed from the depth of wickedness to gentleness. For even now we still see how, in the churches throughout the world, after the coming of Jesus Christ who sprang from the root of Jesse, most people have been refashioned and have changed their very nature from a bestial life. Before, they were wolves of a sort, and in the same way leopards and lions and all the other beasts and reptiles that the prophecy lists, corresponding to the varied vice and wickedness in each. Having changed and been reshaped, as it were, they advanced to such gentleness that they graze together, eating the same food of God's sacred words, with the righteous men of God who are gentlest in character. Because of their innocence of soul, the divine word compared these men to tame and very gentle animals, and to the children recorded here. But if anyone is hard to persuade about this, let him say whether the wording can be preserved in any other way according to its obvious sense. Why, or how, will Lebanon fall with its lofty ones? And let him not take the rod figuratively, nor the flower from it, but let him show how a bodily rod is said to come forth from the root of Jesse, and what sort of flower will come up from it. And if this compels even the very hard-hearted to rise to the spiritual sense, see whether we do not rightly show that the rest too was fulfilled, in its spiritual sense, at the coming of our Savior. These things happened in accordance with the prophecy after the Lord of hosts threw into confusion those who were once glorious among the former people. The prophecy foretells that these men, exalted in their insolence against our Savior, would be crushed and humbled and would fall. And with them, the word says, Lebanon too will fall. It is the word's custom to give this name to Jerusalem and to the worship that was formerly carried out in it in a bodily way. This is clear from Ezekiel, where it is written: "The great eagle, with great wings, long in extent, full of talons, which had the design to enter Lebanon, and took the choice parts of the cedar" (Ezekiel 17:3). Indeed, in explaining the parable, the prophetic word itself clearly teaches that Lebanon is Jerusalem, saying, "Son of man, say now to the rebellious house: Do you not know what these things were? Say: When the king of Babylon comes against Jerusalem, he will take its king and its rulers" (Ezekiel 17:12). It is quite clear, then, how this Lebanon too fell, together with those lofty in insolence, at the coming of our Savior, who sprang from the root of Jesse. Upon him rested the perfection of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and he will come again at his second and glorious coming. He will not judge by appearance, for God does not accept a person's face (Galatians 2:6); nor will he convict by what is said, for he is the one who searches hearts and kidneys (Revelation 2:23) and pierces even to the division of soul and spirit (Hebrews 4:12). At his coming, which has already taken place, the earth was truly filled with the knowledge of the Lord, whereas before no one knew him except those of the circumcision alone. But the prophecy will be brought to fulfillment still more fully when the fullness of the nations has come in and all Israel too is saved together with the rest of the nations. Christ, having risen from the dead, was appointed by God to rule the nations, according to the words, "And there shall be the root of Jesse, and the one who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope." Notice, then, that here neither Israel nor Jacob nor Judah is named at all. It is clearly prophesied that the nations will hope in the one who will rise from the root of Jesse. The wording here agrees with that in Moses, which says, "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he is the expectation" (Genesis 49:10), the expectation not of Israel but of the nations. And whose rest has come to be in the highest honor with God, if not his who heard the Father say to him, "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet" (Psalm 109:1)?

"And a throne will be set right with mercy, and he will sit on it with truth in the tent of David, judging and seeking judgment and hastening righteousness" (Isaiah 16:5). These things too are prophesied about the second coming of Christ. Then the Word of God, once the kingdom over all has been set right for him with mercy and love for humankind, will sit judging with truth in the tent of David. By this name, I think, are meant the church of the saints and of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and all the saints who have come to belong to the portion of the Word of God.

"Behold, the Lord is seated on a light cloud, and he will come into Egypt, and the handmade things of Egypt will be shaken at his presence, and their heart will be overcome within them" (Isaiah 19:1). To take these words as referring to the unbegotten nature of the God of the universe, as though he were going to ride on some cloud and sojourn in the bodily Egypt, I consider neither plausible nor reverent. Therefore the prophecy must be understood of the Word of God, and as already clearly fulfilled at his first coming. Then, on a light cloud, that is, the flesh formed for him from the Holy Spirit, he came into this life, which is figuratively called Egypt. He also came into Egypt itself in a bodily sense, when he was carried there as a child by his mother and Joseph. At that time, for certain ineffable reasons, the demons who had formerly dwelt and worked in the handmade images everywhere were shaken and stirred, thrown into turmoil by his coming. This is what the prophecy shows when it says, "And the handmade things of Egypt will be shaken." But these things will also be fulfilled at his second and glorious reign from heaven, when it is likely that Egypt itself will also be shaken. Then the handmade things of Egypt, as explained above, will be shaken still more, and their heart too, they say, will be overcome within them, when the divine Word subjects to himself and humbles every height that is now raised up against the knowledge of God. All the rest of the prophecy will be explained by figurative interpretation alone.

"In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians, and a pillar to the Lord at its border; and the Lord will be a sign forever in the land of Egypt. For they will cry out to the Lord because of those who afflict them, and he will send them a man who will save them; judging, he will save them. And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day, and they will offer sacrifices and a gift, and they will make vows to God" (Isaiah 19:19). And who else could the man sent by the Lord be, who saved the Egyptians by judging, but the Christ of God, who took the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a man (Philippians 2:8)? Since Egypt is understood figuratively as human life, the Egyptians would be the superstitious, who had already been given over to material things. The God of the universe took pity on them when they were afflicted by the demons who held them under their tyranny, and sent the man mentioned above, who saved them with a salvation befitting God. As a result, those who were formerly shut out from the assembly of the Lord under the law came to know the Lord through his appearing to them, the Lord himself making himself known to them. And it is clear how, in the land of the Egyptians as explained, an altar was established for the Lord out of the assemblies gathered in every place for prayer and the worship of God. Someone keeping close to the wording of "And there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians" might say this: if an altar is a place of sacrifices, where irrational animals are slaughtered for God's sake, then it is most just to say that a greater and truer altar has come to be for God through Christ. It exists both in the whole region of the earth, figuratively called Egypt, because of the martyrs everywhere who were offered to God as sacrifices and, as it were, as victims on behalf of the human race; and in the bodily land of the Egyptians itself, where so many great martyrs glorified God with their own blood. But if those of the circumcision are hard to persuade about what has been set out, let them say when, where and by whom an altar was set up to the Lord in Egypt. Let them say who the man was who saved the Egyptians, and how and when the Lord became known to the Egyptians, so that they abandoned their former error and took up the knowledge of him; for that is what it means to come to know the Lord. All the rest of the prophecy depends on a deeper sense, which this is not the occasion to unfold.

"Lord, in affliction I remembered you; in slight affliction your discipline came upon us. And as a woman in labor draws near to giving birth and cries out in her pain, so have we become to your beloved" (Isaiah 26:16). In the Psalms a title is found, "For the beloved" (Psalm 44); and again it is said, "The king of the powers of the beloved" (Psalm 67:12). In those passages it is shown that the one called God's beloved is none other than Christ. For this reason we have also noted the "beloved" in the passage before us, taking him to be that very one whom a voice from heaven clearly proclaimed, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17).

"Hear the words of the Lord, you afflicted men and rulers of this people who are in Jerusalem. Because you have said, 'We have made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes by, it shall not come upon us; we have made falsehood our hope, and by falsehood we shall be sheltered,' therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am laying in the foundations of Zion a costly stone, chosen, a cornerstone, precious, for its foundations, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame. And I will make judgment into hope, and my mercy into scales" (Isa. 28:14). And how could it not be truly foolish and utterly ridiculous, the notion held by those who expect, in a bodily sense, that the Lord himself will lay one of these stones reckoned costly and precious in the foundations of the bodily Zion, a stone on which whoever believes is prophesied never to be put to shame? Let us therefore shake off the foolish Jewish tales and what the apostle called old wives' fables (1 Tim. 4:7), and receive the divinely inspired prophecies in a manner worthy of God. He says, then, "therefore, behold, I am laying in the foundations of Zion a stone." Therefore on account of what, if not because the rulers of the former people had made agreements with death, and because they had abandoned the covenant of God and in its place made a covenant with Hades, and supposed that on this account they would suffer no harm; and, further, because they had set their hope on falsehood and thought they would be sheltered by falsehood? It is for these very reasons, since those men had fallen away from their hope in God, that he promises to lay the precious stone for those who believe. And to those who had said, "We have made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes by, it shall not come upon us; we have made falsehood our hope, and by falsehood we shall be sheltered," the word says a little further on: "You who trust in vain in falsehood, the storm shall not pass you by, lest it also take away your covenant with death, and your hope in Hades shall not stand; if a rushing storm comes upon you, you will be trampled down by it." It is evident how these things were fulfilled upon that people at the coming of our Saviour. Consistently, then, we hold that the chosen stone indicated here, a wonderful and extraordinary thing, such that those who believe in it shall not be put to shame, is none other than the holy Word of God, on whom, as on a firm foundation, the spiritual and heavenly Zion has been built, which is none other than the church of God. "For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Cor. 3:11). Concerning him it is also said in the Psalms, "The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner" (Ps. 117:22), and he has been called the cornerstone. Daniel too interprets this stone as referring to the kingdom of Christ, where he says, "And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and struck," or "filled, the whole earth" (Dan. 2:35). So those who were building the building according to the letter of the law rejected this stone; but he, though rejected by them, has nonetheless been shown to be the head of the corner of the church from the Gentiles, according to what is said somewhere: "You will make me head of the nations" (Ps. 17:43). Whoever believes in this stone, then, shall not be put to shame, and this prophecy concerning him is also proved true.

"Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time, burning wrath; the oracle with glory; the oracle of his lips full of wrath, and the wrath of his anger will devour like fire" (Isa. 30:27). And what would this so-called name of the Lord be, if not God the Word, through whom all things came to be? I think, then, that this prophecy too hints at what concerns his second and glorious coming.

"Thus says the Lord: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and kinsmen in Jerusalem. For behold, a righteous king shall reign, and rulers shall rule with judgment" (Isa. 31:9). The Christ of God, who said, "But I was set up as king by him," is indicated by these words too. The rulers under him would be either the apostles and those who rule the churches with the judgment of God, or else divine angels, overseers of the salvation of men. And it is on account of this one who reigns over Zion and Jerusalem that "blessed is he who has seed in Zion and kinsmen in Jerusalem"—words which must be understood in a manner worthy of the apostolic spirit, which teaches us about the Jerusalem above and the heavenly mount Zion.

"Be glad, thirsty wilderness; let the desert rejoice and blossom like a lily; and the desert places of the Jordan shall blossom and rejoice; and the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the honour of Carmel; and my people shall see the glory of the Lord and the majesty of God. Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees; give comfort, you who are faint of heart; be strong, do not fear. Behold, our God renders judgment and will render it; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of stammerers shall speak plainly; for water has burst forth in the wilderness, and a ravine in a thirsty land; and the waterless ground shall become marshes, and in the thirsty land there shall be a spring of water" (Isa. 35:1). He foretells that extraordinary healings will take place at the coming of God. Clearly, then, here too the Christ of God has been honoured with the title of God. At his coming the cures foretold were accomplished bodily upon the sufferers, and still more wonderfully they are being worked even now through faith in him, as the whole human race without exception is being freed from the passions of the soul. Water burst forth in the wilderness at the coming of Christ, and a ravine in a thirsty land, when the drinkable and life-giving word gushed up in the land that was long desert and thirsty, the church from the Gentiles. In it, formerly waterless and parched, there suddenly poured forth a spring of the living water of Jesus' words, springing up to eternal life (John 4:14). Watered by this spring, the once-desert is said to blossom like a lily, and is commanded to be glad and rejoice. The reason for the gladness and rejoicing is added as well, since, he says, the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, that is, the glory of Jerusalem. Of Jerusalem it was said in the earlier prophecies that "Lebanon too will fall with its lofty ones"; and when it fell, the glory that was formerly in it was given to the desert that now receives the good news, that is, the church from the Gentiles, together with the former honour of what is called Carmel, which is clearly the former people. These things clearly reached their fulfilment in deeds after the coming of Christ, in accordance both with the prophecy before us and with the words of our Saviour himself, which say that the kingdom of God will be taken away and given to a nation producing its fruits.

"A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every ravine shall be filled, and every mountain and hill brought low; and all the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough ground plains; and the glory of the Lord shall appear, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God, for the Lord has spoken" (Isa. 40:3). John, the forerunner of our Saviour, said to those who asked him who he was, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness," and so on. It is for this reason that we have set out this chapter among the testimonies concerning Christ, since we consider John to be a symbol of the apostolic preaching. For such is the voice crying in the wilderness: something indistinct and inarticulate to those who are only just learning the rudiments. And this voice, raised in what was formerly a wilderness, the church from the Gentiles, commands them to prepare the way of the Lord, and so on. Whoever cares to understand these things will come to know them by investigating them at leisure.

"Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God! The Lord, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with lordship; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. Like a shepherd he will tend his flock, and with his arm he will gather the lambs, and he will comfort those that are with young" (Isa. 40:9). These words too we take to be spoken about the coming of the Word of God, and perhaps rather about the second coming, at which he is prophesied to come as a just judge, bringing the reward that renders to each according to the worth of his deeds. The rest, however, the present occasion does not require us to expound, so we shall turn to another passage.

"Who raised up righteousness from the east, called it to his feet, and it shall go? He will set it before nations and will astonish kings; and he will cast their swords to the ground, and ※ their bows like brushwood driven away; and he will pursue them; the way of his feet shall pass through in peace; it shall not come. Who has worked and done these things? He who calls it from the beginning of the generations has called it. I, God, am first, and for the things to come I am. The nations saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were amazed; they drew near and came together, each one judging to help his neighbour and his brother. And he will say, The craftsman has prevailed, and the smith striking with the hammer, driving at once; at one time he will say, It is a good joint; they fastened them with nails; they will set them up, and it shall not be moved" (Isa. 41:2). What would this righteousness raised up from the east be, as a distinct being with its own subsistence, if not the Christ of God, of whom the apostle says, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Cor. 1:30)? Him the dispensation of the incarnation raised up from the Father's bosom, which is the east of all intelligible light; or else the Father himself did so, who set him before the nations. This was so that their former kings, who were invisible evil powers, might be astonished at the extraordinary nature of the dispensation, seeing so great a Son of God having neither form nor beauty; and so that after such astonishment their swords might be cast to the ground, and their bows like brushwood driven away, so that they should no longer hold weapons of war and fiery darts, with which they formerly waged war on the souls subject to them. After this he says, "and he will pursue them," so that, when they have thus been driven out at the end of all things, the way of his feet may pass through in peace. "And who," he says, "has worked and done these things?" We supply the answer: the goodness and love for humanity of the God of the universe, who calls it—clearly meaning righteousness, which is none other than his wisdom. Beholding it, the nations, which formerly lived without fear of God, feared God; and, called from the extremities and the ends of the inhabited world, they drew near to God, those once far off having come near to the kingdom of heaven. That is why they were also amazed at the extraordinary nature of their salvation; and teaching one another, brother helping brother, they confess their former error concerning idols, saying precisely this: "So it was a carpenter and a smith who, with hammers and nails and human contrivance, set up and made firm those whom we formerly thought to be gods; and they were after all nothing but lifeless wooden images, capable of no movement of their own; our fathers acquired false idols, and there was no profit in them." That these things were accomplished in this way at the coming of our Saviour is established by the testimony of deeds more than of words.

"Jacob my servant, I will uphold him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor let up, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench; but he will bring forth judgment unto truth. He will shine out and not be crushed until he establishes judgment on the earth; and in his name the nations will hope. Thus says the Lord God, who made the heaven and fixed it, who established the earth and what is in it, and gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk on it: I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and strengthen you; and I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring the bound out of their bonds, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison house" (Isa. 42:1). That the words beginning "Jacob my servant, I will uphold him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him" are not prophesied about the Jewish people will be clear to those willing to examine each phrase of the passage; but it is also evident from the exactness of the Hebrew, for neither the name Jacob nor the name Israel appears in it, which is why it has been marked with an obelus in the accurate copies of the Seventy. And that none of the righteous other than our Saviour Jesus Christ—not even the son of Isaac himself, who was called Jacob and Israel—was such that the passage could fit him, no one, I think, doubts. For even if someone should apply "I have put my Spirit upon him" to others, what would he say about "he will bring forth judgment to the nations" and what follows, and especially "and in his name the nations will hope"? And how could it be plausible to apply to the Jewish people, or to Jacob the son of Isaac himself, or to any other of the righteous, the words "I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring the bound out of their bonds, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison house"? But let these difficulties be raised by us against those of the circumcision. The gospel, at any rate, clearly teaches us that this prophecy too was fulfilled in our Saviour Jesus, when the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him how they might destroy him. "But Jesus, knowing it, withdrew from there; and many followed him, and he healed them all, and he ordered them not to make him known" (Matt. 12:14). For to these words the gospel adds, "that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my Spirit upon him," and the rest, as set out in the prophecy. He, then, would be the one who was also called Jacob, since he is the only-begotten Child of God; as it is said elsewhere, "It is a great thing for you to be called my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the dispersion of Israel" (Isa. 49:6). This one, then, having heard from the Father, among other things, "I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations," brought forth judgment to the nations, so that they might order their lives with discerning judgment according to the holy gospel. It is clear how the nations that believed in him have hoped in his name, and how he has been shown to be a light of the nations, so that through the light of his word the eyes of the mind have been opened in those who had long been blinded [?] in them. Moreover, he brought out of their bonds those formerly bound tight with the cords of their own sins, and out of the devil's prison house those who sat in darkness through ignorance of the God of the universe. It remains for the lover of learning to examine each phrase of the prophecy and, in keeping with what we have said, to apply what follows to the Christ of God.

"Be my witnesses, and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I have chosen" (Isa. 43:10). And who would the servant be whom the Lord God has chosen, and whom he counts alongside himself as one who will be a witness among those who bear witness to him, if not the one of whom it was said in the preceding chapter, "Jacob my servant, I will uphold him," and so on? Those words were clearly shown to have been prophesied about our Saviour and Lord Jesus.

"I made the earth and man upon it; with my hand I established the heaven; I gave command to all the stars. I raised him up as king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He will build my city and bring back the captivity of my people, not with gifts nor with ransoms, said the Lord of Hosts. Thus says the Lord of Hosts: Egypt has laboured, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of stature, will cross over to you and will be your slaves; they will follow behind you in fetters, and will cross over to you, and will bow down to you, and will pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Saviour. All who oppose you will be ashamed and confounded, and will go in shame" (Isa. 45:12). The Father raised Christ from the dead so that he should be king with righteousness, reigning on Zion, his heavenly holy mountain. And he raised him for this reason, since all his ways, he says, have been straight, having nothing crooked or twisted (Prov. 8:8); for he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isa. 53:9). This one also built the city of God, both his holy church on earth and the heavenly Jerusalem, bringing back the captivity of his people, which had once come about under the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar and the evil powers subject to him. And he brought back that captivity not by paying ransom to the captors, nor by persuading them with gifts, but by making war on them and subduing them through struggle, so that, made glorious by this achievement, he said, "I have conquered the world" (John 16:53). Witness to these things are the multitudes who through him have turned back from their former error to the knowledge of the true God. Otherwise, let those of the circumcision say to whom they would apply the prophecy before us, which clearly confesses the one prophesied to be God. For "these and those," it says, "will be your slaves, and will follow behind you, and will bow down to you, and will pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no other besides you; for you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Saviour" (Isa. 45:15). For here the word clearly addresses the very one to whom "God is in you" was said, and says to him, "and there is no other besides you; for you are God, and we did not know it." These words are also understood as spoken in the person of those who have recognized the Christ of God made man, in whom God the Father dwelt, according to the saying, "I am in the Father and the Father in me" (John 14:11). Therefore "there is no God besides you" would apply to him alone, since the divinity of the Word alone is united and blended with the Father's kingship, and for this reason a single glory and rule of both is conceived. In the words "Egypt has laboured, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of stature, will cross over to you," I think there is indicated the struggle of certain spiritual opposing powers who took up arms against Christ and were made subject to him; or else of such souls as at first resisted the Word, but later at some point accepted servitude under him for their own benefit. It is about these, I think, that it is said, "they will be your slaves, and will follow behind you bound in fetters, and will pray in you"; while "All who oppose you will be ashamed and confounded, and will go in shame" is prophesied about those who did not repent but remained enemies and adversaries, and were wholly unwilling to take upon themselves the yoke of the word of Christ. So much for the clear evidence concerning Christ. But it would be fitting to set this passage before not only those of the circumcision, but also those who have supposed the Saviour to have been a mere man: the Ebionites, or the followers of Artemon and of Paul of Samosata. For through these words too the divinity of Christ is clearly demonstrated to those who are reluctant to believe it.

"Listen to me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call: I am the first, and I am forever. My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand made the heaven firm; I will call them together, and they will stand and be gathered, and they will hear. Who announced these things to them? ※ Because I, the Lord, love you, I have done your will upon Babylon, to take away the seed of the Chaldeans. I have spoken, and I have called; I have brought him, and I have prospered his way. Come near to me and hear these things: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when it came to pass, I was there. And now the Lord, the Lord, has sent me, and his Spirit." (Isa. 48:12) Since there is a single person speaking these things in the passage, who else could be the Lord who made the heaven and fixed it, and made the earth firm, who says, "I am the first, and I am forever," and who adds in what follows, according to all who have translated the divine Scripture, "And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit"? Who else but the holy Word of God, who after the unbegotten first principle is named the first God of all things that have come into being? Of him it is also written elsewhere, "He sent his word and healed them." For he is the one through whom all things came into being, both those in the heavens and those on the earth, whether visible or invisible. He is the one whom the Lord God the Father sent, and the Holy Spirit with him, to carry out the dispensation for the salvation of humankind. This text would be well suited for use against the Jews, since it teaches that the Lord who created all things is other than the God of the universe, by whom he confesses he has been sent when he says, "And now the Lord has sent me." He would be the one whom the Father addresses with commands at the making of the world: "Let there be light," and "Let this and that come to be," and "Let us make man according to our image." This is why it is also recorded in the Psalms: "For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created." For it is plain that whoever commands something and speaks gives his commands and orders to someone other than himself. To examine every phrase of the passage, however, is not the task of the present treatise.

"Listen to me, you islands, and pay attention, you nations. After a long time it will stand, says the Lord. From my mother's womb he called my name, and he made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the shelter of his hand he hid me. And he said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified.' And I said, 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for futility and for nothing. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my toil is before my God.' And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to gather Jacob and Israel to him: I will be gathered and glorified before the Lord, and my God will be my strength. And he said, 'It is a great thing for you to be called my servant, to establish the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the dispersed of Israel. See, I have made you a covenant of a race, a light of the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth.' Thus says the Lord who rescued you, the God of Israel: 'Sanctify the one who holds his own life cheap, who is abhorred by the nations, the servants of the rulers. Kings will see him, and rulers will rise up, and they will bow down to him for the Lord's sake; for the Holy One of Israel is faithful, and I have chosen you.' Thus says the Lord: 'At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you; I formed you and gave you as a covenant of the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit the desolate places, saying to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Be uncovered." They will feed along all the roads, and their pasture will be on all the paths. They will not hunger or thirst, nor will the scorching heat or the sun strike them; but the one who has mercy on them will comfort them and lead them by springs of water. And I will make every mountain a road, and every path a pasture for them.'" (Isa. 49:1) The people of the circumcision would probably suppose that what the prophecy says is said about themselves, since it says, "And he said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified.'" But besides the fact that the words do not fit them, it is also clearly shown from what follows that these things are prophesied about another Israel. For it is written, "And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to gather Jacob and Israel to him"; and again, "He said to me, 'It is a great thing for you to be called my servant, to establish the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the dispersed of Israel.'" Moreover, the words "See, I have made you a light of the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth" also point to someone extraordinary and wonderful as the subject of the passage. Who could this be but our Lord Jesus Christ, who had already been called Jacob and Israel earlier, in the passages above, in the words, "Jacob my servant, I will help him; Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him"? For he is the only one who truly sees God the Father. He is named Israel, which is interpreted "one who sees God," with respect to his divinity; and Jacob, which means "supplanter," insofar as, having become man, he overcame all the opposing powers. See whether the two passages do not agree with each other, the one before us and the one in which "Jacob my servant" was said with reference to Christ. For just as there it says "Jacob my servant," so here it says "It is a great thing for you to be called my servant"; and just as there it says "Israel my chosen," so here it says "for the Holy One of Israel is faithful, and I have chosen you." And again, there it says, "I have given you as a covenant of a race, a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring those who are bound out of their bonds, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison house"; while in the passage before us it says, "See, I have made you a light of the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit the inheritance of a desert, saying to those in bonds, 'Come out,' and to those in darkness, 'Be uncovered.'" That what is said in the prophecies before us fits no one else but our Savior alone will be clear to anyone who considers the multitude of nations that have set their hope on him, and through him on the God of the universe; for them the Father appointed him as a light. And he says "to establish the earth," that is, to bring the soul, which had long been in turmoil and instability, to its natural stability and composure; and also "to inherit the inheritance of a desert," indicating the church from the nations, which was desolate before his coming and which he received as an inheritance from the one who said to him, "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance." And in keeping with the prophecy about him, he told those in bonds to come out. He did so in the obvious sense in the case of Lazarus, who was bound with grave-cloths and had lain four days in the tomb; saying, "Lazarus, come out" (John 11:43), he set him free to go. He did so also, in a particular instance, in the case of the daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound for eighteen years; her too he freed from her infirmity and sent away whole. And he did so in general whenever he granted forgiveness of their former sins to all who were bound tight by the cords of their own sins, since he alone has authority to forgive sins. Even now, through his teaching, he urges them to come out of their former bonds, saying to each one, "See, you have been made well; sin no more" (John 5:14). Beyond this, even now he commands those still buried in ignorance and wickedness to be uncovered, since he is the Word of God, who searches hearts and minds and discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. But so that we may run through it as briefly as possible, applying the earlier parts too to what is said about Christ, we will take it up again from the beginning and set out our understanding of these as well. In many places, when he calls on Jacob or Israel by name, he clearly addresses the people of the circumcision; here, however, he does not direct the prophecy to them, but summons islands and nations to listen to what will be said. And here indeed is the Lord's promise, spoken about the calling of the nations that were formerly wholly unbelieving and estranged from the worship of God. Among them, in part, are also to be understood the so-called islands: souls that long ago were swamped, as if under the sea, by the surging waves of life and by the bitterest salt currents of vice. We must consider, then, what the Lord himself teaches these about himself. "From my mother's womb," he says, "he called my name." This is clearly said of Christ, for the words are his, as we have learned from the Scripture of the Gospel. When Joseph did not understand Mary's conception, Gabriel, the minister of the Father's will, came to him and said in a dream, among other things, "She will bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus, for he will save his people" (Matt. 1:21). In the prophecy he goes on to say, "and he made my mouth like a sharp sword," and again, "he made me like a chosen arrow." For the word of God is active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4:12), as the inspired apostle taught. It would be most fitting to say to him alone, who became obedient to the Father even to death, "You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified." The words "And I said, 'I have labored in vain,'" and what follows, would be spoken by the Savior because so few live according to his gospel. And since he came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, it is rightly said that he came, in the first place, "to establish the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the dispersion of Israel." Then, because not all of them received him, it goes on, as addressed to him, "See, I have made you a light of the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth." After this the Lord God and Father, who rescued him from all who gathered against him, commands us to sanctify him, saying, "Sanctify the one who holds his own life cheap." For he truly held his own life of no account, emptying himself and becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), taking up our sins and despising the shame, even to death, and death on a cross (Heb. 12:2; Phil. 2:8). Next it says, "who is abhorred by the nations, the servants of the rulers." And it is clear how those enslaved to the rulers of this age abhorred him not only at the time of his passion, when they said, "He is grievous to us even to look at" (Wis. 2:15), but abhor him even now, as they try to overturn his teaching. This is the one, then, whom the Lord commands us to sanctify, foretelling his glorious coming. As for the prophecy that the word adds next in foretelling the calling of the nations, from "I gave you as a covenant of the nations" and what follows: these words are more spiritual and can be explained only by their inner sense, so examining them further is not the task of the present treatise.

"Thus says the Lord: What is this certificate of your mother's divorce, with which I sent her away? Or to which creditor have I sold you? See, you were sold for your sins, and for your lawless deeds I sent your mother away. Why was it that I came, and there was no man who obeyed? Is my hand not strong enough to rescue? Or is it not strong enough to deliver? See, by my rebuke I will make the sea desolate, and I will make rivers into deserts, and their fish will dry up because there is no water, and they will die of thirst. I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and I will make its covering like sackcloth. The Lord, the Lord, gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word. Morning by morning he appointed it for me; he gave me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears. And I do not disobey or contradict. I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting. And the Lord, the Lord, became my helper; therefore I was not put to shame, but I set my face like a solid rock, and I knew that I would not be put to shame, for the one who justified me draws near. Who is the one who contends with me? Let him come near. See, the Lord, the Lord, helps me; who will harm me? See, all of you will grow old like a garment, and a moth will devour you. Who among you fears the Lord? Let him obey the voice of his servant. You who walk in darkness and have no light, trust in the name of the Lord and lean upon God. See, all of you kindle a fire and feed a flame; walk by the light of your fire and by the flame that you have kindled. Because of me these things have happened to you; you will lie down in sorrow." (Isa. 50:1) These words too clearly show the divinity of the Word: both that he existed before the incarnation, and that, once he had become man, he was to suffer the things recorded in the Gospels. For who else could it be who says, "Is my hand not strong," and the rest, up to "I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and its covering like sackcloth," but the Word of God? Having said such great things, he goes on to say, "The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word"; and again he adds the rest, saying, "And I do not disobey or contradict; I have given my back to whips and my cheeks to blows," and so on up to "for the one who justified me draws near." For we say that the Word suffered potentially, sharing in the suffering of the man whom he had assumed. We do not know, then, whether anyone could give an account of the present prophecy without accepting that there is a second hypostasis, that of God the Word, after the first and unbegotten one, the Father and God of the universe. We, at any rate, being rightly persuaded, hold that this is plainly God the Word, who here too says, among other things, "I will clothe the heaven with darkness," and who adds, in the person of the man he had assumed, "The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word." To whom else but the man of our Savior would it be fitting to say also, "Who is the one who contends with me? Let him stand against me"? And of whom would the words from "Who among you fears the Lord? Let him obey the voice of his servant" be spoken, if not of Christ alone? According to the Scriptures he despised shame, emptied himself and humbled himself even to scourging, when, as the prophecy before us foretold of him, Pilate had him flogged and handed him over to be crucified. He endured blows and spitting when the high priest, tearing his clothes at his words, declared that he had blasphemed. For then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists, and others slapped him, saying, "Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?" (Matt. 26:68). The beginning of the chapter seems to be said about the synagogue of the Jews, for it says, "See, you were sold for your sins, and for your lawless deeds I sent your mother away." For he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24) and found no man among them. Indeed, he called them first, but the people did not obey. That is why he says, "Why was it that I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who obeyed?" The words at the end of the passage, coming as they do after their rejection, refer to the calling from the nations, beginning with "Who among you fears the Lord? Let him obey the voice of his servant." For we truly were the ones who walked in darkness, and before the coming of our Savior we had no light; but now, through the grace of God, we trust in the name of the Lord and lean upon God. But to those who did not believe in Christ, to whom it had also been said above, "See, all of you will grow old like a garment, and as a moth it will devour you," the word goes on to say, "See, all of you kindle as it were a fire," and what follows. Here the words "Because of me these things have happened to you" are clearly spoken in the person of Christ, as he reproaches them and exposes the lawlessness that the Jewish people committed against him.

"Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations. Therefore my people will know my name; therefore on that day they will know that I am he who speaks. I am here like springtime upon the mountains, like the feet of one who brings good news of peace, like one who brings good news of good things; for I will make your salvation heard, saying, 'Zion, your God will reign.'" (Isa. 52:5) This prophecy too would most fittingly apply to the Savior, since at his coming the words "For I am he; I who speak am here" were fulfilled. The words from "Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations" are addressed directly to the former people; but those from "Therefore my people will know my name on that day" would be understood of the nations that have believed in him. He, then, is the one who formerly spoke to human beings, sometimes through angels and sometimes through prophets. And as for how he came to them again and proclaimed salvation to all in his own person, the lover of learning will discover what this means by investigating it.

"And the Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations, and all the nations, the ends of the earth, will see the salvation that comes from God. Depart, depart, go out from there, and touch nothing unclean; go out from the midst of her and be set apart, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. For you will not go out in confusion, nor will you go in flight; for the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel is the one who gathers you. Behold, my servant will understand, and he will be exalted and lifted up exceedingly. Just as many will be astonished at you, so your appearance will be without glory among men, and your glory among men; so will many nations marvel at him, and kings will shut their mouths. For those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand" (Isa. 52:10). "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground; he has no form and no glory. We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men. He was a man under affliction, who knew how to bear sickness; because his face is turned away, he was dishonoured and not esteemed. This one bears our sins and suffers pain for our sake, and we reckoned him to be in toil, in affliction and under a blow. But he was wounded for our sins and made sick for our iniquities; the chastisement that brings us peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. All of us went astray like sheep; each man strayed in his own way, and the Lord handed him over for our sins. And because of his affliction he does not open his mouth. Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgement was taken away; who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was any deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord wills to cleanse him from his wound. If you make an offering for sin, your soul will see a long-lived offspring. And the Lord wills by his hand to take away the toil of his soul, to show him light and to form him with understanding, to justify the righteous one who serves many well; and he himself will bear their sins. Therefore he will inherit many and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was handed over to death and he was counted among the lawless; and he himself bore the sins of many and was handed over because of their iniquities" (Isa. 53:1). "Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout and be glad, you who are not in labour, for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband" (Isa. 54:1). When else, if not at the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ, did the Father and God of the universe reveal before the nations his great arm, which is none other than his Word? Having seen the salvation granted to them by God, the nations are commanded to depart from their former error, and no longer to touch the unclean things in which they used to wallow, entangled in shameful and defiled practices. And since it is no small matter to separate oneself from the way of life handed down from one's fathers and from the common society of men, the Lord himself promises for this reason to go along with those who carry his vessels and to gather them; and by the vessels he plainly means the sacred doctrines and the divine words. Again, just as in the earlier prophecies Christ was in various ways called the servant of God, so he is here too. And it is prophesied that he will understand and be exalted and be greatly glorified, his humanity being meant, since it is of this that these things are said. And truly many were astonished and perplexed at him, supposing him to be a man like themselves. They were astonished indeed when they saw him clothed in no eminence or worldly glory, when he had laid aside the form of God, emptied himself and taken the form of a servant, and yet performed wonders worthy of astonishment and amazement, so that those who saw them said in their amazement, "Is this not the son of Joseph? Are not his mother and his brothers here with us?" (John 6:42; Matt. 13:55). And to this day a great many are astonished and perplexed at him, seeing that his teaching has spread, and is still spreading, over the whole world, and observing the unwavering and unshakeable disposition of those who have believed in him. Yet while they marvel at these things, they do not understand the divine power by which he worked, and is still able to work, such great things. And truly kings shut and closed their mouths at him, whether those who gathered together at the time of his passion (of whom it was said, "The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together" [Ps. 2:2]), or the rulers of the nations in successive ages. They shut their mouths because, although they often tried to hinder his word and his teaching, he nonetheless prevailed and shone out, glorified and lifted on high, so as to make himself known not only to those who had received the prophecies about him from their fathers but, most astonishing of all, to those to whom nothing had ever been announced about him, that is, to us of the nations. We had heard nothing at all from our ancestors and had learned nothing beforehand of his coming, yet we understood him when he came and accepted the prophecies about him. Foreseeing this in the Spirit, the prophet cries out in wonder, "Lord, who has believed our report?" This is not the same as "No one has believed our report"; for great multitudes from the nations, and even some of the circumcision, have plainly believed the report about Christ.
