"And to whom," he says, "has the arm of the Lord", that is, the pre-existent Word of God, "been revealed?" The passage itself teaches this at the beginning of the prophecy, where it says, "And the Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations." Next it says, "We announced him before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground; he has no form and no glory; and we saw him, and he had no form or beauty", and what follows. These things too were fulfilled when, having emptied himself of the form of God, he did not choose an appearance that men would think handsome and comely, nor did he pass through human life with glory among men or clothed in any worldly eminence. Rather, taking the form of a slave and a servant, he humbled himself and truly became a man, "under affliction and knowing how to bear sickness", while the glorious and divine face of his Godhead was turned away and hidden. That is why he was dishonoured by those who perceived only his humanity, and they esteemed him not merely not as the Son of God, but not even as an ordinary righteous man. And those who perceived these things by the Spirit say, as though narrating and teaching the reason for such a dispensation, "This one bears our sins and suffers pain for our sake"; for, being prophets, they saw how he would become the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). To this is added, "But we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow and in affliction; but he was wounded for our iniquities." For he was in effect wounded when they took up stones to throw at him. "And he was made sick," it says, "for our sins"; for Christ, sharing the weakness of the weak even more than Paul, could have said, "Who is weak, and I am not weak?" (2 Cor. 11:29). The prophet acknowledges that the one of whom he speaks will suffer all these things for his sake and for the sake of the whole people: "He was wounded," he says, "for our iniquities, and made sick for our sins"; and counting himself among them, he adds, "By his bruise we were healed." And seeing clearly the error into which the whole people of the circumcision fell concerning him, and that there is no man who does not sin, even if he seems the most righteous of all, he goes on, "All of us went astray like sheep; each man strayed in his own way; and the Lord handed him over for our sins," with what follows, all of which is shown beyond dispute to have been fulfilled in our Saviour Jesus alone. So it is right to marvel at the hardness of heart of those of the former people who refuse to accept him on the pretext of what they themselves did against him. They are in the habit of laughing at these things and mocking them, as though he suffered what was unworthy of God's care for him, even though the prophet, besides what has already been said, plainly cries out about him that "like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth," and that "his life is taken from the earth." And who would not be amazed to hear the prophet add to all that has been listed, "Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death"? What excuse could they devise against this, those who heard the voice of Christ with their very ears and did not understand, and looked upon his coming with their very eyes and did not see? For what other righteous man could they point to who was led to death because of their sins? Or who has there ever been who bore the sins of the whole people, and of the prophets themselves, and suffered pain for them, so that they confess that they were all healed by his bruise, saying, "This one bears our sins and suffers pain for our sake, and by his bruise we were healed"? And who that shares human nature could be such as to have sinned in neither word nor deed, so that the divine Scripture speaks truly of him: "He committed no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth"? And on what charge does the word foretell that one so attested would be led like a sheep to the slaughter and condemned to death because of the iniquities of the people? Let them say too whether the Christ they expect to come will certainly suffer all the things the prophecies declare about him, or whether nothing of the kind will happen to him. But if they stumble at faith in our Saviour because of what befell him, they would not say such things of the one they are expecting. By their reckoning, then, it is time to declare the divine utterances unfulfilled and, plainly, false. But not by ours: nothing about him was announced or handed down to us from our fathers, yet we have seen him and received him, in keeping with what is said elsewhere: "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." Throughout the whole prophecy the things concerning him are set out more fully and more clearly. And the destruction that overtook those who plotted against him is also made known through the words, "And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death; because he committed no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth." For it is saying that they killed him although he was such a one, and that for this reason they would suffer such things. Immediately after this, the Church from the nations again receives good news, being compared with the former people and preferred to it, in the words, "Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labour, for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband." The contents of this passage call for much searching and examination; whoever heeds the Saviour's command, "Search the Scriptures, for in them you think you have eternal life, and it is they that bear witness about me" (John 5:39), will come to know what is in them by searching more carefully.

"Listen to me, and you will eat good things, and your soul will delight in good things. Give ear, and follow my ways; hear me, and your soul will live among good things, and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the sure holy things of David. Behold, I have given him as a witness among the nations, a ruler and a commander among the nations. Behold, nations that do not know you will call upon you, and peoples who do not know you will flee to you for refuge, for the sake of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you" (Isa. 55:2). To those who understand what is said, the word [offers?] spiritual nourishment, divine and heavenly delight, and also life, not the indifferent life of the flesh but the everlasting life of the soul. It further promises to make with them an everlasting covenant, which, it says, will contain the sure holy things of David. What, then, would this new and everlasting covenant be, which is prophesied to be given to those addressed here, after the temporary covenant given through Moses? It is the new scripture of the sacred Gospels, which contains the holy things of David because of Jesus, the Christ of God, who was born of David's seed. And God says that he has given him as a witness not to Israel but to the nations, to rule over them and to command them, and not over the former people of the circumcision. These nations, which previously did not know him at all, called upon him as Saviour and God once they recognised that he was the Son of God. Indeed, we who had never known him fled to him for refuge, escaping our former error and our slavery to the opposing powers. These things, the prophecy says, will happen for the sake of the Lord his God, because he glorified him. And how the Father glorified him is clear from the voice that came to him from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again" (John 12:28). Consider whether the words here, "Nations that do not know you will call upon you, and peoples who have not known you will flee to you for refuge," are not akin to those of the preceding section, where it was said, "Those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." Similar to these are also the words in the seventeenth Psalm, spoken in the person of Christ: "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me" (Ps. 17:43). We, then, believing the prophecies to be true, are convinced that they were fulfilled at the coming of our Saviour. For we are aware how we ourselves, who were once wandering nations, driven by cruel demons into every kind of idolatry, neither knowing the only true God nor heeding the prophetic voice, have come through the teaching of our Saviour Jesus to the knowledge of the God of the universe. We have believed the divinely inspired Scriptures and have received the Word of God whom they prophesied, though before we did not know him at all. Since we have received such great benefits through our Saviour's teaching, how could we not rightly receive him and honour him as divine, seeing that he is the Son of God and our own Saviour?

"See how the righteous one is taken away, and no one takes it to heart; righteous men are taken away, and no one considers it. For the righteous one has been taken away from the presence of injustice; his burial will be in peace; he has been taken from the midst. But you, come here, you lawless sons, offspring of adulterers and of a harlot! In whom have you taken your delight? Against whom have you opened your mouth? Against whom have you let loose your tongue? Are you not children of destruction, a lawless offspring?" (Isa. 57:1). The Christ of God alone has truly been shown to be such, beyond all who have ever been called righteous. That is why he alone could properly be called righteous, so that the prophecy says of him, "See how the righteous one is taken away." From what he is taken away, it adds in the words, "For the righteous one has been taken away from the presence of injustice." And who it is that takes him away we can hear from him himself, when he says, "No one takes my life from me; I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again" (John 10:18). Then it says, "His burial is in peace." Here it should be noted that the prophetic Scripture points not only to his death but also to his burial. This is why the holy apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says, "For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried" (1 Cor. 15:3). Which Scriptures, if not those that say, "Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death," and "His burial is in peace"? And it is not only the righteous one already mentioned who has been taken away from the midst of injustice; "righteous men too," it says, "are taken away." These would be Christ's holy apostles and his wonderful martyrs, who are themselves also called righteous by sharing in his righteousness. Yet while these things were being accomplished, no one, it says, saw and no one considered: plainly it means those whose hearts had grown dull and who had shut their eyes so as not to see. To them the next part of the prophecy is addressed, beginning, "But you, come here, you lawless sons, offspring of adulterers and of a harlot."

"And those from the west will fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his glorious name; for wrath will come from the Lord like a raging river; it will come with fury. And the deliverer will come for the sake of Zion, and will turn ungodliness away from Jacob, says the Lord. And this is my covenant with them: my Spirit which is upon you, and the words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, or from the mouth of your offspring, says the Lord, from now on and forever" (Isa. 59:19). Here again the word prophesies the calling of the Church from the nations, which was established through our Saviour. For who else would those from the west be? And through whom did nations of every kind fear the name of the Lord, if not through the teaching of Jesus, by which they abandoned their former error in the darkness of ignorance and fled for refuge to the God of the universe? And who is the one prophesied to come from Zion to deliver Jacob and turn him away from his former ungodliness, if not the one who came to save the lost sheep of the house of Israel that had fallen into ungodliness? To them, it says, he will grant by covenant the Spirit of God that is in Christ and the words of eternal life, which the Father has put into the mouth of the Son; and these, it says, will not depart either from him or from the mouth of his offspring, from now on and for all time to come. These would be the words of the gospel of the new covenant. Although so many have plotted against them long ago and are still plotting against them now, they have not failed and will not fail from the mouth of the Church established from the rational and spiritual offspring of Christ. For the Lord has spoken and declared that he will not blot them out, from now on and forever. That is why, as John says, the gospel of Christ is seen to be an eternal gospel (Rev. 14:6).

"The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; the Lord has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense of our God; to comfort all who mourn, so that those who mourn Zion may be given glory instead of ashes, the oil of gladness to those who mourn, a garment of glory instead of a spirit of weariness; and they shall be called generations of righteousness, a planting of the Lord for glory" (Isa. 61:1). Jesus, the Christ of God, who came forth from the root of Jesse, on whom the seven spirits of God came to rest, loved righteousness and hated lawlessness, and so was anointed by God his Father with what is called the spiritual oil of gladness. At the time when he had become man, he once took Isaiah into his hands and read the present passage. Then, closing the book (Luke 4:20), he said, "Today this scripture has been fulfilled." For he truly was the one sent from the Father to bring the good news of the kingdom of heaven to the poor in spirit, to whom he also said, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 5:3). He was also sent to heal the broken-hearted, of whom it is said, "A broken and humbled heart God will not despise" (Ps. 50:17). Besides this, he came to proclaim forgiveness of sins to those who had long ago been taken captive by the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar. That is why he said so confidently to the paralytic, "Child, your sins are forgiven" (Matt. 9:2). Some had their mind's eyes damaged and had been blinded by the spiritual foreigners and Babylonians, as Samson and Zedekiah were, and he came to give these people recovery of sight as well. Among those he healed were also, in part, the bodily blind, whom he made to see when they believed in him and cried out, "Have mercy on us, Son of David" (Matt. 20:31). He is the one who proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, which he announced after John had been shut up in prison. He also taught about the kingdom of God and about our judgment, in which each person will receive the penalty their deeds deserve. In addition, he came to comfort those who mourn with the praiseworthy mourning that is according to God. To them he also promised blessedness, saying, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matt. 5:4). Further, he came so that glory might be given to those who mourn Zion. And who could these be but those who seek their own homeland and continually rekindle the memory of the heavenly city? Such was the man who knew himself to be a sojourner and a stranger on earth and lamented, "Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged" (Ps. 119:5). Such too were those who wept by the rivers of Babylon when they remembered Zion. To these people, then, the Christ of God will fulfill the comfort he promised to those who mourn. He will give them glory once they are freed from mourning. In place of the ashes they covered themselves with while mourning in this present life, he will provide the oil of gladness. He will anoint them too with the oil of exultation, so that they may share in his anointing and his kingdom, and so that they too may say, "For we have become sharers of [?]" (Heb. 3:14). Christ is further prophesied to give those who mourn Zion "a garment of glory in place of the spirit of weariness." This is because they have grown weary of the affairs of this life, as if displeased with what human beings do. They mourn especially for this reason. They do so not only because they see God's promises from afar, but also because, in their sympathy and love for humanity, they suffer and grieve along with their own weak members. They all but cry out, in the spirit of the apostle, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" (2 Cor. 11:29).

"Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness; he has placed a turban on me as on a bridegroom, and adorned me with ornaments like a bride. And as the earth makes its flowers grow, and as a garden makes its seeds spring up, so the Lord, the Lord, will make righteousness and exultation spring up before all the nations" (Isa. 61:10). The soul of our Lord Jesus Christ is the soul of which he said, "My soul is very sorrowful" (Matt. 26:38), and, "Now my soul is troubled" (John 12:27). It rejoices and is glad in nothing created, but only in the Father and Lord. For he clothed him with the garment of divinity and with the tunic of true and perfect gladness. Moreover, Christ was the bridegroom of the church, the bride that has no spot or wrinkle, and so the Father placed a turban on him as on a bridegroom. His soul, for its part, was the bride of the Godhead, which is above all reproach, and so he adorned it like a bride with the fitting ornament of the Spirit of the Lord. He also cultivated it like fertile and good land, and again like a garden that grows and flourishes with the shoots in it, the shoots with which the great paradise of God is said to be planted. These things will come to pass, he says, because the Lord is righteous, and is God not only of the Jews but also of the nations, and he has made his own righteousness spring up, that is, his Christ, before all the nations that believe through him.

"Raise a signal to the nations. For behold, the Lord has made it heard to the end of the earth: Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your Savior has come, having his reward with him and his work before his face; and he shall call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord; and you shall be called a city sought after, and not forsaken" (Isa. 62:10). "Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimson garments from Bozrah, so beautiful in his robe, with force and strength? 'I speak righteousness and the judgment of salvation.' Why are your garments red, and your clothing as if from a trodden winepress? 'It is full of what has been trodden down, and of the nations there is no man with me, and I trampled them in my wrath'" (Isa. 63:1). Here again the prophecy orders that a signal be taken up concerning the church drawn from the nations. It promises that the Lord will make something heard to the end of the earth. This was fulfilled at the coming of our Savior Jesus, when the voice of his apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world. Next it says, "Say to the daughters of Zion." This means the churches drawn from the nations, for these would be the daughters of the heavenly Zion, which is our mother, according to the apostle. "Behold, your Savior comes, having his reward" (Gal. 4:26), and what follows. These words point to Christ's second coming. Then he will come as judge, to give each person the rewards for their present labors, and the requital for whatever wicked deeds each has done now. After this the word speaks as if asking a question: "Who is this who comes from Edom" (which is interpreted "earthly"), "with crimson garments from Bozrah, so beautiful in his robe?" He seems to have said this in wonder at the Savior's beauty. Even after the incarnation, the self-emptying and the time spent on earth, and even after the passion and the descent to the dead, that beauty remained lovely and radiant. It was marred in no way, and it took on no filth, no stain or spot, from the material and bodily condition of earthly and human affairs. He was also struck with amazement at his strength, because he had defeated the whole army of the devil. So he adds, "so beautiful in his robe, with force and strength?" The Savior replies to this question and teaches who he is: "I speak righteousness and the judgment of salvation." Then the word speaks to him again, with the passion in view: "Why are your garments red?" and so on. For as the Lamb of God, who took the sins of the world upon himself, he put on garments made red by our sins. That is why the prophet Zechariah also says, "And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments" (Zech. 3:4). These were garments made of our sins. On their account it was said a little earlier, "He bears our sins and suffers pain for us." For he himself committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22). The Savior answers the question again and teaches why his garments became red, saying, "from the nations." He alone subdued these nations, with no human being working alongside him, and he trampled down the whole opposing power of the evil spirits that were at war with him.

"And the Lord remembered the days of old: he who brought up from the earth the great shepherd of the sheep, who put the Holy Spirit within them" (Isa. 63:11). And who else could the shepherd of God's sheep be, the one whom the Lord brought up from the earth, but our Savior, who came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel? For he is the good shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep. The Father brought him up from the earth and highly exalted him, granting him the name that is above every name.

"The city of your holy one has become a wilderness; Zion has become like a wilderness, Jerusalem a curse. The house, our sanctuary, and the glory that our fathers blessed, has been burned with fire, and all our glorious things have fallen in ruin. And in all this you held back, Lord, and kept silent, and humbled us exceedingly" (Isa. 64:10). "I became manifest to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am,' to a nation that did not call on my name. But over you I spread out my hands all day long, toward a disobedient and contrary people, who did not walk in the true way but followed their sins" (Isa. 65:1). Here too the rejection of Israel is prophesied first, and then the election of the nations through Christ is indicated. The prophet has offered a prayer in the person of the people, and the word answers him. It exposes the hardness and disobedience of the former people and shows its own love for humanity. "How can you say these things," it says, "as though I were reluctant to save you? Why, I openly presented myself even to those who did not ask for me or seek me." And indeed it is plain how the Word of God, previously unknown to the nations, became manifest to them at the consummation of the ages, through the goodness and love for humanity of the Father and God of all. Because of their error concerning idols, they had never asked him for what they needed. Yet he was found by us, who did not seek him. He also answered those who did not call upon his name by becoming man, all but crying out, "Here I am." These things, then, the word clearly prophesies about the calling of the nations. Next it adds something meant to put the Jewish people to shame: "But over you I spread out my hands toward a disobedient and contrary people." These words can also point to the posture of his suffering on the cross.

So much, then, for the passages from Isaiah. Having now set out the subject of the Selections in four books, in this ninth treatise of the General Elementary Introduction, we shall try in the tenth to offer another approach suited to those whose reasoning has been harmed by the godless heresies.
